title: The Lion And The Mouse
body:
A LION was awakened from sleep by a Mouse running over his face. Rising up angrily, he caught him and was about to kill him, when the Mouse piteously entreated, saying: “If you would only spare my life, I would be sure to repay your kindness.” The Lion laughed and let him go. It happened shortly after this that the Lion was caught by some hunters, who bound him by strong ropes to the ground. The Mouse, recognizing his roar, came and gnawed the rope with his teeth, and set him free, exclaiming:

“You ridiculed the idea of my ever being able to help you, not expecting to receive from me any repayment of your favour; now you know that it is possible for even a Mouse to confer benefits on a Lion.”
moral: A kindness is never wasted.
body_child: A big lion was sleeping. A little mouse ran over his face. The lion woke up and caught the mouse. 'Please let me go,' said the mouse. 'One day I will help you.' The lion laughed, but he let the mouse go. Later, hunters caught the lion in a rope net. The lion roared. The mouse heard him and ran to help. He chewed the ropes until they broke. The lion was free! Even a little friend can be a big help.
moral_elaborated: Even a small friend can help a big friend. Always be kind to others. You never know when you might need help too.

title: The Wolf And The Lamb
body: WOLF, meeting with a Lamb astray from the fold, resolved not to lay violent hands on him, but to find some plea to justify to the Lamb the Wolf’s right to eat him. He thus addressed him: “Sirrah, last year you grossly insulted me.” “Indeed,” bleated the Lamb in a mournful tone of voice, “I was not then born.” Then said the Wolf, “You feed in my pasture.” “No, good sir,” replied the Lamb, “I have not yet tasted grass.” Again said the Wolf, “You drink of my well.” “No,” exclaimed the Lamb, “I never yet drank water, for as yet my mother’s milk is both food and drink to me.” Upon which the Wolf seized him and ate him up, saying, “Well! I won’t remain supperless, even though you refute every one of my imputations.”
moral: The tyrant will always find a pretext for his tyranny.
body_child: A hungry wolf saw a little lamb. The wolf wanted to eat the lamb, but he wanted a reason to be mean. He said, 'You were mean to me last year!' The lamb said, 'I was not even born then!' Then the wolf said, 'You are eating my grass.' The lamb said, 'I only drink my mother's milk.' The wolf did not care. He ate the lamb anyway. Mean people will always find a reason to do bad things.
moral_elaborated: Mean people often make up excuses to be mean. It is hard to argue with someone who just wants to be a bully. Stay away from people who are not fair.

title: The Ass And The Grasshopper
body: AN ASS having heard some Grasshoppers chirping, was highly enchanted; and, desiring to possess the same charms of melody, demanded what sort of food they lived on to give them such beautiful voices. They replied, “The dew.” The Ass resolved that he would live only upon dew, and in a short time died of hunger.
moral: What is food for one may be poison for another.
body_child: A donkey heard some grasshoppers singing. He loved their music. He asked them, 'What do you eat to sing so well?' The grasshoppers said, 'We only drink the dew.' The donkey wanted to sing like them. He stopped eating his hay and only drank dew. Soon, the donkey became very hungry and sick. We should not try to be something we are not.
moral_elaborated: Everyone is different and needs different things. Do not try to change who you are just to be like someone else. Be happy being yourself.

title: The Wolf and the Crane
body: A WOLF who had a bone stuck in his throat hired a Crane, for a large sum, to put her head into his mouth and draw out the bone. When the Crane had extracted the bone and demanded the promised payment, the Wolf, grinning and grinding his teeth, exclaimed: “Why, you have surely already had a sufficient recompense, in having been permitted to draw out your head in safety from the mouth and jaws of a wolf.”
moral: In serving the wicked, expect no reward, and be thankful if you escape injury for your pains.
body_child: A wolf had a bone stuck in his throat. It hurt very much. He asked a bird called a crane to help him. 'I will pay you if you pull the bone out,' said the wolf. The crane put her long neck into the wolf's mouth and pulled out the bone. When she asked for her pay, the wolf laughed. 'You are lucky I did not bite your head off!' he said. The crane learned that mean people do not keep their promises.
moral_elaborated: Do not expect a reward from someone who is mean. Be happy if you can just get away safely. Some people are not thankful when you help them.

title: The Father And His Sons
body: A FATHER had a family of sons who were perpetually quarreling among themselves. When he failed to heal their disputes by his exhortations, he determined to give them a practical illustration of the evils of disunion; and for this purpose he one day told them to bring him a bundle of sticks. When they had done so, he placed the faggot into the hands of each of them in succession, and ordered them to break it in pieces. They tried with all their strength, and were not able to do it. He next opened the faggot, took the sticks separately, one by one, and again put them into his sons’ hands, upon which they broke them easily. He then addressed them in these words: “My sons, if you are of one mind, and unite to assist each other, you will be as this faggot, uninjured by all the attempts of your enemies; but if you are divided among yourselves, you will be broken as easily as these sticks.”
moral: Union gives strength.
body_child: A father had many sons. They were always fighting. The father wanted to teach them a lesson. He gave them a bundle of sticks and said, 'Break this.' No one could break the bundle. Then the father gave them one stick at a time. The sons broke the sticks easily. 'See,' said the father. 'When you are together, you are strong. When you fight and stay apart, you are weak like a single stick.'
moral_elaborated: We are much stronger when we work together. If we fight, we become easy to hurt. Always try to help your friends and family.

title: The Bat And The Weasels
body: A BAT who fell upon the ground and was caught by a Weasel pleaded to be spared his life. The Weasel refused, saying that he was by nature the enemy of all birds. The Bat assured him that he was not a bird, but a mouse, and thus was set free. Shortly afterwards the Bat again fell to the ground and was caught by another Weasel, whom he likewise entreated not to eat him. The Weasel said that he had a special hostility to mice. The Bat assured him that he was not a mouse, but a bat, and thus a second time escaped.
moral: It is wise to turn circumstances to good account.
body_child: A bat fell and a weasel caught him. 'I eat all birds!' said the weasel. The bat said, 'I am not a bird, I am a mouse!' The weasel let him go. Later, another weasel caught the bat. 'I eat all mice!' said this weasel. The bat said, 'I am not a mouse, I am a bat!' This weasel let him go too. The bat was very smart and saved his own life twice.
moral_elaborated: Use your brain to get out of trouble. It is good to be quick and smart when things go wrong. Being clever can save the day.

title: The Cock and the Jewel
body: A COCK, scratching for food for himself and his hens, found a precious stone and exclaimed: “If your owner had found thee, and not I, he would have taken thee up, and have set thee in thy first estate; but I have found thee for no purpose. I would rather have one barleycorn than all the jewels in the world.”
moral: A piece of corn is better to a cock than a diamond.
body_child: A rooster was looking for food in the dirt. He found a bright, shiny jewel. 'This is very pretty,' said the rooster. 'A person would love this jewel. But I am a hungry rooster. I would rather find one small piece of corn than a whole bag of jewels.' The rooster knew what was truly important to him.
moral_elaborated: Something valuable to one person might not be useful to you. We should value what we really need. A simple thing can be better than a fancy thing.

title: The Swallow and the Crow
body: THE SWALLOW and the Crow had a contention about their plumage. The Crow put an end to the dispute by saying, “Your feathers are all very well in the spring, but mine protect me against the winter.”
moral: Fair weather friends are not worth much.
body_child: A swallow and a crow were talking about their feathers. The swallow had pretty, colorful feathers. 'Look how beautiful I am!' said the swallow. The crow had plain black feathers. 'Your feathers are nice for the spring,' said the crow. 'But my thick feathers keep me warm in the cold winter.' The crow knew that being strong is better than just looking pretty.
moral_elaborated: It is better to be prepared for hard times than to just look good. Pretty things do not always help when life gets tough. Choose things that are useful and strong.

title: The Kingdom of the Lion
body: THE BEASTS of the field and forest had a Lion as their king. He was neither wrathful, cruel, nor tyrannical, but just and gentle as a king could be. During his reign he made a royal proclamation for a general assembly of all the birds and beasts, and drew up conditions for a universal league, in which the Wolf and the Lamb, the Panther and the Kid, the Tiger and the Stag, the Dog and the Hare, should live together in perfect peace and amity. The Hare said, “Oh, how I have longed to see this day, in which the weak shall take their place with impunity by the side of the strong.” And after the Hare said this, he ran for his life.
moral: The weak cannot trust the promises of the strong.
body_child: A kind lion was the king of the forest. He wanted all animals to be friends. He said, 'The wolf will not eat the lamb. The dog will not chase the rabbit.' Everyone agreed to be peaceful. A little rabbit said, 'I am so happy that the strong will now be nice to the weak.' But then the rabbit got scared and ran away. He knew that some animals might forget the rules.
moral_elaborated: Even if there are rules for peace, you must still be careful. Not everyone will keep their promises. It is okay to be cautious to stay safe.

title: The Traveler and His Dog
body: A TRAVELER about to set out on a journey saw his Dog stand at the door stretching himself. He asked him sharply: “Why do you stand there gaping? Everything is ready but you, so come with me instantly.” The Dog, wagging his tail, replied: “O, master! I am quite ready; it is you for whom I am waiting.”
moral: The loiterer often blames delay on his more active friend.
body_child: A man was getting ready for a trip. He saw his dog waiting by the door. The man was running late and felt grumpy. 'Why are you just standing there?' the man yelled. 'We are waiting for you!' The dog wagged his tail and said, 'I have been ready for a long time. I am just waiting for you to walk out the door!'
moral_elaborated: Sometimes people blame others for their own delays. Make sure you are ready before you get mad at your friends. It is important to be honest about who is slow.

title: The Ants and the Grasshopper
body: THE ANTS were spending a fine winter’s day drying grain collected in the summertime. A Grasshopper, perishing with famine, passed by and earnestly begged for a little food. The Ants inquired of him, “Why did you not treasure up food during the summer?” He replied, “I had not leisure enough. I passed the days in singing.” They then said in derision: “If you were foolish enough to sing all the summer, you must dance supperless to bed in the winter.”
moral: It is best to prepare for the days of necessity.
body_child: The ants worked hard all summer to save food for the winter. One cold day, a hungry grasshopper came by. 'Please give me some food,' he said. The ants asked, 'What did you do all summer?' The grasshopper said, 'I sang songs all day.' The ants said, 'If you sang all summer, you can dance all winter!' They did not give him any food. It is important to work and prepare for the future.
moral_elaborated: Work hard now so you have what you need later. It is good to have fun, but you must do your chores first. Being prepared makes life easier.

title: The Hare and the Tortoise
body: A HARE one day ridiculed the short feet and slow pace of the Tortoise, who replied, laughing: “Though you be swift as the wind, I will beat you in a race.” The Hare, believing her assertion to be simply impossible, assented to the proposal; and they agreed that the Fox should choose the course and fix the goal. On the day appointed for the race the two started together. The Tortoise never for a moment stopped, but went on with a slow but steady pace straight to the end of the course. The Hare, lying down by the wayside, fell fast asleep. At last waking up, and moving as fast as he could, he saw the Tortoise had reached the goal, and was comfortably dozing after her fatigue.
moral: Slow but steady wins the race.
body_child: A fast rabbit made fun of a slow turtle. 'I can beat you in a race!' said the turtle. The rabbit laughed and said, 'Let's go!' The rabbit ran very fast. He got tired and took a nap. The turtle never stopped. He walked slowly, step by step. When the rabbit woke up, the turtle was already at the finish line! The turtle won because he did not give up.
moral_elaborated: You do not have to be the fastest to win. If you keep going and do not quit, you will reach your goal. It is better to be steady than to be lazy.

title: The Charcoal-Burner And The Fuller
body: A CHARCOAL-BURNER carried on his trade in his own house. One day he met a friend, a Fuller, and entreated him to come and live with him, saying that they should be far better neighbors and that their housekeeping expenses would be lessened. The Fuller replied, “The arrangement is impossible as far as I am concerned, for whatever I should whiten, you would immediately blacken again with your charcoal.”
moral: Like will draw like.
body_child: A man who made black coal lived in a small house. He asked his friend, who cleaned white clothes, to move in. 'We can save money!' said the coal-maker. The friend said, 'I cannot live with you. I work hard to make things white. Your black coal dust would make everything dirty again!' They knew their jobs did not go well together.
moral_elaborated: It is hard to work with someone who does the opposite of what you do. Choose your partners carefully so you can help each other. Some things just do not mix well.

title: The Boy Hunting Locusts
body: A BOY was hunting for locusts. He had caught a goodly number, when he saw a Scorpion, and mistaking him for a locust, reached out his hand to take him. The Scorpion, showing his sting, said: “If you had but touched me, my friend, you would have lost me, and all your locusts too!”
moral: Look before you leap.
body_child: A boy was catching bugs in the field. He found many grasshoppers. Then he saw a scorpion. He thought it was just another bug and tried to grab it. The scorpion showed his sharp sting. 'Stop!' said the scorpion. 'If you touch me, I will sting you. Then you will lose all your bugs and get hurt too!' The boy learned to look closely before touching.
moral_elaborated: Always look carefully before you grab something. Some things might look safe but can be dangerous. It is better to be safe than sorry.

title: The Fisherman Piping
body: A FISHERMAN skilled in music took his flute and his nets to the seashore. Standing on a projecting rock, he played several tunes in the hope that the fish, attracted by his melody, would of their own accord dance into his net, which he had placed below. At last, having long waited in vain, he laid aside his flute, and casting his net into the sea, made an excellent haul of fish. When he saw them leaping about in the net upon the rock he said: “O you most perverse creatures, when I piped you would not dance, but now that I have ceased you do so merrily.”
moral: There is a time and place for everything.
body_child: A fisherman loved to play his flute. He thought the fish would like his music and jump into his net. He played many songs, but no fish came. Then he put away his flute and threw his net into the water. He caught many fish! When the fish wiggled in the net, he said, 'You did not dance for my music, but you are dancing now!' He learned that music does not catch fish.
moral_elaborated: To get a job done, you must use the right tools. Singing and playing are fun, but they will not do your work for you. Do what works best for the task.

title: The Dog and the Shadow
body: A DOG, crossing a bridge over a stream with a piece of flesh in his mouth, saw his own shadow in the water and took it for that of another Dog, with a piece of meat double his own in size. He immediately let go of his own, and fiercely attacked the other Dog to get his larger piece from him. He thus lost both: that which he grasped at in the water, because it was a shadow; and his own, because the stream swept it away.
moral: It is not wise to be greedy.
body_child: A dog was carrying a big piece of meat. He walked over a bridge and looked down. He saw his own shadow in the water. He thought it was another dog with a even bigger piece of meat! He dropped his meat to grab the other piece. But there was no other dog. His meat fell into the river and was gone. The dog had nothing because he was greedy.
moral_elaborated: Be happy with what you have. If you try to take too much, you might lose everything. Greed can make you lose what is already yours.

title: Hercules and the Wagoner
body: A CARTER was driving a wagon along a country lane, when the wheels sank down deep into a rut. The rustic driver, stupefied and aghast, stood looking at the wagon, and did nothing but utter loud cries to Hercules to come and help him. Hercules, it is said, appeared and thus addressed him: “Put your shoulders to the wheels, my man. Goad on your bullocks, and never more pray to me for help, until you have done your best to help yourself, or depend upon it you will henceforth pray in vain.”
moral: Self-help is the best help.
body_child: A man was driving a wagon. The wheels got stuck in the deep mud. The man just stood there and cried for help. He called for a strong god named Hercules to save him. Hercules appeared and said, 'Get to work! Push the wheels yourself. I will not help you until you try to help yourself.' The man learned that he had to try hard before asking for help.
moral_elaborated: You must try your best before you ask others for help. Hard work is the first step to solving a problem. People are more likely to help those who try.

title: The Mole and His Mother
body: A MOLE, a creature blind from birth, once said to his Mother: “I am sure than I can see, Mother!” In the desire to prove to him his mistake, his Mother placed before him a few grains of frankincense, and asked, “What is it?” The young Mole said, “It is a pebble.” His Mother exclaimed: “My son, I am afraid that you are not only blind, but that you have lost your sense of smell.”
moral: Do not boast of things you cannot do.
body_child: A little mole cannot see very well. One day he said, 'Mother, I can see now!' His mother wanted to see if he was telling the truth. She put something that smelled very sweet in front of him. 'What is this?' she asked. The mole said, 'It is a rock.' His mother sighed. 'You cannot see, and now you cannot smell either!' The little mole was just pretending.
moral_elaborated: It is better to be honest about what you can and cannot do. Do not brag about things that are not true. People will know if you are pretending.

title: The Herdsman and the Lost Bull
body: A HERDSMAN tending his flock in a forest lost a Bull-calf from the fold. After a long and fruitless search, he made a vow that, if he could only discover the thief who had stolen the Calf, he would offer a lamb in sacrifice to Hermes, Pan, and the Guardian Deities of the forest. Not long afterwards, as he ascended a small hillock, he saw at its foot a Lion feeding on the Calf. Terrified at the sight, he lifted his eyes and his hands to heaven, and said: “Just now I vowed to offer a lamb to the Guardian Deities of the forest if I could only find out who had robbed me; but now that I have discovered the thief, I would willingly add a full-grown Bull to the Calf I have lost, if I may only secure my own escape from him in safety.”
moral: Be careful what you wish for.
body_child: A man lost his young bull in the woods. He was very upset. He said, 'I will give a gift to the gods if I can just find the thief!' Then he saw a big lion eating his bull. The man was very scared. 'I found the thief, but now I want to run away!' he cried. He realized that finding the thief was much scarier than he thought it would be.
moral_elaborated: Be careful what you ask for, because you might just get it. Sometimes the truth is scarier than not knowing. Think about what might happen if your wish comes true.

title: The Fawn and His Mother
body: A YOUNG FAWN once said to his Mother, “You are larger than a dog, and swifter, and more used to running, and you have your horns as a defense; why, then, O Mother! do the hounds frighten you so?” She smiled, and said: “I know full well, my son, that all you say is true. I have the advantages you mention, but when I hear even the bark of a single dog I feel ready to faint, and fly away as fast as I can.”
moral: No arguments will give courage to the coward.
body_child: A young deer asked his mother a question. 'Mother, you are big and fast. You have sharp horns. Why are you afraid of dogs?' His mother smiled. 'You are right, my son,' she said. 'I am big and strong. But when I hear a dog bark, I get very scared. I just want to run away as fast as I can!' Even if you look strong, you can still feel scared inside.
moral_elaborated: Being strong on the outside does not always mean you are brave. Fear is something everyone feels sometimes. It is hard to be brave even when you have everything you need.

title: The Ass, the Fox, and the Lion
body: THE ASS and the Fox, having entered into partnership together for their mutual protection, went out into the forest to hunt. They had not proceeded far when they met a Lion. The Fox, seeing imminent danger, approached the Lion and promised to contrive for him the capture of the Ass if the Lion would pledge his word not to harm the Fox. Then, upon assuring the Ass that he would not be injured, the Fox led him to a deep pit and arranged that he should fall into it. The Lion, seeing that the Ass was secured, immediately clutched the Fox, and attacked the Ass at his leisure.
body_child: A Donkey and a Fox went into the woods together. They saw a big Lion and were scared. The Fox told the Lion, "I will help you catch the Donkey if you do not hurt me." The Fox led the Donkey into a deep hole. But once the Donkey was stuck, the Lion caught the Fox first. Then he ate the Donkey too.
moral: Traitors often destroy themselves.
moral_elaborated: If you try to trick a friend to save yourself, you might get hurt too. It is important to be a loyal friend. Being mean to others often brings trouble to you in the end.

title: The Flies and the Honey-Pot
body: A NUMBER of Flies were attracted to a jar of honey which had been overturned in a housekeeper’s room, and placing their feet in it, ate greedily. Their feet, however, became so smeared with the honey that they could not use their wings, nor release themselves, and were suffocated. Just as they were expiring, they exclaimed, “O foolish creatures that we are, for the sake of a little pleasure we have destroyed ourselves.”
body_child: Some flies found a jar of sweet honey on the floor. They were very hungry and began to eat it. Soon, their feet got stuck in the sticky honey. They could not fly away or get out. They were very sad and said, "We were silly! We wanted a sweet snack, but now we are trapped."
moral: Pleasure bought with pains, hurts.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes things that look fun can actually be dangerous. You should think before you jump into something just because you want it right now. Too much of a good thing can cause big trouble.

title: The Lioness
body: A CONTROVERSY prevailed among the beasts of the field as to which of the animals deserved the most credit for producing the greatest number of whelps at a birth. They rushed clamorously into the presence of the Lioness and demanded of her the settlement of the dispute. “And you,” they said, “how many sons have you at a birth?” The Lioness laughed at them, and said: “Why! I have only one; but that one is altogether a thoroughbred Lion.”
body_child: All the animals were arguing. They wanted to know who had the most babies at one time. They went to the Lioness and asked, "How many babies do you have?" The Lioness laughed and said, "I only have one. But my one baby is a strong, brave Lion!"
moral: The value is in the worth, not in the number.
moral_elaborated: It is better to have one very good thing than many things that are not as good. Quality is more important than how many things you have. One great friend is better than many friends who do not care.

title: The Farmer and the Snake
body: ONE WINTER a Farmer found a Snake stiff and frozen with cold. He had compassion on it, and taking it up, placed it in his bosom. The Snake was quickly revived by the warmth, and resuming its natural instincts, bit its benefactor, inflicting on him a mortal wound. “Oh,” cried the Farmer with his last breath, “I am rightly served for pitying a scoundrel.”
body_child: One cold winter day, a farmer found a snake in the snow. The snake was frozen and still. The kind farmer put the snake inside his coat to warm it up. When the snake got warm, it bit the farmer. The farmer was sad that he helped something that was mean to him.
moral: The greatest kindness will not bind the ungrateful.
moral_elaborated: Some people might still be mean even if you are very nice to them. You should be kind, but you also need to be careful. Not everyone will thank you for your help.

title: The Man and the Lion
body:
A MAN and a Lion traveled together through the forest. They soon began to boast of their respective superiority to each other in strength and prowess. As they were disputing, they passed a statue carved in stone, which represented “a Lion strangled by a Man.” The traveler pointed to it and said: “See there! How strong we are, and how we prevail over even the king of beasts.” The Lion replied: “This statue was made by one of you men. If we Lions knew how to erect statues, you would see the Man placed under the paw of the Lion.”

One story is good, till another is told.
body_child: A Man and a Lion were walking in the forest. They both said they were the strongest. They saw a stone statue of a man winning a fight against a lion. The man said, "See? Humans are stronger!" The Lion said, "A man made that statue. If a lion made it, the lion would be the winner!"
moral: There are two sides to every story.
moral_elaborated: People see things in their own way. Just because someone tells a story doesn't mean it's the only truth. You should listen to both sides before you decide what to believe.

title: The Pomegranate, Apple-Tree, and Bramble
body: THE POMEGRANATE and Apple-Tree disputed as to which was the most beautiful. When their strife was at its height, a Bramble from the neighboring hedge lifted up its voice, and said in a boastful tone: “Pray, my dear friends, in my presence at least cease from such vain disputings.”
body_child: An Apple tree and a Pomegranate tree were arguing. Each one said, "I am the most beautiful tree!" They argued for a long time. Then, a prickly Bramble bush spoke up from a nearby hedge. "Please, my dear friends," the Bramble said. "Stop your silly fighting while I am here!"
moral: The least valuable are often the most boastful.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes people who are not very important try to act like they are the most important. The little bush wanted to sound as big as the trees. It is better to be humble than to act like you are better than everyone else.

title: The Farmer and the Stork
body: A FARMER placed nets on his newly-sown plowlands and caught a number of Cranes, which came to pick up his seed. With them he trapped a Stork that had fractured his leg in the net and was earnestly beseeching the Farmer to spare his life. “Pray save me, Master,” he said, “and let me go free this once. My broken limb should excite your pity. Besides, I am no Crane, I am a Stork, a bird of excellent character; and see how I love and slave for my father and mother. Look too, at my feathers—they are not the least like those of a Crane.” The Farmer laughed aloud and said, “It may be all as you say, I only know this: I have taken you with these robbers, the Cranes, and you must die in their company.”
body_child: A farmer put nets in his field to catch birds that stole his seeds. He caught many big birds called Cranes. He also caught a Stork. The Stork had a broken leg and begged the farmer to let him go. "I am a good bird!" the Stork said. "I take care of my parents and my feathers are different from the Cranes." The farmer laughed. He said, "I caught you with the birds who steal. You must stay with them."
moral: Birds of a feather flock together.
moral_elaborated: You are known by the friends you choose. If you hang out with people who do bad things, others will think you are bad too. It is important to choose good friends.

title: The Mountain in Labor
body: A MOUNTAIN was once greatly agitated. Loud groans and noises were heard, and crowds of people came from all parts to see what was the matter. While they were assembled in anxious expectation of some terrible calamity, out came a Mouse.
body_child: A giant mountain started making loud noises. It groaned and shook. Many people came to see what was happening. They were scared that something big and scary would come out of the mountain. Everyone watched and waited. Suddenly, a tiny little mouse popped out of a hole.
moral: Don’t make much ado about nothing.
moral_elaborated: Do not make a big deal out of something small. Sometimes we get very worried about things that are not scary at all. It is better to wait and see before getting upset.

title: The Bear and the Fox
body: A BEAR boasted very much of his philanthropy, saying that of all animals he was the most tender in his regard for man, for he had such respect for him that he would not even touch his dead body. A Fox hearing these words said with a smile to the Bear, “Oh! that you would eat the dead and not the living.”
body_child: A Bear bragged that he was very kind to humans. He said, "I respect people so much that I never touch a person when they are dead." A Fox heard this and smiled. The Fox said, "I wish you would eat the dead people instead of hunting the living ones!"
moral: It is better to be kind to the living than the dead.
moral_elaborated: It is more important to be nice to people while they are still here. Saying you are kind does not matter if you are actually mean to others. True kindness is shown by how we treat people every day.

title: The Tortoise and the Eagle
body: A TORTOISE, lazily basking in the sun, complained to the sea-birds of her hard fate, that no one would teach her to fly. An Eagle, hovering near, heard her mistake and demanded what reward she would give him if he would take her aloft and float her in the air. “I will give you,” she said, “all the riches of the Red Sea.” “I will teach you to fly then,” said the Eagle; and taking her up in his talons he carried her almost to the clouds suddenly he let her go, and she fell on a lofty mountain, dashing her shell to pieces. The Tortoise exclaimed in the moment of death: “I have deserved my present fate; for what had I to do with wings and clouds, who can with difficulty move about on the earth?”
body_child: A Tortoise was resting in the sun. She was sad because she could not fly. An Eagle asked her, "What will you give me if I teach you to fly?" The Tortoise said she would give him many treasures. The Eagle picked her up and flew high into the clouds. Then he let her go. The Tortoise fell and hit a mountain. Before she died, she said, "I should have stayed on the ground where I belong."
moral: If men had all they wished, they would be often ruined.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes the things we want can actually hurt us. We should be happy with who we are. It is dangerous to try to do things that we are not meant to do.

title: The Fox and the Goat
body: A FOX one day fell into a deep well and could find no means of escape. A Goat, overcome with thirst, came to the same well, and seeing the Fox, inquired if the water was good. Concealing his sad plight under a merry guise, the Fox indulged in a lavish praise of the water, saying it was excellent beyond measure, and encouraging him to descend. The Goat, mindful only of his thirst, thoughtlessly jumped down, but just as he drank, the Fox informed him of the difficulty they were both in and suggested a scheme for their common escape. “If,” said he, “you will place your forefeet upon the wall and bend your head, I will run up your back and escape, and will help you out afterwards.” The Goat readily assented and the Fox leaped upon his back. Steadying himself with the Goat’s horns, he safely reached the mouth of the well and made off as fast as he could. When the Goat upbraided him for breaking his promise, he turned around and cried out, “You foolish old fellow! If you had as many brains in your head as you have hairs in your beard, you would never have gone down before you had inspected the way up, nor have exposed yourself to dangers from which you had no means of escape.”
body_child: A Fox fell into a deep well and could not get out. A thirsty Goat came by and asked if the water was good. The Fox lied and said the water was great, so the Goat jumped in. Then the Fox said, "Let me climb on your back to get out, and then I will help you." The Fox climbed out and ran away, telling the Goat he should have thought about how to get out before he jumped in.
moral: Look before you leap.
moral_elaborated: Always think about what might happen before you do something. Do not rush into a situation without a plan to stay safe. It is important to be careful and think ahead.

title: The Raven and the Swan
body: A RAVEN saw a Swan and desired to secure for himself the same beautiful plumage. Supposing that the Swan’s splendid white color arose from his washing in the water in which he swam, the Raven left the altars in the neighborhood where he picked up his living, and took up residence in the lakes and pools. But cleansing his feathers as often as he would, he could not change their color, while through want of food he perished.
body_child: A black Raven wanted to have white feathers like a Swan. He thought the Swan was white because he lived in the water. The Raven moved to a lake and washed himself all day long. His feathers stayed black, and he could not find any food to eat, so he grew very weak and died.
moral: Change of habit cannot alter Nature.
moral_elaborated: You cannot change who you are just by changing where you live. Be happy with yourself instead of trying to be someone else. Trying to be something you are not can lead to trouble.

title: The Thirsty Pigeon
body: A PIGEON, oppressed by excessive thirst, saw a goblet of water painted on a signboard. Not supposing it to be only a picture, she flew towards it with a loud whir and unwittingly dashed against the signboard, jarring herself terribly. Having broken her wings by the blow, she fell to the ground, and was caught by one of the bystanders.
body_child: A very thirsty Pigeon saw a picture of a glass of water on a sign. She thought the water was real and flew toward it very fast. She hit the sign so hard that she broke her wings and fell down. Because she was hurt, a person nearby caught her.
moral: Zeal should not outrun discretion.
moral_elaborated: Do not let your excitement make you act without thinking first. Take a moment to look closely at things so you don't make a mistake. Being in too much of a hurry can cause accidents.

title: The Dog in the Manger
body: A DOG lay in a manger, and by his growling and snapping prevented the oxen from eating the hay which had been placed for them. “What a selfish Dog!” said one of them to his companions; “he cannot eat the hay himself, and yet refuses to allow those to eat who can.”
body_child: A Dog was sleeping in a wooden box full of hay meant for cows. When the hungry cows came to eat, the Dog growled and bit at them. The cows were sad because the Dog could not eat hay, but he would not let the cows eat it either.
moral: Do not grudge others what you cannot enjoy yourself.
moral_elaborated: Do not stop other people from having something that you do not even need. It is mean to be selfish with things you cannot use. It is better to share and be kind to others.

title: The Oxen and the Axle-Trees
body: A HEAVY WAGON was being dragged along a country lane by a team of Oxen. The Axle-trees groaned and creaked terribly; whereupon the Oxen, turning round, thus addressed the wheels: “Hullo there! why do you make so much noise? We bear all the labor, and we, not you, ought to cry out.”
body_child: Some strong Oxen were pulling a heavy wagon down a road. The wheels of the wagon made a very loud, squeaky noise. The Oxen looked back and said, "Why are you complaining? We are the ones doing all the hard work, so we should be the ones making noise!"
moral: Those who suffer most cry out the least.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes the people doing the hardest work are the ones who complain the least. People who make the most noise are often not the ones doing the real work. Remember to thank the people who work hard quietly.

title: The Farmer and the Cranes
body: SOME CRANES made their feeding grounds on some plowlands newly sown with wheat. For a long time the Farmer, brandishing an empty sling, chased them away by the terror he inspired; but when the birds found that the sling was only swung in the air, they ceased to take any notice of it and would not move. The Farmer, on seeing this, charged his sling with stones, and killed a great number. The remaining birds at once forsook his fields, crying to each other, “It is time for us to be off to Liliput: for this man is no longer content to scare us, but begins to show us in earnest what he can do.”
body_child: A farmer wanted to keep birds away from his new seeds. At first, he just made noise to scare them, and the birds did not leave. Then, the farmer used stones, and the birds got very scared. They flew away because they saw the farmer was serious about protecting his field.
moral: If words suffice not, blows must follow.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes just talking is not enough to stop someone from doing something wrong. You may need to take action to make them listen. Doing something is often stronger than just talking.

title: The Sick Lion
body: A LION, unable from old age and infirmities to provide himself with food by force, resolved to do so by artifice. He returned to his den, and lying down there, pretended to be sick, taking care that his sickness should be publicly known. The beasts expressed their sorrow, and came one by one to his den, where the Lion devoured them. After many of the beasts had thus disappeared, the Fox discovered the trick and presenting himself to the Lion, stood on the outside of the cave, at a respectful distance, and asked him how he was. “I am very middling,” replied the Lion, “but why do you stand without? Pray enter within to talk with me.” “No, thank you,” said the Fox. “I notice that there are many prints of feet entering your cave, but I see no trace of any returning.”
body_child: An old lion was too weak to hunt for food. He went into his cave and pretended to be sick. When other animals came to visit him, he caught them and ate them. A smart fox stayed outside because he saw that no animals ever came back out.
moral: He is wise who is warned by the misfortunes of others.
moral_elaborated: You can learn from what happens to other people. If you see others get into trouble, you can be smart and stay safe. Paying attention helps you avoid the same mistakes.

title: The Bear and the Two Travelers
body: TWO MEN were traveling together, when a Bear suddenly met them on their path. One of them climbed up quickly into a tree and concealed himself in the branches. The other, seeing that he must be attacked, fell flat on the ground, and when the Bear came up and felt him with his snout, and smelt him all over, he held his breath, and feigned the appearance of death as much as he could. The Bear soon left him, for it is said he will not touch a dead body. When he was quite gone, the other Traveler descended from the tree, and jocularly inquired of his friend what it was the Bear had whispered in his ear. “He gave me this advice,” his companion replied. “Never travel with a friend who deserts you at the approach of danger.”
body_child: Two friends were walking when a bear surprised them. One friend climbed a tree to hide. The other friend lay flat on the ground and acted dead. The bear sniffed him and left. His friend asked what the bear said, and he replied, 'Never travel with a friend who leaves you when things get scary.'
moral: Misfortune tests the sincerity of friends.
moral_elaborated: You find out who your real friends are when you are in trouble. A true friend stays to help you instead of running away. Hard times show you who really cares about you.

title: The Fox Who Had Lost His Tail
body: A FOX caught in a trap escaped, but in so doing lost his tail. Thereafter, feeling his life a burden from the shame and ridicule to which he was exposed, he schemed to convince all the other Foxes that being tailless was much more attractive, thus making up for his own deprivation. He assembled a good many Foxes and publicly advised them to cut off their tails, saying that they would not only look much better without them, but that they would get rid of the weight of the brush, which was a very great inconvenience. One of them interrupting him said, “If you had not yourself lost your tail, my friend, you would not thus counsel us.”
body_child: A fox lost his tail in a trap and felt very embarrassed. He told the other foxes they should all cut off their tails to look better. One fox saw through the trick. He said the first fox only wanted them to lose their tails because he had already lost his.
moral: Distrust those who offer advice for their own benefit.
moral_elaborated: Be careful when someone gives you advice that only helps them. They might be trying to trick you into being just like them. Always think about why someone is telling you to do something.

title: The Cat and the Cock
body: A CAT caught a Cock, and pondered how he might find a reasonable excuse for eating him. He accused him of being a nuisance to men by crowing in the nighttime and not permitting them to sleep. The Cock defended himself by saying that he did this for the benefit of men, that they might rise in time for their labours. The Cat replied, “Although you abound in specious apologies, I shall not remain supperless;”
body_child: A cat caught a rooster and tried to find a reason to eat him. He said the rooster was too noisy at night. The rooster said he only crowed to help people wake up for work. The cat did not care and ate him anyway because he was hungry.
moral: and he made a meal of him.
moral_elaborated: Mean people will often find any excuse to do something bad. Even if you have a good answer, they might not listen to you. It is hard to argue with someone who has already decided to be unfair.

title: The Wolf in Sheep’s Clothing
body: ONCE UPON A TIME a Wolf resolved to disguise his appearance in order to secure food more easily. Encased in the skin of a sheep, he pastured with the flock deceiving the shepherd by his costume. In the evening he was shut up by the shepherd in the fold; the gate was closed, and the entrance made thoroughly secure. But the shepherd, returning to the fold during the night to obtain meat for the next day, mistakenly caught up the Wolf instead of a sheep, and killed him instantly.
body_child: A wolf wanted to eat some sheep. He put on a sheep's skin to hide. He went into the field with the other sheep. The shepherd did not see him. At night, the shepherd locked the wolf in the pen with the sheep. Later, the shepherd needed meat. He went into the dark pen and picked up the wolf by mistake. He killed the wolf because he thought it was a sheep.
moral: Harm seek, harm find.
moral_elaborated: If you try to hurt others, you might get hurt yourself. Being mean or tricky often leads to trouble. It is better to be kind and honest.

title: The Goat and the Goatherd
body: A GOATHERD had sought to bring back a stray goat to his flock. He whistled and sounded his horn in vain; the straggler paid no attention to the summons. At last the Goatherd threw a stone, and breaking its horn, begged the Goat not to tell his master. The Goat replied, “Why, you silly fellow, the horn will speak though I be silent.”
body_child: A boy was looking for a lost goat. He whistled and called, but the goat did not come back. The boy got angry and threw a stone at the goat. The stone broke the goat's horn. The boy was scared and told the goat not to tell anyone. The goat said, "Everyone will see my broken horn! You cannot hide what happened."
moral: Do not attempt to hide things which cannot be hid.
moral_elaborated: You should not try to hide the truth when it is easy for everyone to see. If you make a mistake, it is better to be honest about it. Some things are impossible to keep a secret.

title: The Boasting Traveler
body: A MAN who had traveled in foreign lands boasted very much, on returning to his own country, of the many wonderful and heroic feats he had performed in the different places he had visited. Among other things, he said that when he was at Rhodes he had leaped to such a distance that no man of his day could leap anywhere near him as to that, there were in Rhodes many persons who saw him do it and whom he could call as witnesses. One of the bystanders interrupted him, saying: “Now, my good man, if this be all true there is no need of witnesses. Suppose this to be Rhodes, and leap for us.”
body_child: A man went on a long trip. When he came home, he told many big stories. He said he jumped very far in a place called Rhodes. He said many people saw him do it. A man listening to him said, "We do not need to go to Rhodes. Show us your jump right here!"
moral: Actions speak louder than words.
moral_elaborated: It is better to show what you can do than to just talk about it. People believe you more when they see you do something. Bragging does not prove anything.

title: The Lion in Love
body: A LION demanded the daughter of a woodcutter in marriage. The Father, unwilling to grant, and yet afraid to refuse his request, hit upon this expedient to rid himself of his importunities. He expressed his willingness to accept the Lion as the suitor of his daughter on one condition: that he should allow him to extract his teeth, and cut off his claws, as his daughter was fearfully afraid of both. The Lion cheerfully assented to the proposal. But when the toothless, clawless Lion returned to repeat his request, the Woodman, no longer afraid, set upon him with his club, and drove him away into the forest.
body_child: A big lion loved a woodcutter's daughter. He asked the father if he could marry her. The father was scared of the lion's teeth and claws. He told the lion, "You must let me pull your teeth and cut your claws first." The lion agreed because he loved the girl. But when the lion had no teeth or claws, the father was not afraid anymore. He chased the lion away with a big stick.
moral: Do not give up your strength for someone else.
moral_elaborated: Be careful when someone asks you to change who you are. If you give away what makes you strong, you might get hurt. Always keep yourself safe.

title: The Miser
body: A MISER sold all that he had and bought a lump of gold, which he buried in a hole in the ground by the side of an old wall and went to look at daily. One of his workmen observed his frequent visits to the spot and decided to watch his movements. He soon discovered the secret of the hidden treasure, and digging down, came to the lump of gold, and stole it. The Miser, on his next visit, found the hole empty and began to tear his hair and to make loud lamentations. A neighbor, seeing him overcome with grief and learning the cause, said, “Pray do not grieve so; but go and take a stone, and place it in the hole, and fancy that the gold is still lying there. It will do you quite the same service; for when the gold was there, you had it not, as you did not make the slightest use of it.”
body_child: A man had a lot of gold. He buried it in a hole in the ground. He went to look at it every day but never spent it. A worker saw him and stole the gold. The man cried when he found the gold was gone. A neighbor said, "Do not be sad. Put a rock in the hole and pretend it is gold. Since you never used the gold anyway, a rock is just as good!"
moral: Money is worth nothing if you do not use it.
moral_elaborated: Having things is only useful if you actually use them to help yourself or others. Saving things forever without using them is like having nothing at all. Use what you have wisely.

title: The Porker, the Sheep, and the Goat
body: A young Pig was shut up in a fold-yard with a Goat and a Sheep. On one occasion the shepherd laid hold of him, when he grunted, and squeaked, and resisted violently. The Sheep and the Goat complained of his distressing cries, and said, “He often handles us, and we do not cry out.” To this he replied, “Your handling and mine are very different things. He catches you only for your wool, or your milk, but he lays hold on me for my very life.”
body_child: A little pig lived in a yard with a sheep and a goat. One day, a man grabbed the pig. The pig started to squeal and kick. The sheep and the goat told him to be quiet. They said, "The man catches us all the time, but we do not cry." The pig said, "He catches you for your wool. He catches me to eat me!"
moral: It is easy to be calm when you are not the one in danger.
moral_elaborated: It is easy to stay quiet when nothing bad is happening to you. We should not judge others when they are scared. They might have a very good reason to be upset.

title: The Boy and the Filberts
body: A BOY put his hand into a pitcher full of filberts. He grasped as many as he could possibly hold, but when he tried to pull out his hand, he was prevented from doing so by the neck of the pitcher. Unwilling to lose his filberts, and yet unable to withdraw his hand, he burst into tears and bitterly lamented his disappointment. A bystander said to him, “Be satisfied with half the quantity, and you will readily draw out your hand.”
body_child: A boy put his hand into a jar full of nuts. He grabbed a huge handful. But when he tried to pull his hand out, it got stuck. He did not want to let go of the nuts, so he started to cry. A man told him, "Just take half of the nuts. Then your hand will come out easily."
moral: Do not attempt too much at once.
moral_elaborated: If you try to take too much at one time, you might end up with nothing. It is better to take a little bit and be happy. Being greedy can cause problems.

title: The Frogs Asking for a King
body: THE FROGS, grieved at having no established Ruler, sent ambassadors to Jupiter entreating for a King. Perceiving their simplicity, he cast down a huge log into the lake. The Frogs were terrified at the splash occasioned by its fall and hid themselves in the depths of the pool. But as soon as they realized that the huge log was motionless, they swam again to the top of the water, dismissed their fears, climbed up, and began squatting on it in contempt. After some time they began to think themselves ill-treated in the appointment of so inert a Ruler, and sent a second deputation to Jupiter to pray that he would set over them another sovereign. He then gave them an Eel to govern them. When the Frogs discovered his easy good nature, they sent yet a third time to Jupiter to beg him to choose for them still another King.
body_child: The frogs wanted a king to rule them. They asked for help. A big log was thrown into their pond. At first, the frogs were scared. Then they saw the log did not move, so they hopped on it. They wanted a better king, so they asked again. Next, they got an eel, but he was too nice. They asked a third time for a new king.
moral: Be content with what you have, or you may get something worse.
moral_elaborated: Be happy with what you have right now. If you keep asking for more and more, you might get something that is not good for you. Sometimes simple things are the best.

title: The Laborer and the Snake
body: A SNAKE, having made his hole close to the porch of a cottage, inflicted a mortal bite on the Cottager’s infant son. Grieving over his loss, the Father resolved to kill the Snake. The next day, when it came out of its hole for food, he took up his axe, but by swinging too hastily, missed its head and cut off only the end of its tail. After some time the Cottager, afraid that the Snake would bite him also, endeavored to make peace, and placed some bread and salt in the hole. The Snake, slightly hissing, said: “There can henceforth be no peace between us; for whenever I see you I shall remember the loss of my tail, and whenever you see me you will be thinking of the death of your son.”
body_child: A snake lived near a house and bit a man's baby. The father was very sad and tried to hit the snake with an axe. He missed the snake's head and cut off its tail. Later, the man tried to be friends with the snake by giving it food. The snake said, "We can never be friends. I will always remember my tail, and you will always remember your son."
moral: No one truly forgets injuries in the presence of him who caused the injury.
moral_elaborated: It is very hard to forget when someone hurts you. Even if you try to be nice later, the sad memory stays. Some things are very hard to forgive.

title: The Lion, the Mouse, and the Fox
body: A LION, fatigued by the heat of a summer’s day, fell fast asleep in his den. A Mouse ran over his mane and ears and woke him from his slumbers. He rose up and shook himself in great wrath, and searched every corner of his den to find the Mouse. A Fox seeing him said: “A fine Lion you are, to be frightened of a Mouse.” “’Tis not the Mouse I fear,” said the Lion; “I resent his familiarity and ill-breeding.”
body_child: A lion was sleeping in his cave on a hot day. A tiny mouse ran over his head and woke him up. The lion was very angry and looked everywhere for the mouse. A fox saw him and laughed. "Are you really scared of a tiny mouse?" the fox asked. The lion said, "I am not scared. I am mad because the mouse was rude to me."
moral: Little liberties are great offenses.
moral_elaborated: Even small things can be very rude. We should always respect others, no matter how big or small they are. Being polite is important to everyone.

title: The Horse and Groom
body: A GROOM used to spend whole days in currycombing and rubbing down his Horse, but at the same time stole his oats and sold them for his own profit. “Alas!” said the Horse, “if you really wish me to be in good condition, you should groom me less, and feed me more.”
moral: A man is known by his deeds, not by his words.
body_child: A worker brushed his horse every day to make him look nice and shiny. But the worker also stole the horse's food to sell it for money. The horse became very thin and hungry. The horse said, "If you want me to be healthy, please feed me more and brush me less!"
moral_elaborated: It is more important to take care of someone's needs than to just make them look good. True kindness means being helpful, not just acting like you are. Always do what is right for others.

title: The Ass and the Mule
body: A MULETEER set forth on a journey, driving before him an Ass and a Mule, both well laden. The Ass, as long as he traveled along the plain, carried his load with ease, but when he began to ascend the steep path of the mountain, felt his load to be more than he could bear. He entreated his companion to relieve him of a small portion, that he might carry home the rest; but the Mule paid no attention to the request. The Ass shortly afterwards fell down dead under his burden. Not knowing what else to do in so wild a region, the Muleteer placed upon the Mule the load carried by the Ass in addition to his own, and at the top of all placed the hide of the Ass, after he had skinned him. The Mule, groaning beneath his heavy burden, said to himself: “I am treated according to my deserts. If I had only been willing to assist the Ass a little in his need, I should not now be bearing, together with his burden, himself as well.”
moral: Help others in their time of need, or you may suffer too.
body_child: A donkey and a mule were carrying heavy bags up a steep mountain. The donkey was very tired and asked the mule to help him. The mule said no. Soon, the donkey fell down and died. The owner then put all of the donkey’s bags on the mule’s back and the mule had to carry everything alone.
moral_elaborated: When we help our friends, we make the work easier for everyone. If we are selfish, we might end up having to do all the work ourselves later. It is always better to be kind and share the load.

title: The Ass and the Lapdog
body: A MAN had an Ass, and a Maltese Lapdog, a very great beauty. The Ass was left in a stable and had plenty of oats and hay to eat, just as any other Ass would. The Lapdog knew many tricks and was a great favourite with his master, who often fondled him and seldom went out to dine without bringing him home some tidbit to eat. The Ass, on the contrary, had much work to do in grinding the corn-mill and in carrying wood from the forest or burdens from the farm. He often lamented his own hard fate and contrasted it with the luxury and idleness of the Lapdog, till at last one day he broke his cords and halter, and galloped into his master’s house, kicking up his heels without measure, and frisking and fawning as well as he could. He next tried to jump about his master as he had seen the Lapdog do, but he broke the table and smashed all the dishes upon it to atoms. He then attempted to lick his master, and jumped upon his back. The servants, hearing the strange hubbub and perceiving the danger of their master, quickly relieved him, and drove out the Ass to his stable with kicks and clubs and cuffs. The Ass, as he returned to his stall beaten nearly to death, thus lamented: “I have brought it all on myself! Why could I not have been contented to labor with my companions, and not wish to be idle all the day like that useless little Lapdog!”
moral: Do not try to be something you are not.
body_child: A man had a pet dog and a big donkey. The dog did tricks and got treats, while the donkey had to work hard. The donkey wanted to be like the dog, so he ran into the house and tried to jump on his master. He broke the table and all the dishes! The servants chased the donkey back to the barn, and he realized he should just be himself.
moral_elaborated: Every person and animal is special in their own way. You do not need to act like someone else to be liked. Just be yourself and do your best at your own job.

title: The Oxen and the Butchers
body: THE OXEN once upon a time sought to destroy the Butchers, who practiced a trade destructive to their race. They assembled on a certain day to carry out their purpose, and sharpened their horns for the contest. But one of them who was exceedingly old (for many a field had he plowed) thus spoke: “These Butchers, it is true, slaughter us, but they do so with skillful hands, and with no unnecessary pain. If we get rid of them, we shall fall into the hands of unskillful operators, and thus suffer a double death: for you may be assured, that though all the Butchers should perish, yet will men never want beef.”
moral: Do not be in a hurry to change one evil for another.
body_child: Some oxen wanted to get rid of the butchers who worked with them. They began to sharpen their horns to fight. But an old ox told them to stop. He said that if they got rid of the current butchers, the new people who came along might be even worse. He told them to think carefully before making a change.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes we think a change will make things better, but it could actually make things worse. Think carefully before you try to change a bad situation. It is important to look before you leap.

title: The Shepherd’s Boy and the Wolf
body: A SHEPHERD-BOY, who watched a flock of sheep near a village, brought out the villagers three or four times by crying out, “Wolf! Wolf!” and when his neighbors came to help him, laughed at them for their pains. The Wolf, however, did truly come at last. The Shepherd-boy, now really alarmed, shouted in an agony of terror: “Pray, do come and help me; the Wolf is killing the sheep;” but no one paid any heed to his cries, nor rendered any assistance. The Wolf, having no cause of fear, at his leisure lacerated or destroyed the whole flock.
moral: There is no believing a liar, even when he speaks the truth.
body_child: A boy was bored while watching his sheep. He yelled "Wolf!" just to trick the people in town. When they ran to help, he laughed at them. Later, a real wolf came! The boy cried for help, but the people thought he was lying again. Nobody came to help, and the wolf took the sheep.
moral_elaborated: If you tell lies, people will stop trusting you. Even when you tell the truth, they might think you are still joking. It is always best to be honest so people can believe you.

title: The Boys and the Frogs
body: SOME BOYS, playing near a pond, saw a number of Frogs in the water and began to pelt them with stones. They killed several of them, when one of the Frogs, lifting his head out of the water, cried out: “Pray stop, my boys: what is sport to you, is death to us.”
moral: One man's pleasure is another man's pain.
body_child: Some boys played near a pond. They saw frogs in the water and threw stones at them. They hurt the frogs. One frog put its head up and said, "Please stop! You are having fun, but you are hurting us."
moral_elaborated: What is fun for you might hurt someone else. Always think about other people's feelings before you act. Be kind to all living things.

title: The Salt Merchant and His Ass
body: A PEDDLER drove his Ass to the seashore to buy salt. His road home lay across a stream into which his Ass, making a false step, fell by accident and rose up again with his load considerably lighter, as the water melted the sack. The Peddler retraced his steps and refilled his panniers with a larger quantity of salt than before. When he came again to the stream, the Ass fell down on purpose in the same spot, and, regaining his feet with the weight of his load much diminished, brayed triumphantly as if he had obtained what he desired. The Peddler saw through his trick and drove him for the third time to the coast, where he bought a cargo of sponges instead of salt. The Ass, again playing the fool, fell down on purpose when he reached the stream, but the sponges became swollen with water, greatly increasing his load.
moral: And thus his trick recoiled on him, for he now carried on his back a double burden.
body_child: A man and his donkey went to get salt. On the way home, the donkey fell in a river. The salt melted and the bag got light. The donkey was happy! Next time, the donkey fell on purpose to make the bag light again. The man saw the trick. He filled the bags with sponges. The donkey fell in the water again, but the sponges got heavy with water. The donkey had to carry a very heavy load!
moral_elaborated: If you try to be lazy or play tricks, it might make things harder for you. It is better to do your work honestly. Tricks can end up hurting you in the end.

title: The Mischievous Dog
body: A DOG used to run up quietly to the heels of everyone he met, and to bite them without notice. His master suspended a bell about his neck so that the Dog might give notice of his presence wherever he went. Thinking it a mark of distinction, the Dog grew proud of his bell and went tinkling it all over the marketplace. One day an old hound said to him: “Why do you make such an exhibition of yourself? That bell that you carry is not, believe me, any order of merit, but on the contrary a mark of disgrace, a public notice to all men to avoid you as an ill mannered dog.”
moral: Notoriety is often mistaken for fame.
body_child: There was a dog that liked to bite people. His master put a bell on his neck. The bell would ring so people knew he was coming. The dog thought the bell was a prize. He showed it to everyone. An old dog said, "Why are you proud? That bell is not a trophy. It is there to tell people you are a mean dog."
moral_elaborated: Being famous for doing bad things is not good. It is better to be known for being kind and helpful. Do not be proud of a bad reputation.

title: The Goatherd and the Wild Goats
body: A GOATHERD, driving his flock from their pasture at eventide, found some Wild Goats mingled among them, and shut them up together with his own for the night. The next day it snowed very hard, so that he could not take the herd to their usual feeding places, but was obliged to keep them in the fold. He gave his own goats just sufficient food to keep them alive, but fed the strangers more abundantly in the hope of enticing them to stay with him and of making them his own. When the thaw set in, he led them all out to feed, and the Wild Goats scampered away as fast as they could to the mountains. The Goatherd scolded them for their ingratitude in leaving him, when during the storm he had taken more care of them than of his own herd. One of them, turning about, said to him: “That is the very reason why we are so cautious; for if you yesterday treated us better than the Goats you have had so long, it is plain also that if others came after us, you would in the same manner prefer them to ourselves.”
moral: Old friends cannot with impunity be sacrificed for new ones.
body_child: A man had some goats. One night, some wild goats joined them. The man gave the wild goats more food than his own goats. He wanted them to stay forever. When the snow melted, the wild goats ran away. The man was angry. A wild goat said, "We are leaving because you treated us better than your old friends. If new goats come, you would treat them better than us, too!"
moral_elaborated: Always take good care of your old friends. Do not ignore them just to make new friends. If you are not loyal to old friends, new friends will not trust you.

title: The Man and His Two Sweethearts
body: A MIDDLE-AGED MAN, whose hair had begun to turn gray, courted two women at the same time. One of them was young, and the other well advanced in years. The elder woman, ashamed to be courted by a man younger than herself, made a point, whenever her admirer visited her, to pull out some portion of his black hairs. The younger, on the contrary, not wishing to become the wife of an old man, was equally zealous in removing every gray hair she could find. Thus it came to pass that between them both he very soon found that he had not a hair left on his head.
moral: Those who seek to please everybody please nobody.
body_child: A man had hair that was turning gray. Two women liked him. One woman was young and did not like gray hair. She pulled out his gray hairs. The other woman was old and did not like black hair. She pulled out his black hairs. Soon, the man had no hair left at all!
moral_elaborated: You cannot make everyone happy all the time. If you try to change for everyone, you might lose what makes you special. It is better to just be yourself.

title: The Sick Stag
body: A SICK STAG lay down in a quiet corner of its pasture-ground. His companions came in great numbers to inquire after his health, and each one helped himself to a share of the food which had been placed for his use; so that he died, not from his sickness, but from the failure of the means of living.
body_child: A sick deer lay down to rest. Many friends came to see him. Each friend ate a little bit of his food. Soon, all his food was gone. The deer died because he had nothing left to eat.
moral: Evil companions bring more hurt than profit.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes friends can hurt us even if they do not mean to. In this story, the friends ate the food the sick deer needed to get better. It is important to have friends who truly help us.

title: The Boy and the Nettles
body: A BOY was stung by a Nettle. He ran home and told his Mother, saying, “Although it hurts me very much, I only touched it gently.” “That was just why it stung you,” said his Mother. “The next time you touch a Nettle, grasp it boldly, and it will be soft as silk to your hand, and not in the least hurt you.”
body_child: A boy touched a plant that stings. He ran home and told his mother. He said he touched it very lightly. His mother said to grab it tight next time. If he was brave, the plant would not hurt his hand.
moral: Whatever you do, do with all your might.
moral_elaborated: When you have a hard job to do, do it with a lot of energy. If you are shy or scared, the job might feel harder. Being brave and strong helps you finish your work.

title: The Astronomer
body: AN ASTRONOMER used to go out at night to observe the stars. One evening, as he wandered through the suburbs with his whole attention fixed on the sky, he fell accidentally into a deep well. While he lamented and bewailed his sores and bruises, and cried loudly for help, a neighbor ran to the well, and learning what had happened said: “Hark ye, old fellow, why, in striving to pry into what is in heaven, do you not manage to see what is on earth?”
body_child: A man loved to look at the stars at night. He walked around while looking at the sky. He did not see a deep hole and fell inside. A neighbor heard him and said he should look at the ground before looking at the stars.
moral: Take care of the things that are near you first.
moral_elaborated: It is good to have big dreams, but you must also watch where you are going. If you do not pay attention to what is near you, you might get hurt. Always look at the path in front of you.

title: The Wolves and the Sheep
body: “WHY SHOULD there always be this fear and slaughter between us?” said the Wolves to the Sheep. “Those evil-disposed Dogs have much to answer for. They always bark whenever we approach you and attack us before we have done any harm. If you would only dismiss them from your heels, there might soon be treaties of peace and reconciliation between us.” The Sheep, poor silly creatures, were easily beguiled and dismissed the Dogs, whereupon the Wolves destroyed the unguarded flock at their own pleasure.
body_child: The wolves told the sheep they wanted to be friends. They said the dogs were mean for barking at them. The sheep believed the wolves and sent the dogs away. With the dogs gone, the wolves ate the sheep.
moral: Never trust the advice of an enemy.
moral_elaborated: Some people may try to trick you into leaving your friends who protect you. You should be careful about who you listen to. Do not trust someone who wants to hurt you.

title: The Cat and the Birds
body: A CAT, hearing that the Birds in a certain aviary were ailing dressed himself up as a physician, and, taking his cane and a bag of instruments becoming his profession, went to call on them. He knocked at the door and inquired of the inmates how they all did, saying that if they were ill, he would be happy to prescribe for them and cure them. They replied, “We are all very well, and shall continue so, if you will only be good enough to go away, and leave us as we are.”
body_child: A cat heard that some birds were sick. He dressed up like a doctor. He went to the birds and asked to help them. The birds knew it was the cat. They told him they were fine and to go away.
moral: A villain may disguise himself, but he will not deceive the wise.
moral_elaborated: Just because someone looks nice or acts helpful doesn't mean they are a friend. Use your brain to see if someone is trying to trick you. Wise people can see through a person's costume.

title: The Vain Jackdaw
body: JUPITER DETERMINED, it is said, to create a sovereign over the birds, and made proclamation that on a certain day they should all present themselves before him, when he would himself choose the most beautiful among them to be king. The Jackdaw, knowing his own ugliness, searched through the woods and fields, and collected the feathers which had fallen from the wings of his companions, and stuck them in all parts of his body, hoping thereby to make himself the most beautiful of all. When the appointed day arrived, and the birds had assembled before Jupiter, the Jackdaw also made his appearance in his many feathered finery. But when Jupiter proposed to make him king because of the beauty of his plumage, the birds indignantly protested, and each plucked from him his own feathers, leaving the Jackdaw nothing but a Jackdaw.
moral: It is not only fine feathers that make fine birds.
body_child: A king wanted to pick the most beautiful bird to be the leader. A Jackdaw wanted to win, but he was not very pretty. He found colorful feathers on the ground and stuck them to his body. When he went to see the king, he looked very fancy. But the other birds saw their own feathers and pulled them off. The Jackdaw was just a plain bird again.
moral_elaborated: Do not try to be someone you are not. Real beauty comes from who you are inside, not what you wear. It is always better to be yourself.

title: The Kid and the Wolf
body: A KID standing on the roof of a house, out of harm’s way, saw a Wolf passing by and immediately began to taunt and revile him. The Wolf, looking up, said, “Sirrah! I hear thee: yet it is not thou who mockest me, but the roof on which thou art standing.”
moral: Time and place often give the advantage to the weak over the strong.
body_child: A young goat was standing on top of a tall roof. A Wolf walked by on the ground below. The goat started to yell mean things at the Wolf because he felt safe. The Wolf looked up and said, 'You are not brave. It is only the high roof that makes you feel strong.'
moral_elaborated: Sometimes people feel brave only because they are in a safe spot. It is easy to be mean when you know nothing can hurt you. True courage is different from just being safe.

title: The Old Woman and the Physician
body: AN OLD WOMAN having lost the use of her eyes, called in a Physician to heal them, and made this bargain with him in the presence of witnesses: that if he should cure her blindness, he should receive from her a sum of money; but if her infirmity remained, she should give him nothing. This agreement being made, the Physician, time after time, applied his salve to her eyes, and on every visit took something away, stealing all her property little by little. And when he had got all she had, he healed her and demanded the promised payment. The Old Woman, when she recovered her sight and saw none of her goods in her house, would give him nothing. The Physician insisted on his claim, and, as she still refused, summoned her before the Judge. The Old Woman, standing up in the Court, argued: “This man here speaks the truth in what he says; for I did promise to give him a sum of money if I should recover my sight: but if I continued blind, I was to give him nothing. Now he declares that I am healed. I on the contrary affirm that I am still blind; for when I lost the use of my eyes, I saw in my house various chattels and valuable goods: but now, though he swears I am cured of my blindness, I am not able to see a single thing in it.”
moral: He who plays a trick may be tricked in return.
body_child: An old woman could not see well, so she called a doctor. She promised to pay him if he fixed her eyes. Every time the doctor visited, he stole something from her house while she was blind. When she could see again, she saw that all her things were gone. She refused to pay him. She told the judge, 'I am still blind because I cannot see any of my furniture!'
moral_elaborated: If you try to cheat someone, you might lose in the end. The doctor was greedy and stole, so he did not get paid. Honesty is always the best way to do business.

title: The Ox and the Frog
body: AN OX drinking at a pool trod on a brood of young frogs and crushed one of them to death. The Mother coming up, and missing one of her sons, inquired of his brothers what had become of him. “He is dead, dear Mother; for just now a very huge beast with four great feet came to the pool and crushed him to death with his cloven heel.” The Frog, puffing herself out, inquired, “if the beast was as big as that in size.” “Cease, Mother, to puff yourself out,” said her son, “and do not be angry; for you would, I assure you, sooner burst than successfully imitate the hugeness of that monster.”
moral: Self-conceit leads to self-destruction.
body_child: A big Ox stepped on a tiny frog by a pond. The mother frog came home and asked what happened. Her other children said a giant monster crushed their brother. The mother frog puffed herself up with air. She asked, 'Was the monster this big?' Her children told her to stop. They knew she could never be as big as the giant Ox.
moral_elaborated: Do not try to be bigger or more important than you really are. It is dangerous to pretend to be something impossible. Be happy with who you are.

title: The Farmer and His Sons
body: A FATHER, being on the point of death, wished to be sure that his sons would give the same attention to his farm as he himself had given it. He called them to his bedside and said, “My sons, there is a great treasure hid in one of my vineyards.”
moral: Industry is itself a treasure.
body_child: A father was very old. He told his sons that a treasure was hidden in their farm. After he died, the sons dug up every inch of the dirt to find the gold. They never found any coins. However, because they worked the soil so well, the grapes grew better than ever before. Their hard work was the real treasure.
moral_elaborated: Working hard is the best way to get good things. Even if you don't find gold, your effort will help you succeed. Hard work pays off in the end.

title: The Heifer and the Ox
body: A HEIFER saw an Ox hard at work harnessed to a plow, and tormented him with reflections on his unhappy fate in being compelled to labor. Shortly afterwards, at the harvest festival, the owner released the Ox from his yoke, but bound the Heifer with cords and led him away to the altar to be slain in honour of the occasion. The Ox saw what was being done, and said with a smile to the Heifer: “For this you were allowed to live in idleness, because you were presently to be sacrificed.”
body_child: A young cow saw an old ox working hard on a farm. She laughed at him for having to work so much. Later, there was a big feast. The farmer let the ox rest, but he took the young cow away to be cooked for the meal. The ox said, "You were allowed to be lazy only because you were being saved for this day."
moral: Idleness can lead to a quick end.
