moral_elaborated: It is better to be busy and useful than to be lazy. Sometimes hard work keeps us safe. Being lazy does not always lead to a happy ending.

title: The Fighting Cocks and the Eagle
body: TWO GAME COCKS were fiercely fighting for the mastery of the farmyard. One at last put the other to flight. The vanquished Cock skulked away and hid himself in a quiet corner, while the conqueror, flying up to a high wall, flapped his wings and crowed exultingly with all his might. An Eagle sailing through the air pounced upon him and carried him off in his talons. The vanquished Cock immediately came out of his corner, and ruled henceforth with undisputed mastery.
body_child: Two roosters fought to see who would be the boss of the farm. One rooster lost and hid in a corner. The winner flew up to a high wall to brag. He flapped his wings and cheered loudly. A big eagle saw him and carried him away. The rooster who lost came out of his corner and became the new boss.
moral: Pride goes before destruction.
moral_elaborated: Bragging about winning can lead to trouble. It is better to be quiet and humble after you win. Showing off can attract bad things to you.

title: The Charger and the Miller
body: A CHARGER, feeling the infirmities of age, was sent to work in a mill instead of going out to battle. But when he was compelled to grind instead of serving in the wars, he bewailed his change of fortune and called to mind his former state, saying, “Ah! Miller, I had indeed to go campaigning before, but I was barbed from counter to tail, and a man went along to groom me; and now I cannot understand what ailed me to prefer the mill before the battle.” “Forbear,” said the Miller to him, “harping on what was of yore, for it is the common lot of mortals to sustain the ups and downs of fortune.”
body_child: A brave war horse grew old and weak. He was sent to work at a mill to grind grain. He was sad because he used to be a hero in battles. He told the miller he missed his old life. The miller said, "Do not complain about the past. Life has good times and hard times for everyone."
moral: Be prepared for the changes of life.
moral_elaborated: Life will not always stay the same. We must be ready for things to change as we get older. Try to be brave during both the good and bad times.

title: The Fox and the Monkey
body: A MONKEY once danced in an assembly of the Beasts, and so pleased them all by his performance that they elected him their King. A Fox, envying him the honour, discovered a piece of meat lying in a trap, and leading the Monkey to the place where it was, said that she had found a store, but had not used it, she had kept it for him as treasure trove of his kingdom, and counseled him to lay hold of it. The Monkey approached carelessly and was caught in the trap; and on his accusing the Fox of purposely leading him into the snare, she replied, “O Monkey, and are you, with such a mind as yours, going to be King over the Beasts?”
body_child: A monkey danced so well that the other animals made him King. A fox was jealous. She found some meat inside a trap. She told the monkey she found a treasure for him. The monkey was not careful and got caught in the trap. The fox said, "You are not smart enough to be a king."
moral: A leader must have wisdom.
moral_elaborated: You should always think before you act. Being good at one thing does not mean you can do everything. Always look for danger before you try to grab a prize.

title: The Horse and His Rider
body: A HORSE SOLDIER took the utmost pains with his charger. As long as the war lasted, he looked upon him as his fellow-helper in all emergencies and fed him carefully with hay and corn. But when the war was over, he only allowed him chaff to eat and made him carry heavy loads of wood, subjecting him to much slavish drudgery and ill-treatment. War was again proclaimed, however, and when the trumpet summoned him to his standard, the Soldier put on his charger its military trappings, and mounted, being clad in his heavy coat of mail. The Horse fell down straightway under the weight, no longer equal to the burden, and said to his master, “You must now go to the war on foot, for you have transformed me from a Horse into an Ass; and how can you expect that I can again turn in a moment from an Ass to a Horse?”
body_child: A soldier took great care of his horse during a war. When the war ended, he treated the horse badly. He gave the horse poor food and made him carry heavy wood. Soon, another war started. The horse was now too weak to carry the soldier. The horse said, "You treated me poorly when you didn't need me, so now I cannot help you."
moral: Treat others well if you want their help later.
moral_elaborated: Always take care of the people and animals that help you. If you are mean to your friends when you are safe, they cannot help you when you are in trouble. Kindness should never stop.

title: The Belly and the Members
body: THE MEMBERS of the Body rebelled against the Belly, and said, “Why should we be perpetually engaged in administering to your wants, while you do nothing but take your rest, and enjoy yourself in luxury and self-indulgence?”
moral: The Members carried out their resolve and refused their assistance to the Belly. The whole Body quickly became debilitated, and the hands, feet, mouth, and eyes, when too late, repented of their folly.
body_child: The parts of the body were mad at the belly. They said, "We do all the work while you just sit there and eat!" They stopped giving the belly food. Soon, the hands and feet felt very weak. They learned that every part of the body must work together to stay healthy.
moral_elaborated: We all need each other to get things done. Even if someone's job looks easy, it is still very important. When we do not work together, everyone loses.

title: The Widow and Her Little Maidens
body: A WIDOW who was fond of cleaning had two little maidens to wait on her. She was in the habit of waking them early in the morning, at cockcrow. The maidens, aggravated by such excessive labor, resolved to kill the cock who rouse their mistress so early. When they had done this, they found that they had only prepared for themselves greater troubles, for their mistress, no longer hearing the hour from the cock, woke them up to their work in the middle of the night.
moral: Sometimes our solutions only make things worse.
body_child: A woman made her two helpers wake up very early when the rooster crowed. The helpers did not like waking up early, so they killed the rooster. They thought they could sleep more. Instead, the woman woke them up even earlier in the middle of the night!
moral_elaborated: Don't try to get out of work by making a bad choice. Sometimes the thing you complain about is actually helping you. If you act without thinking, you might make your problem bigger.

title: The Vine and the Goat
body: A VINE was luxuriant in the time of vintage with leaves and grapes. A Goat, passing by, nibbled its young tendrils and its leaves. The Vine addressed him and said: “Why do you thus injure me without a cause, and crop my leaves? Is there no young grass left? But I shall not have to wait long for my just revenge; for if you now should crop my leaves, and cut me down to my root, I shall provide the wine to pour over you when you are led as a victim to the sacrifice.”
moral: Those who do wrong will be punished.
body_child: A goat was eating the leaves off a vine. The vine asked, "Why are you hurting me when there is grass to eat?" The vine told the goat that it would have its revenge. Later, when the goat was taken away, the vine's grapes were used to make the drink for the ceremony.
moral_elaborated: If you are mean to others, bad things might happen to you too. It is important to be kind to the things that help us. Doing something bad to others often comes back to haunt you.

title: Jupiter and the Monkey
body: JUPITER ISSUED a proclamation to all the beasts of the forest and promised a royal reward to the one whose offspring should be deemed the handsomest. The Monkey came with the rest and presented, with all a mother’s tenderness, a flat-nosed, hairless, ill-featured young Monkey as a candidate for the promised reward. A general laugh saluted her on the presentation of her son. She resolutely said, “I know not whether Jupiter will allot the prize to my son, but this I do know, that he is at least in the eyes of me his mother, the dearest, handsomest, and most beautiful of all.”
moral: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
body_child: A king promised a prize to the animal with the cutest baby. A mother monkey brought her baby, but the other animals laughed at him. The mother did not care what they thought. She said her baby was the most beautiful one to her.
moral_elaborated: Every mother thinks her child is special and beautiful. It does not matter what other people think. Love makes us see the best in the people we care about.

title: The Hawk, the Kite, and the Pigeons
body: THE PIGEONS, terrified by the appearance of a Kite, called upon the Hawk to defend them. He at once consented. When they had admitted him into the cote, they found that he made more havoc and slew a larger number of them in one day than the Kite could pounce upon in a whole year.
moral: Avoid a remedy that is worse than the disease.
body_child: Some pigeons were scared of a big bird called a Kite. They asked a Hawk to protect them. The Hawk said yes, but then he started eating the pigeons himself! He was much scarier than the Kite they were afraid of.
moral_elaborated: Be careful who you ask for help. Sometimes the person you think will help you can cause even more trouble. Always think before you pick a new friend.

title: The Dolphins, the Whales, and the Sprat
body: THE DOLPHINS and Whales waged a fierce war with each other. When the battle was at its height, a Sprat lifted its head out of the waves and said that he would reconcile their differences if they would accept him as an umpire. One of the Dolphins replied, “We would far rather be destroyed in our battle with each other than admit any interference from you in our affairs.”
body_child: The Dolphins and the Whales were having a big fight. A tiny fish called a Sprat swam up to them. He said, "Stop fighting! I can help you be friends." A Dolphin looked at him and said, "We would rather keep fighting than let a tiny fish like you tell us what to do!"
moral: The small should not meddle in the affairs of the great.
moral_elaborated: It is not a good idea to tell much bigger or more powerful people what to do. They might get angry because they think they are more important than you. It is often safer to stay out of their arguments.

title: The Swallow, the Serpent, and the Court of Justice
body: A SWALLOW, returning from abroad and especially fond of dwelling with men, built herself a nest in the wall of a Court of Justice and there hatched seven young birds. A Serpent gliding past the nest from its hole in the wall ate up the young unfledged nestlings. The Swallow, finding her nest empty, lamented greatly and exclaimed: “Woe to me a stranger! that in this place where all others’ rights are protected, I alone should suffer wrong.”
body_child: A mother bird made a nest on the wall of a courthouse. She had seven babies. One day, a snake came out of a hole and ate all the babies. The mother bird was very sad. She cried, "I thought I would be safe at a courthouse where everyone follows the rules. But I am the only one who got hurt!"
moral: Justice is not always found where it is most expected.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes bad things happen even in places that are supposed to be safe. We feel extra sad when we think we are protected but get hurt anyway. Not everyone follows the rules, even in a house of rules.

title: The Two Pots
body: A RIVER carried down in its stream two Pots, one made of earthenware and the other of brass. The Earthen Pot said to the Brass Pot, “Pray keep at a distance and do not come near me, for if you touch me ever so slightly, I shall be broken in pieces, and besides, I by no means wish to come near you.”
body_child: Two pots were floating down a river. One was made of clay and the other was made of heavy metal. The metal pot wanted to float together. But the clay pot said, "Please stay away! If you touch me, I will break into tiny pieces. I must stay away to be safe."
moral: Equals make the best friends.
moral_elaborated: It is safest to play with friends who are similar to you. If a very strong friend is too rough, they might accidentally hurt a friend who is not as strong. Being around people like ourselves helps keep us safe.

title: The Shepherd and the Wolf
body: A SHEPHERD once found the whelp of a Wolf and brought it up, and after a while taught it to steal lambs from the neighboring flocks. The Wolf, having shown himself an apt pupil, said to the Shepherd, “Since you have taught me to steal, you must keep a sharp lookout, or you will lose some of your own flock.”
body_child: A man found a baby wolf and raised it. He taught the wolf how to steal sheep from other people. The wolf learned very fast. One day the wolf said to the man, "You taught me how to steal. Now you better watch your own sheep, or I will steal them too!"
moral: A bad lesson can come back to hurt the teacher.
moral_elaborated: If you teach someone how to be mean or do bad things, they might do those bad things to you. It is always better to teach others how to be kind. What you teach others can come back to you.

title: The Crab and Its Mother
body: A CRAB said to her son, “Why do you walk so one-sided, my child? It is far more becoming to go straight forward.” The young Crab replied: “Quite true, dear Mother; and if you will show me the straight way, I will promise to walk in it.” The Mother tried in vain, and submitted without remonstrance to the reproof of her child.
body_child: A mother crab said to her son, "Why do you walk sideways? You should walk straight forward." The young crab said, "Okay, Mother! If you show me how to walk straight, I will do it." The mother tried to walk straight, but she could only go sideways. She realized she could not tell her son to do what she could not do herself.
moral: Example is more powerful than precept.
moral_elaborated: It is better to show people how to act instead of just telling them. Children usually do what their parents do, not just what they say. Always try to set a good example for others to follow.

title: The Father and His Two Daughters
body: A MAN had two daughters, the one married to a gardener, and the other to a tile-maker. After a time he went to the daughter who had married the gardener, and inquired how she was and how all things went with her. She said, “All things are prospering with me, and I have only one wish, that there may be a heavy fall of rain, in order that the plants may be well watered.” Not long after, he went to the daughter who had married the tilemaker, and likewise inquired of her how she fared; she replied, “I want for nothing, and have only one wish, that the dry weather may continue, and the sun shine hot and bright, so that the bricks might be dried.” He said to her, “If your sister wishes for rain, and you for dry weather, with which of the two am I to join my wishes?”
body_child: A father had two daughters. One daughter was married to a gardener. The other was married to a brick maker. The father visited the first daughter. She said, "I hope it rains so the plants grow." Then he visited the second daughter. She said, "I hope the sun stays hot so my bricks can dry." The father did not know what to wish for. If it rained, it would help one daughter but hurt the other.
moral: You cannot please everyone at the same time.
moral_elaborated: People want different things. Sometimes, what is good for one person is bad for another. It is impossible to make everyone happy at once.

title: The Thief and His Mother
body: A BOY stole a lesson-book from one of his schoolfellows and took it home to his Mother. She not only abstained from beating him, but encouraged him. He next time stole a cloak and brought it to her, and she again commended him. The Youth, advanced to adulthood, proceeded to steal things of still greater value. At last he was caught in the very act, and having his hands bound behind him, was led away to the place of public execution. His Mother followed in the crowd and violently beat her breast in sorrow, whereupon the young man said, “I wish to say something to my Mother in her ear.” She came close to him, and he quickly seized her ear with his teeth and bit it off. The Mother upbraided him as an unnatural child, whereon he replied, “Ah! if you had beaten me when I first stole and brought to you that lesson-book, I should not have come to this, nor have been thus led to a disgraceful death.”
body_child: A young boy stole a book from school. He took it home to his mother. She did not punish him. She told him he did a good job. When he grew up, he stole bigger and more expensive things. Finally, he was caught. He was very sad and told his mother it was her fault. He said if she had stopped him when he was little, he would not be a thief today.
moral: Nip evil in the bud.
moral_elaborated: It is important to learn right from wrong when you are young. If we are not stopped from doing small bad things, we might do bigger bad things later. Parents should help children learn from their mistakes early.

title: The Old Man and Death
body: AN OLD MAN was employed in cutting wood in the forest, and, in carrying the faggots to the city for sale one day, became very wearied with his long journey. He sat down by the wayside, and throwing down his load, besought “Death” to come. “Death” immediately appeared in answer to his summons and asked for what reason he had called him. The Old Man hurriedly replied, “That, lifting up the load, you may place it again upon my shoulders.”
body_child: An old man was carrying heavy wood. He was very tired from his long walk. He sat down and cried out, "I wish Death would come and take me!" Suddenly, Death appeared and asked, "Why did you call me?" The old man was scared. He said quickly, "I just wanted you to help me put this heavy wood back on my shoulders!"
moral: We all love life, even when it is hard.
moral_elaborated: Even when things are very difficult, we still want to keep going. We often find that we are stronger than we think. Life is very special and we should not give up on it.

title: The Fir-Tree and the Bramble
body: A FIR-TREE said boastingly to the Bramble, “You are useful for nothing at all; while I am everywhere used for roofs and houses.” The Bramble answered: “You poor creature, if you would only call to mind the axes and saws which are about to hew you down, you would have reason to wish that you had grown up a Bramble, not a Fir-Tree.”
body_child: A tall Fir-Tree was mean to a small bush. The tree said, "I am useful to build big houses, but you are not useful for anything!" The little bush replied, "Wait until the woodcutters come with their sharp saws. Then you will wish you were a small bush like me. No one wants to chop me down!"
moral: Better poverty without care, than riches with.
moral_elaborated: It is better to have a simple life and be safe than to be important and in danger. Being fancy can sometimes bring big problems. Be happy with who you are.

title: The Æthiop
body: THE PURCHASER of a black servant was persuaded that the color of his skin arose from dirt contracted through the neglect of his former masters. On bringing him home he resorted to every means of cleaning, and subjected the man to incessant scrubbings. The servant caught a severe cold, but he never changed his color or complexion.
body_child: A man bought a servant with dark skin. He thought the man was just dirty. He took the man home and tried to wash him many times. He used lots of soap and water. The man got a very bad cold from all the washing. Even after all that work, his skin stayed the same color.
moral: What’s bred in the bone will stick to the flesh.
moral_elaborated: You cannot change the way someone is born. It is best to accept people just as they are. Trying to change nature will not work and might even cause harm.

title: The Mouse, the Frog, and the Hawk
body: A MOUSE who always lived on the land, by an unlucky chance formed an intimate acquaintance with a Frog, who lived for the most part in the water. The Frog, one day intent on mischief, bound the foot of the Mouse tightly to his own. Thus joined together, the Frog first of all led his friend the Mouse to the meadow where they were accustomed to find their food. After this, he gradually led him towards the pool in which he lived, until reaching the very brink, he suddenly jumped in, dragging the Mouse with him. The Frog enjoyed the water amazingly, and swam croaking about, as if he had done a good deed. The unhappy Mouse was soon suffocated by the water, and his dead body floated about on the surface, tied to the foot of the Frog. A Hawk observed it, and, pouncing upon it with his talons, carried it aloft. The Frog, being still fastened to the leg of the Mouse, was also carried off a prisoner, and was eaten by the Hawk.
body_child: A land mouse and a water frog became friends. One day, the frog played a mean trick and tied the mouse's foot to his own. He jumped into a deep pond and pulled the mouse under the water. The poor mouse could not breathe and died. A hungry hawk saw the mouse floating and flew down to grab him. Because the frog was still tied to the mouse, the hawk caught the frog too. The hawk ate them both.
moral: Harm hatch, harm catch.
moral_elaborated: If you try to hurt someone else, you might end up getting hurt too. Being mean to others often brings trouble to yourself. It is better to be a kind friend.

title: The Fisherman and His Nets
body: A FISHERMAN, engaged in his calling, made a very successful cast and captured a great haul of fish. He managed by a skillful handling of his net to retain all the large fish and to draw them to the shore; but he could not prevent the smaller fish from falling back through the meshes of the net into the sea.
body_child: A fisherman threw a big net into the ocean and caught many fish. He pulled the net to the shore. The big fish were too large to escape and stayed in the net. But the tiny fish were small enough to swim through the holes. They fell back into the water and were safe.
moral: The little are often safe while the great are in danger.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes being small and simple is better than being big and important. Small things can escape from dangers that big things cannot. This shows that everyone has their own special strength.

title: The Wolf and the Sheep
body: A WOLF, sorely wounded and bitten by dogs, lay sick and maimed in his lair. Being in want of food, he called to a Sheep who was passing, and asked him to fetch some water from a stream flowing close beside him. “For,” he said, “if you will bring me drink, I will find means to provide myself with meat.” “Yes,” said the Sheep, “if I should bring you the draught, you would doubtless make me provide the meat also.”
body_child: A wolf was hurt and stayed in his cave. He was very hungry and thirsty. He saw a sheep walk by and asked for some water. The wolf said that if he had water, he would find his own food. The smart sheep knew the wolf was lying. The sheep said if he went near the wolf, he would become the wolf's dinner!
moral: Hypocritical speeches are easily seen through.
moral_elaborated: It is easy to tell when someone is lying to get what they want. You should be careful around people who try to trick you with nice words. Trust your feelings when something sounds like a trick.

title: The Old Woman and the Wine-Jar
body: AN OLD WOMAN found an empty jar which had lately been full of prime old wine and which still retained the fragrant smell of its former contents. She greedily placed it several times to her nose, and drawing it backwards and forwards said, “O most delicious! How nice must the Wine itself have been, when it leaves behind in the very vessel which contained it so sweet a perfume!”
body_child: An old woman found an empty jar. It used to be full of sweet wine. Even though it was empty, the jar still smelled very good. She smelled it many times and smiled. She thought about how wonderful the wine must have been to leave such a lovely smell behind.
moral: The memory of a good deed lives.
moral_elaborated: Good things leave behind happy memories even after they are gone. When you do something kind, people will remember it for a long time. Your good actions are like a sweet smell that stays in a room.

title: The Man Bitten by a Dog
body: A MAN who had been bitten by a Dog went about in quest of someone who might heal him. A friend, meeting him and learning what he wanted, said, “If you would be cured, take a piece of bread, and dip it in the blood from your wound, and go and give it to the Dog that bit you.” The Man who had been bitten laughed at this advice and said, “Why? If I should do so, it would be as if I should beg every Dog in the town to bite me.”
body_child: A dog bit a man. The man looked for help to get better. A friend told him to give a treat to the dog that bit him. The man laughed and said that was a bad idea. He knew that if he gave the mean dog a treat, other dogs would want to bite him too!
moral: Benefits bestowed upon the evil-disposed increase their means of injuring you.
moral_elaborated: If you reward someone for being mean, they will keep being mean to you. It is important not to give prizes for bad behavior. Treat others well, but do not let bullies think they can get rewards for hurting people.

title: The Huntsman and the Fisherman
body: A HUNTSMAN, returning with his dogs from the field, fell in by chance with a Fisherman who was bringing home a basket well laden with fish. The Huntsman wished to have the fish, and their owner experienced an equal longing for the contents of the game-bag. They quickly agreed to exchange the produce of their day’s sport. Each was so well pleased with his bargain that they made for some time the same exchange day after day. Finally a neighbor said to them, “If you go on in this way, you will soon destroy by frequent use the pleasure of your exchange, and each will again wish to retain the fruits of his own sport.”
body_child: A hunter met a fisherman on the road. The hunter had meat and the fisherman had fish. They decided to swap their food. They were both very happy. They swapped their food every day for a long time. A neighbor told them they might get tired of it. He said they would soon want their own food again.
moral: Abstain and enjoy.
moral_elaborated: If you do the same thing every day, it might stop being fun. It is good to take a break from things you like. This helps you enjoy them more later.

title: The Fox and the Crow
body: A CROW having stolen a bit of meat, perched in a tree and held it in her beak. A Fox, seeing this, longed to possess the meat himself, and by a wily stratagem succeeded. “How handsome is the Crow,” he exclaimed, “in the beauty of her shape and in the fairness of her complexion! Oh, if her voice were only equal to her beauty, she would deservedly be considered the Queen of Birds!” This he said deceitfully; but the Crow, anxious to refute the reflection cast upon her voice, set up a loud caw and dropped the flesh. The Fox quickly picked it up, and thus addressed the Crow: “My good Crow, your voice is right enough, but your wit is wanting.”
body_child: A crow had a piece of meat in her mouth. She sat in a tree. A fox saw her and wanted the meat. He told the crow she was very beautiful. He asked her to sing a song. The crow opened her mouth to say 'Caw!' and the meat fell down. The fox ate it and told the crow she was not very smart.
moral: Do not trust flatterers.
moral_elaborated: Be careful when someone says too many nice things to you just to get what they want. They might be trying to trick you. Always think before you trust them.

title: The Widow and the Sheep
body: A CERTAIN poor widow had one solitary Sheep. At shearing time, wishing to take his fleece and to avoid expense, she sheared him herself, but used the shears so unskillfully that with the fleece she sheared the flesh. The Sheep, writhing with pain, said, “Why do you hurt me so, Mistress? What weight can my blood add to the wool? If you want my flesh, there is the butcher, who will kill me in an instant; but if you want my fleece and wool, there is the shearer, who will shear and not hurt me.”
body_child: A woman had one sheep. She wanted to cut the sheep's wool herself to save money. She did not know how to do it right and hurt the sheep. The sheep said, 'Why are you hurting me? If you want wool, go to someone who knows how to cut it safely.'
moral: The least outlay is not always the greatest gain.
moral_elaborated: Trying to save money by doing a job yourself can sometimes lead to big mistakes. It is better to pay a professional to do a job the right way. This keeps everyone safe and happy.

title: The Playful Ass
body: AN ASS climbed up to the roof of a building, and frisking about there, broke in the tiling. The owner went up after him and quickly drove him down, beating him severely with a thick wooden cudgel. The Ass said, “Why, I saw the Monkey do this very thing yesterday, and you all laughed heartily, as if it afforded you very great amusement.”
body_child: A donkey climbed onto a roof. He jumped around and broke the tiles. The owner was angry and hit the donkey to make him get down. The donkey was sad. He said, 'Yesterday I saw the monkey do the same thing and you laughed!'
moral: Do not copy others blindly.
moral_elaborated: Just because something looks funny when someone else does it, doesn't mean you should do it too. We are all different. Always think about whether an action is right for you.

title: The Stag in the Ox-Stall
body: A STAG, roundly chased by the hounds and blinded by fear to the danger he was running into, took shelter in a farmyard and hid himself in a shed among the oxen. An Ox gave him this kindly warning: “O unhappy creature! why should you thus, of your own accord, incur destruction and trust yourself in the house of your enemy?” The Stag replied: “Only allow me, friend, to stay where I am, and I will undertake to find some favourable opportunity of effecting my escape.” At the approach of the evening the herdsman came to feed his cattle, but did not see the Stag; and even the farm-bailiff with several laborers passed through the shed and failed to notice him. The Stag, congratulating himself on his safety, began to express his sincere thanks to the Oxen who had kindly helped him in the hour of need. One of them again answered him: “We indeed wish you well, but the danger is not over. There is one other yet to pass through the shed, who has as it were a hundred eyes, and until he has come and gone, your life is still in peril.” At that moment the master himself entered, and having had to complain that his oxen had not been properly fed, he went up to their racks and cried out: “Why is there such a scarcity of fodder? There is not half enough straw for them to lie on. Those lazy fellows have not even swept the cobwebs away.”
body_child: A deer was hiding from hunters. He ran into a barn and hid in the straw. An ox told him it was a bad idea to stay there. The farm workers came in but did not see the deer. The deer felt safe and thanked the oxen. But then the owner of the farm came in. He looked at everything very closely. He saw the deer's horns in the hay and caught him.
moral: While he thus examined everything in turn, he spied the tips of the antlers of the Stag peeping out of the straw. Then summoning his laborers, he ordered that the Stag should be seized and killed.
moral_elaborated: A leader often notices small details that others miss. You should always be careful even if you think you are safe. It is hard to hide from someone who is very observant.

title: The Two Dogs
body: A MAN had two dogs: a Hound, trained to assist him in his sports, and a Housedog, taught to watch the house. When he returned home after a good day’s sport, he always gave the Housedog a large share of his spoil. The Hound, feeling much aggrieved at this, reproached his companion, saying, “It is very hard to have all this labor, while you, who do not assist in the chase, luxuriate on the fruits of my exertions.” The Housedog replied, “Do not blame me, my friend, but find fault with the master, who has not taught me to labor, but to depend for subsistence on the labor of others.”
moral: Children are not to be blamed for the faults of their parents.
body_child: A man had two dogs. One dog was a hunter. The other dog stayed home to guard the house. When the hunter came home, the master gave the house dog a lot of food. The hunter was mad. He said, "I do all the work while you just sit here!" The house dog said, "Do not be mad at me. Be mad at our master. He taught me how to wait for food, not how to hunt."
moral_elaborated: You should not be angry with someone for what they were taught. If a person was never shown how to do something, it is not their fault. Blame the person who should have taught them.

title: The Wild Ass and the Lion
body: A WILD ASS and a Lion entered into an alliance so that they might capture the beasts of the forest with greater ease. The Lion agreed to assist the Wild Ass with his strength, while the Wild Ass gave the Lion the benefit of his greater speed. When they had taken as many beasts as their necessities required, the Lion undertook to distribute the prey, and for this purpose divided it into three shares. “I will take the first share,” he said, “because I am King: and the second share, as a partner with you in the chase: and the third share (believe me) will be a source of great evil to you, unless you willingly resign it to me, and set off as fast as you can.”
moral: Might makes right.
body_child: A Wild Ass and a Lion worked together to hunt for food. The Lion was strong. The Ass was very fast. They caught many animals. Then the Lion divided the food into three parts. He said, "I take the first part because I am King. I take the second part because I helped you. You should give me the third part too, or I will hurt you." The Ass had to run away with nothing.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes people who are strong take everything for themselves just because they can. They use their power to get what they want, even if it is not fair. It is hard to argue with someone who is much stronger than you.

title: The Lion and the Dolphin
body: A LION roaming by the seashore saw a Dolphin lift up its head out of the waves, and suggested that they contract an alliance, saying that of all the animals they ought to be the best friends, since the one was the king of beasts on the earth, and the other was the sovereign ruler of all the inhabitants of the ocean. The Dolphin gladly consented to this request. Not long afterwards the Lion had a combat with a wild bull, and called on the Dolphin to help him. The Dolphin, though quite willing to give him assistance, was unable to do so, as he could not by any means reach the land. The Lion abused him as a traitor. The Dolphin replied, “Nay, my friend, blame not me, but Nature, which, while giving me the sovereignty of the sea, has quite denied me the power of living upon the land.”
moral: Choose friends who can help you in your time of need.
body_child: A Lion and a Dolphin decided to be best friends. The Lion ruled the land and the Dolphin ruled the sea. One day, the Lion was in a big fight with a wild bull. He asked the Dolphin for help. The Dolphin wanted to help, but he could not leave the water. The Lion was angry. The Dolphin said, "Do not be mad at me. I was born to live in the sea, not on the land."
moral_elaborated: Even if a friend wants to help you, they might not be able to. Some friends have different skills or live in different places. You should pick helpers who can actually reach you when things get hard.

title: The Eagle and the Arrow
body: AN EAGLE sat on a lofty rock, watching the movements of a Hare whom he sought to make his prey. An archer, who saw the Eagle from a place of concealment, took an accurate aim and wounded him mortally. The Eagle gave one look at the arrow that had entered his heart and saw in that single glance that its feathers had been furnished by himself. “It is a double grief to me,” he exclaimed, “that I should perish by an arrow feathered from my own wings.”
moral: We often provide the means for our own destruction.
body_child: An Eagle sat on a high rock. He was looking for food. A man with a bow and arrow shot the Eagle. As the Eagle was dying, he looked at the arrow. He saw that the arrow had feathers from his own wings on it. The Eagle was very sad. He was hurt by something that came from his own body.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes the things we do or make can come back to hurt us. It is extra sad when we help create the problem that causes us trouble. We should be careful about what we leave behind.

title: The Sick Kite
body: A KITE, sick unto death, said to his mother: “O Mother! do not mourn, but at once invoke the gods that my life may be prolonged.” She replied, “Alas! my son, which of the gods do you think will pity you? Is there one whom you have not outraged by filching from their very altars a part of the sacrifice offered up to them?”
moral: We must make friends in prosperity if we would have their help in adversity.
body_child: A bird called a Kite was very sick. He asked his mother to pray to the gods to help him get well. His mother said, "Why would the gods help you? You have stolen food from them many times." The Kite had no one to help him because he had been mean before he got sick.
moral_elaborated: Be kind to others when things are going well. If you are mean when you are strong, no one will want to help you when you are weak. It is important to have friends before you need them.

title: The Lion and the Boar
body: ON A SUMMER DAY, when the great heat induced a general thirst among the beasts, a Lion and a Boar came at the same moment to a small well to drink. They fiercely disputed which of them should drink first, and were soon engaged in the agonies of a mortal combat. When they stopped suddenly to catch their breath for a fiercer renewal of the fight, they saw some Vultures waiting in the distance to feast on the one that should fall first. They at once made up their quarrel, saying, “It is better for us to make friends, than to become the food of Crows or Vultures.”
body_child: It was a very hot day. A Lion and a Boar were both very thirsty. They found a small well but started to fight over who would drink first. While they were fighting, they saw big birds waiting to eat whoever lost. They decided to stop fighting and be friends so the birds wouldn't eat them.
moral: It is better to be friends than to fight and lose everything.
moral_elaborated: When you fight with others, you might both get hurt. It is much better to work together and be kind. That way, everyone stays safe and happy.

title: The Mice in Council
body: THE MICE summoned a council to decide how they might best devise means of warning themselves of the approach of their great enemy the Cat. Among the many plans suggested, the one that found most favour was the proposal to tie a bell to the neck of the Cat, so that the Mice, being warned by the sound of the tinkling, might run away and hide themselves in their holes at his approach. But when the Mice further debated who among them should thus “bell the Cat,” there was no one found to do it.
body_child: The mice had a meeting to talk about how to stay safe from the cat. One mouse said, "Let's put a bell on the cat! Then we can hear her coming." All the mice thought this was a great idea. But then they asked who would put the bell on the cat, and no one was brave enough to do it.
moral: It is easy to propose impossible remedies.
moral_elaborated: It is very easy to come up with a good idea. However, it is much harder to actually do the work to make it happen. A plan is only good if you can really do it.

title: The One-Eyed Doe
body: A DOE blind in one eye was accustomed to graze as near to the edge of the cliff as she possibly could, in the hope of securing her greater safety. She turned her sound eye towards the land that she might get the earliest tidings of the approach of hunter or hound, and her injured eye towards the sea, from whence she entertained no anticipation of danger. Some boatmen sailing by saw her, and taking a successful aim, mortally wounded her. Yielding up her last breath, she gasped forth this lament: “O wretched creature that I am! to take such precaution against the land, and after all to find this seashore, to which I had come for safety, so much more perilous.”
body_child: A deer was blind in one eye. She stood by the ocean to eat grass. She kept her good eye on the land to watch for hunters. She thought she was safe because she did not think anyone would come from the water. But some men in a boat saw her and shot her from the sea.
moral: Danger often comes from where we least expect it.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes we only look for danger in one place and forget to look everywhere else. We should try to be careful all around us. You never know where a problem might start.

title: The Mice and the Weasels
body: THE WEASELS and the Mice waged a perpetual war with each other, in which much blood was shed. The Weasels were always the victors. The Mice thought that the cause of their frequent defeats was that they had no leaders set apart from the general army to command them, and that they were exposed to dangers from lack of discipline. They therefore chose as leaders Mice that were most renowned for their family descent, strength, and counsel, as well as those most noted for their courage in the fight, so that they might be better marshaled in battle array and formed into troops, regiments, and battalions. When all this was done, and the army disciplined, and the herald Mouse had duly proclaimed war by challenging the Weasels, the newly chosen generals bound their heads with straws, that they might be more conspicuous to all their troops. Scarcely had the battle begun, when a great rout overwhelmed the Mice, who scampered off as fast as they could to their holes. The generals, not being able to get in on account of the ornaments on their heads, were all captured and eaten by the Weasels.
body_child: The mice were losing a war against the weasels. They picked leaders to help them win. The leaders wore big straw hats so everyone could see them. When the weasels attacked, the mice ran to hide in their holes. The leaders could not fit inside because of their big hats, and they were caught by the weasels.
moral: The more honour the more danger.
moral_elaborated: Being an important leader can be fun, but it also comes with more risks. Sometimes being special or famous makes it harder to stay safe. It is important to be careful even when you are in charge.

title: The Shepherd and the Sea
body: A SHEPHERD, keeping watch over his sheep near the shore, saw the Sea very calm and smooth, and longed to make a voyage with a view to commerce. He sold all his flock, invested it in a cargo of dates, and set sail. But a very great tempest came on, and the ship being in danger of sinking, he threw all his merchandise overboard, and barely escaped with his life in the empty ship. Not long afterwards when someone passed by and observed the unruffled calm of the Sea, he interrupted him and said, “It is again in want of dates, and therefore looks quiet.”
body_child: A man who watched sheep saw the ocean was very calm. He sold all his sheep and bought a boat full of fruit to sell. A giant storm came and he lost everything. Later, the ocean looked calm again. The man said the ocean was only acting nice so it could take more things from people.
moral: Do not trust a calm sea or a fair-weather friend.
moral_elaborated: Just because something looks nice and safe now does not mean it will stay that way. You should not give up everything you have for something risky. Always be careful of things that can change quickly.

title: The Ass, the Cock, and the Lion
body: AN ASS and a Cock were in a straw-yard together when a Lion, desperate from hunger, approached the spot. He was about to spring upon the Ass, when the Cock (to the sound of whose voice the Lion, it is said, has a singular aversion) crowed loudly, and the Lion fled away as fast as he could. The Ass, observing his trepidation at the mere crowing of a Cock summoned courage to attack him, and galloped after him for that purpose. He had run no long distance, when the Lion, turning about, seized him and tore him to pieces.
body_child: A donkey and a rooster were in a farmyard together. A hungry lion came near to eat the donkey. Suddenly, the rooster crowed very loudly. Lions are scared of that sound, so the lion ran away. The donkey thought he was brave and chased the lion. But the lion turned around and caught the donkey.
moral: False confidence often leads into danger.
moral_elaborated: Do not think you are stronger than you really are. Just because someone else scared an enemy does not mean you can too. Being too proud can lead to trouble.

title: The Rivers and the Sea
body: THE RIVERS joined together to complain to the Sea, saying, “Why is it that when we flow into your tides so potable and sweet, you work in us such a change, and make us salty and unfit to drink?” The Sea, perceiving that they intended to throw the blame on him, said, “Pray cease to flow into me, and then you will not be made briny.”
body_child: Many rivers went to talk to the Sea. They asked, "Why do you make our fresh water so salty?" The Sea knew they were trying to blame him for the salt. The Sea said, "If you do not like the salt, then stop flowing into me."
moral: Don't complain about the results of your own actions.
moral_elaborated: If you choose to do something, do not complain about what happens because of it. The rivers chose to go into the sea. They should not be surprised when their water changes.

title: The Wild Boar and the Fox
body: A WILD BOAR stood under a tree and rubbed his tusks against the trunk. A Fox passing by asked him why he thus sharpened his teeth when there was no danger threatening from either huntsman or hound. He replied, “I do it advisedly; for it would never do to have to sharpen my weapons just at the time I ought to be using them.”
body_child: A wild pig stood by a tree. He rubbed his long teeth against the wood to make them sharp. A fox walked by and asked, "Why are you doing that? There are no hunters near us today." The pig said, "I do this now so I am ready. I cannot wait to sharpen my teeth when a hunter is already here!"
moral: To be well prepared for war is the best guarantee of peace.
moral_elaborated: It is smart to get ready before you have a problem. If you wait until the last minute, it will be too late. Always be prepared for what might happen.

title: The Milk-Woman and Her Pail
body: A FARMER’S daughter was carrying her Pail of milk from the field to the farmhouse, when she fell a-musing. “The money for which this milk will be sold, will buy at least three hundred eggs. The eggs, allowing for all mishaps, will produce two hundred and fifty chickens. The chickens will become ready for the market when poultry will fetch the highest price, so that by the end of the year I shall have money enough from my share to buy a new gown. In this dress I will go to the Christmas parties, where all the young fellows will propose to me, but I will toss her head and refuse them every one.”
body_child: A girl was carrying a pail of milk on her head. She started to dream about the future. She thought, "I will sell this milk and buy eggs. The eggs will turn into chickens. I will sell the chickens and buy a beautiful new dress." She was so happy that she tossed her head. The pail fell down, and all the milk spilled on the ground.
moral: At this moment she tossed her head in unison with her thoughts, when down fell the milk pail to the ground, and all her imaginary schemes perished in a moment.
moral_elaborated: Do not plan how to spend money before you actually have it. It is better to focus on what you are doing right now. If you dream too much, you might make a mistake and lose everything.

title: The Bee and Jupiter
body: A BEE from Mount Hymettus, the queen of the hive, ascended to Olympus to present Jupiter some honey fresh from her combs. Jupiter, delighted with the offering of honey, promised to give whatever she should ask. She therefore besought him, saying, “Give me, I pray thee, a sting, that if any mortal shall approach to take my honey, I may kill him.” Jupiter was much displeased, for he loved the race of man, but could not refuse the request because of his promise. He thus answered the Bee: “You shall have your request, but it will be at the peril of your own life. For if you use your sting, it shall remain in the wound you make, and then you will die from the loss of it.”
body_child: A queen bee brought some honey to the king of the gods. The king was very happy. He told the bee she could have anything she wanted. The bee said, "Give me a sting. I want to kill anyone who tries to take my honey." The king was sad because he loved people. He told the bee, "You will have a sting. But if you use it, you will die too."
moral: Evil wishes, like chickens, come home to roost.
moral_elaborated: If you wish for something bad to happen to others, it might happen to you instead. It is better to be kind. Mean wishes often hurt the person who makes them.

title: The Wolf and the Housedog
body: A WOLF, meeting a big well-fed Mastiff with a wooden collar about his neck asked him who it was that fed him so well and yet compelled him to drag that heavy log about wherever he went. “The master,” he replied. Then said the Wolf: “May no friend of mine ever be in such a plight; for the weight of this chain is enough to spoil the appetite.”
body_child: A hungry wolf met a big, strong dog. The dog wore a heavy wooden collar. The wolf asked who fed the dog so well. The dog said his master fed him but made him wear the collar. The wolf said he would rather be hungry than wear a heavy chain. He wanted to be free.
moral: Freedom is more valuable than comfort.
moral_elaborated: It is better to be free than to have lots of food but live in a cage. Being able to go where you want is very important. No treat is worth losing your freedom.

title: The Three Tradesmen
body: A GREAT CITY was besieged, and its inhabitants were called together to consider the best means of protecting it from the enemy. A Bricklayer earnestly recommended bricks as affording the best material for an effective resistance. A Carpenter, with equal enthusiasm, proposed timber as a preferable method of defense. Upon which a Currier stood up and said, “Sirs, I differ from you altogether: there is no material for resistance equal to a covering of hides; and nothing so good as leather.”
body_child: A city was in danger from an enemy. The people met to talk about how to protect it. A man who made bricks said to use bricks. A man who worked with wood said to use wood. Then a man who made leather said that leather was the best way to stop the enemy.
moral: Every man for himself.
moral_elaborated: People often think their own way is the only right way. They choose things that help themselves instead of thinking about what is best for everyone. It is hard to see the big picture when you only think about your own work.

title: The Ass Carrying the Image
body: AN ASS once carried through the streets of a city a famous wooden Image, to be placed in one of its Temples. As he passed along, the crowd made lowly prostration before the Image. The Ass, thinking that they bowed their heads in token of respect for himself, bristled up with pride, gave himself airs, and refused to move another step. The driver, seeing him thus stop, laid his whip lustily about his shoulders and said, “O you perverse dull-head! it is not yet come to this, that men pay worship to an Ass.”
body_child: A donkey carried a beautiful statue through the town. People bowed down as the statue passed by. The donkey thought the people were bowing to him! He felt very proud and stopped walking. His driver hit him and said, "They are not bowing to you, they are bowing to the statue!"
moral: They are not wise who give to themselves the credit due to others.
moral_elaborated: Do not take credit for things you did not do. Sometimes people are being nice to the work you are doing, not to you. Stay humble and do not get too proud.

title: The Master and His Dogs
body: A CERTAIN MAN, detained by a storm in his country house, first of all killed his sheep, and then his goats, for the maintenance of his household. The storm still continuing, he was obliged to slaughter his yoke oxen for food. On seeing this, his Dogs took counsel together, and said, “It is time for us to be off, for if the master spare not his oxen, who work for his gain, how can we expect him to spare us?”
body_child: A man was stuck at home during a big storm. He had no food, so he killed his sheep to eat. Then he killed his goats. Finally, he killed his big oxen that helped him farm. The dogs saw this and got scared. They said they must run away because if the master killed his helpful oxen, he would kill the dogs too.
moral: He is not to be trusted as a friend who mistreats his own family.
moral_elaborated: If someone is mean to the people who help them, they will be mean to you too. You should stay away from people who do not treat their friends with kindness. Watch how people treat others to see if they are a good friend.

title: The Old Hound
body: A HOUND, who in the days of his youth and strength had never yielded to any beast of the forest, encountered in his old age a boar in the chase. He seized him boldly by the ear, but could not retain his hold because of the decay of his teeth, so that the boar escaped. His master, quickly coming up, was very much disappointed, and fiercely abused the dog. The Hound looked up and said, “It was not my fault master: my spirit was as good as ever, but I could not help my infirmities. I rather deserve to be praised for what I have been, than to be blamed for what I am.”
body_child: An old hunting dog tried to catch a wild pig. He was very brave, but his teeth were old and weak. The pig got away. His master was very angry and yelled at him. The dog said, "I tried my best, but my body is old. Please remember how good I was when I was young and strong."
moral: Respect your elders for their past service.
moral_elaborated: We should be kind to others when they get old and weak. Even if they cannot do everything they used to do, they still deserve respect. Remember the good things they have done throughout their lives.

title: The Two Travelers and the Axe
body: TWO MEN were journeying together. One of them picked up an axe that lay upon the path, and said, “I have found an axe.” “Nay, my friend,” replied the other, “do not say ‘I,’ but ‘We’ have found an axe.” They had not gone far before they saw the owner of the axe pursuing them, and he who had picked up the axe said, “We are undone.” “Nay,” replied the other, “keep to your first mode of speech, my friend; what you thought right then, think right now. Say ‘I,’ not ‘We’ are undone.”
moral: He who shares the danger ought to share the prize.
body_child: Two friends were walking. One man found an axe on the ground. He said, "I found an axe!" His friend said, "You should say *we* found it." Soon, the owner of the axe chased them. The first man said, "We are in trouble!" The friend said, "No, you said you found it alone. Now you can be in trouble alone."
moral_elaborated: If you want a friend to help you when things go wrong, you must share with them when things go well. True friends share both the good times and the bad times.

title: The Old Lion
body: A LION, worn out with years and powerless from disease, lay on the ground at the point of death. A Boar rushed upon him, and avenged with a stroke of his tusks a long-remembered injury. Shortly afterwards the Bull with his horns gored him as if he were an enemy. When the Ass saw that the huge beast could be assailed with impunity, he let drive at his forehead with his heels. The expiring Lion said, “I have reluctantly brooked the insults of the brave, but to be compelled to endure such treatment from thee, a disgrace to Nature, is indeed to die a double death.”
moral: It is cowardly to attack those who cannot defend themselves.
body_child: An old lion was very sick and weak. A wild pig came and hit him. Then a bull came and poked him with its horns. Finally, a donkey came and kicked the lion in the head. The dying lion was very sad. He did not mind the strong animals, but it hurt his feelings that even a weak donkey would kick him when he was down.
moral_elaborated: We should not be mean to people who are old or weak. It is easy to act tough when someone cannot fight back, but it is not the right thing to do.

title: The Wolf and the Shepherds
body: A WOLF, passing by, saw some Shepherds in a hut eating a haunch of mutton for their dinner. Approaching them, he said, “What a clamor you would raise if I were to do as you are doing!”
moral: People often judge others for doing the same things they do.
body_child: A wolf walked by a small house. He saw some men inside eating a sheep for dinner. The wolf said, "If I were the one eating a sheep, you would yell at me and chase me. But you are doing the exact same thing!"
moral_elaborated: Sometimes people tell you not to do something, even though they do it too. We should be fair when we judge other people. Do not get mad at others for things that you do yourself.

title: The Seaside Travelers
body: SOME TRAVELERS, journeying along the seashore, climbed to the summit of a tall cliff, and looking over the sea, saw in the distance what they thought was a large ship. They waited in the hope of seeing it enter the harbor, but as the object on which they looked was driven nearer to shore by the wind, they found that it could at the most be a small boat, and not a ship. When however it reached the beach, they discovered that it was only a large faggot of sticks, and one of them said to his companions, “We have waited for no purpose, for after all there is nothing to see but a load of wood.”
moral: Our mere anticipations of life outrun its realities.
body_child: Some friends stood on a high cliff by the ocean. They saw something far away in the water and thought it was a giant ship. As the wind blew it closer, it looked like a small boat. When it finally hit the beach, it was just a pile of wood. The friends were sad because they expected something great, but it was just a bunch of sticks.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes we imagine things will be much bigger or better than they really are. It is important to wait and see the truth before getting too excited. Real life is not always as fancy as our dreams.

title: The Ass and His Shadow
body: A TRAVELER hired an Ass to convey him to a distant place. The day being intensely hot, and the sun shining in its strength, the Traveler stopped to rest, and sought shelter from the heat under the Shadow of the Ass. As this afforded only protection for one, and as the Traveler and the owner of the Ass both claimed it, a violent dispute arose between them as to which of them had the right to the Shadow. The owner maintained that he had let the Ass only, and not his Shadow. The Traveler asserted that he had, with the hire of the Ass, hired his Shadow also. The quarrel proceeded from words to blows, and while the men fought, the Ass galloped off.
moral: In quarreling about the shadow we often lose the substance.
body_child: A man paid to use a donkey for a trip. It was a very hot day. The man sat in the donkey's shadow to stay cool. The owner of the donkey got mad. He said the man paid for the donkey, but not for the shadow. They started to fight and hit each other. While they were fighting, the donkey ran away. Now both men had nothing.
moral_elaborated: When you fight over small, silly things, you might lose the thing you really need. It is better to share or get along than to lose everything because of an argument.

title: The Ass and His Masters
body: AN ASS, belonging to an herb-seller who gave him too little food and too much work made a petition to Jupiter to be released from his present service and provided with another master. Jupiter, after warning him that he would repent his request, caused him to be sold to a tile-maker. Shortly afterwards, finding that he had heavier loads to carry and harder work in the brick-field, he petitioned for another change of master. Jupiter, telling him that it would be the last time that he could grant his request, ordained that he be sold to a tanner. The Ass found that he had fallen into worse hands, and noting his master’s occupation, said, groaning: “It would have been better for me to have been either starved by the one, or to have been overworked by the other of my former masters, than to have been bought by my present owner, who will even after I am dead tan my hide, and make me useful to him.”
body_child: A donkey worked for a man who did not give him enough food. He asked a god for a new boss. He got a new boss who made him work even harder. He asked for another boss again. This new boss was a man who made leather from animal skins. The donkey was sad because he knew his life would only get harder. He realized he should have stayed with his first boss.
moral: He that is discontented in one place will seldom be happy in another.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes we think things are bad and want a big change. But if we keep complaining, things might get even harder. It is good to be happy with what we have.

title: Mercury and the Sculptor
body: MERCURY once determined to learn in what esteem he was held among mortals. For this purpose he assumed the character of a man and visited in this disguise a Sculptor’s studio having looked at various statues, he demanded the price of two figures of Jupiter and Juno. When the sum at which they were valued was named, he pointed to a figure of himself, saying to the Sculptor, “You will certainly want much more for this, as it is the statue of the Messenger of the Gods, and author of all your gain.” The Sculptor replied, “Well, if you will buy these, I’ll fling you that into the bargain.”
body_child: A god named Mercury wanted to know if people liked him. He went to a shop that sold statues. He dressed like a normal man so no one would know who he was. He saw statues of other gods and asked how much they cost. Then he pointed to a statue of himself. He thought it would cost a lot of money. The artist said, "If you buy the others, I will give you that one for free!"
moral: Vanity is often greeted with contempt.
moral_elaborated: Mercury thought he was very important and special. He was surprised when the artist thought his statue was not worth any money. Do not act like you are better than everyone else.

title: The Fox and the Woodcutter
body: A FOX, running before the hounds, came across a Woodcutter felling an oak and begged him to show him a safe hiding-place. The Woodcutter advised him to take shelter in his own hut, so the Fox crept in and hid himself in a corner. The huntsman soon came up with his hounds and inquired of the Woodcutter if he had seen the Fox. He declared that he had not seen him, and yet pointed, all the time he was speaking, to the hut where the Fox lay hidden. The huntsman took no notice of the signs, but believing his word, hastened forward in the chase. As soon as they were well away, the Fox departed without taking any notice of the Woodcutter: whereon he called to him and reproached him, saying, “You ungrateful fellow, you owe your life to me, and yet you leave me without a word of thanks.” The Fox replied, “Indeed, I should have thanked you fervently if your deeds had been as good as your words, and if your hands had not been traitors to your speech.”
body_child: A fox was running away from hunters. He asked a woodcutter for a place to hide. The man told the fox to hide in his hut. When the hunters came, the man said he did not see the fox, but he pointed his finger at the hut! The hunters did not see him pointing and left. The fox walked away without saying thank you. He told the man, "I would thank you if your actions were as kind as your words."
moral: Actions speak louder than words.
moral_elaborated: The man said he was helping the fox, but his hands tried to show the hunters where the fox was. True friends help with what they do, not just what they say. Always make sure your actions match your words.

title: The Oak and the Reeds
body: A VERY LARGE OAK was uprooted by the wind and thrown across a stream. It fell among some Reeds, which it thus addressed: “I wonder how you, who are so light and weak, are not entirely crushed by these strong winds.” They replied, “You fight and contend with the wind, and consequently you are destroyed; while we on the contrary bend before the least breath of air, and therefore remain unbroken, and escape.”
body_child: A big, strong oak tree fell down in a storm. It landed near some thin reeds by a river. The tree asked, "How did you stay up in the wind when you are so small and weak?" The reeds said, "You tried to fight the wind, and you broke. We bowed down when the wind blew, so we did not break."
moral: Stoop to conquer.
moral_elaborated: Being stiff and stubborn can sometimes cause things to break. It is often better to be flexible and go with the flow. If you learn to bend, you can get through hard times.

title: The Lion in a Farmyard
body: A LION entered a farmyard. The Farmer, wishing to catch him, shut the gate. When the Lion found that he could not escape, he flew upon the sheep and killed them, and then attacked the oxen. The Farmer, beginning to be alarmed for his own safety, opened the gate and released the Lion. On his departure the Farmer grievously lamented the destruction of his sheep and oxen, but his wife, who had been a spectator to all that took place, said, “On my word, you are rightly served, for how could you for a moment think of shutting up a Lion along with you in your farmyard when you know that you shake in your shoes if you only hear his roar at a distance?”
body_child: A lion walked into a farm. The farmer wanted to catch him, so he shut the gate. The lion got angry because he was trapped. He started eating the farmer's sheep and cows. The farmer got scared and let the lion out. His wife said, "It was silly to lock a scary lion in with your animals! You should have known he would be dangerous."
moral: He who provokes a dangerous enemy should not complain of the consequences.
moral_elaborated: The farmer tried to trap something very dangerous and got hurt. He should have known that a lion would cause trouble. Do not go looking for trouble with things that are much stronger than you.

title: The Wolf and the Lion
body: A WOLF, having stolen a lamb from a fold, was carrying him off to his lair. A Lion met him in the path, and seizing the lamb, took it from him. Standing at a safe distance, the Wolf exclaimed, “You have unrighteously taken that which was mine from me!” To which the Lion jeeringly replied, “It was righteously yours, eh? The gift of a friend?”
body_child: A wolf stole a lamb from a farm. He was taking the lamb to his home. A lion met him on the path. The lion grabbed the lamb and took it from the wolf. The wolf stood far away. He yelled, "You took what was mine! That's not fair!" The lion laughed and replied, "Was it really yours? Did a friend give it to you?"
moral: One who takes things unfairly cannot complain when they are taken away.
moral_elaborated: The wolf stole the lamb, so it wasn't truly his to begin with. When the stronger lion took it, the wolf had no real right to complain. This teaches us that if you get something the wrong way, you might lose it, and you can't be upset.

title: The Birdcatcher, the Partridge, and the Cock
body: A BIRDCATCHER was about to sit down to a dinner of herbs when a friend unexpectedly came in. The bird-trap was quite empty, as he had caught nothing, and he had to kill a pied Partridge, which he had tamed for a decoy. The bird entreated earnestly for his life: “What would you do without me when next you spread your nets? Who would chirp you to sleep, or call for you the covey of answering birds?” The Birdcatcher spared his life, and determined to pick out a fine young Cock just attaining to his comb. But the Cock expostulated in piteous tones from his perch: “If you kill me, who will announce to you the appearance of the dawn? Who will wake you to your daily tasks or tell you when it is time to visit the bird-trap in the morning?” He replied, “What you say is true. You are a capital bird at telling the time of day. But my friend and I must have our dinners.”
body_child: A man who caught birds was going to eat a simple dinner. Then, a friend came to visit him. The man had no birds in his trap. He had to kill a tame partridge bird to feed his friend. The partridge begged, "Please don't kill me! Who will help you catch birds next time?" The man let the partridge live. Then he decided to kill a young rooster instead. The rooster cried, "If you kill me, who will wake you up in the morning?" The man said, "You are right. You are good at telling time. But my friend and I need to eat dinner."
moral: Necessity knows no law.
moral_elaborated: When you really need something, like food, you might have to make tough choices. The birdcatcher needed to feed his friend. Sometimes, what we need to survive is more important than other rules.

title: The Ant and the Dove
body: AN ANT went to the bank of a river to quench its thirst, and being carried away by the rush of the stream, was on the point of drowning. A Dove sitting on a tree overhanging the water plucked a leaf and let it fall into the stream close to her. The Ant climbed onto it and floated in safety to the bank. Shortly afterwards a birdcatcher came and stood under the tree, and laid his lime-twigs for the Dove, which sat in the branches. The Ant, perceiving his design, stung him in the foot.
body_child: An ant went to a river to drink water. The strong water pulled the ant away. The ant was almost drowning. A dove was sitting in a tree over the water. The dove pulled off a leaf and dropped it near the ant. The ant climbed onto the leaf and floated safely to the river bank. Soon after, a man who caught birds came. He stood under the tree and set a trap for the dove. The ant saw what the man was doing. The ant stung the man's foot.
moral: One good turn deserves another.
moral_elaborated: The dove helped the ant when the ant was in trouble. Later, the ant helped the dove when the dove was in danger. This fable teaches us to be kind, because acts of kindness often come back to help us.

title: The Hares and the Frogs
body: THE HARES, oppressed by their own exceeding timidity and weary of the perpetual alarm to which they were exposed, with one accord determined to put an end to themselves and their troubles by jumping from a lofty precipice into a deep lake below. As they scampered off in large numbers to carry out their resolve, the Frogs lying on the banks of the lake heard the noise of their feet and rushed helter-skelter to the deep water for safety. On seeing the rapid disappearance of the Frogs, one of the Hares cried out to his companions: “Stay, my friends, do not do as you intended; for you now see that there are creatures who are still more timid than ourselves.”
body_child: The hares were always scared. They were tired of being afraid all the time. So, they all decided to jump off a tall cliff into a deep lake. They wanted to end their troubles. As many hares ran to the cliff, frogs by the lake heard them. The frogs quickly jumped into the water to be safe. A hare saw the frogs disappear so fast. He called to his friends, "Stop! Don't jump! Look! There are animals even more scared than us!"
moral: There is always someone worse off than yourself.
moral_elaborated: The hares thought they were the most scared animals. But when they saw the frogs run, they realized others were even more timid. This story reminds us that even when things are hard, we can find comfort knowing that others might have bigger problems than we do.

title: The Monkey and the Fishermen
body: A MONKEY perched upon a lofty tree saw some Fishermen casting their nets into a river, and narrowly watched their proceedings. The Fishermen after a while gave up fishing, and on going home to dinner left their nets upon the bank. The Monkey, who is the most imitative of animals, descended from the treetop and endeavored to do as they had done. Having handled the net, he threw it into the river, but became tangled in the meshes and drowned. With his last breath he said to himself, “I am rightly served; for what business had I who had never handled a net to try and catch fish?”
body_child: A monkey sat in a tall tree. He watched some fishermen throw their nets into the river. The fishermen stopped fishing and went home to eat. They left their nets on the river bank. Monkeys like to copy what they see. So, the monkey climbed down from the tree. He tried to do what the fishermen did. He grabbed the net and threw it into the river. But he got caught in the net and drowned. As he took his last breath, he thought, "This is what I get. Why did I try to catch fish when I never learned how to use a net?"
moral: Imitation is dangerous without skill.
moral_elaborated: The monkey tried to do something he didn't know how to do. He copied the fishermen but didn't have their skills. It's important to learn things properly and not just copy others if it's something dangerous.

title: The Swan and the Goose
body: A CERTAIN rich man bought in the market a Goose and a Swan. He fed the one for his table and kept the other for the sake of its song. When the time came for killing the Goose, the cook went to get him at night, when it was dark, and he was not able to distinguish one bird from the other. By mistake he caught the Swan instead of the Goose.
moral: The Swan, threatened with death, burst forth into song and thus made himself known by his voice, and preserved his life by his melody.
body_child: A rich man bought two birds: a goose and a swan. He wanted to eat the goose, but he liked to hear the swan sing. One night, it was time to cook the goose. The cook went to get it in the dark. He couldn't tell the birds apart. By mistake, he grabbed the swan instead of the goose!
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, your special talents can help you. The swan used its beautiful voice to show who it was. This saved its life from the cook!

title: The Doe and the Lion
body: A DOE hard pressed by hunters sought refuge in a cave belonging to a Lion. The Lion concealed himself on seeing her approach, but when she was safe within the cave, sprang upon her and tore her to pieces. “Woe is me,” exclaimed the Doe, “who have escaped from man, only to throw myself into the mouth of a wild beast?”
moral: In avoiding one evil, care must be taken not to fall into another.
body_child: Hunters chased a deer. The deer ran into a cave to hide. A lion lived in that cave! The lion hid when the deer came in. When the deer felt safe, the lion jumped out and caught her. The deer cried, "Oh no! I ran from people, but now a lion will eat me!"
moral_elaborated: When you try to escape one problem, be careful. Make sure you don't run into an even bigger problem. Always think about what might happen next.

title: The Fisherman and the Little Fish
body: A FISHERMAN who lived on the produce of his nets, one day caught a single small Fish as the result of his day’s labor. The Fish, panting convulsively, thus entreated for his life: “O Sir, what good can I be to you, and how little am I worth? I am not yet come to my full size. Pray spare my life, and put me back into the sea. I shall soon become a large fish fit for the tables of the rich, and then you can catch me again, and make a handsome profit of me.” The Fisherman replied, “I should indeed be a very simple fellow if, for the chance of a greater uncertain profit, I were to forego my present certain gain.”
moral: Don't give up a small, sure gain for the chance of a larger, uncertain one.
body_child: A fisherman caught only one tiny fish all day. The fish begged him, "Please let me go! I am too small to eat now. Put me back in the sea, and I will grow big! Then you can catch me again and sell me for lots of money!" The fisherman said, "No way! I won't give up what I have now for something I might get later."
moral_elaborated: It's often better to keep what you have for sure. Don't give up something good that you know is yours. Waiting for something bigger later might mean you get nothing at all.

title: The Hunter and the Woodman
body: A HUNTER, not very bold, was searching for the tracks of a Lion. He asked a man felling oaks in the forest if he had seen any marks of his footsteps or knew where his lair was. “I will,” said the man, “at once show you the Lion himself.” The Hunter, turning very pale and chattering with his teeth from fear, replied, “No, thank you. I did not ask that; it is his track only I am in search of, not the Lion himself.”
moral: The hero is brave in deeds as well as words.
body_child: A hunter was looking for a lion, but he wasn't very brave. He asked a man chopping wood, "Have you seen lion footprints? Or do you know where a lion sleeps?" The woodman said, "Yes! I can show you the lion right now!" The hunter turned white. His teeth chattered with fear. He said, "No, thank you! I just want to see its footprints, not the lion itself!"
moral_elaborated: It's easy to sound brave and talk big. But a truly brave person shows it with their actions, not just their words. True heroes are brave when it really matters.

title: The Swollen Fox
body: A VERY HUNGRY FOX, seeing some bread and meat left by shepherds in the hollow of an oak, crept into the hole and made a hearty meal. When he finished, he was so full that he was not able to get out, and began to groan and lament his fate. Another Fox passing by heard his cries, and coming up, inquired the cause of his complaining. On learning what had happened, he said to him, “Ah, you will have to remain there, my friend, until you become such as you were when you crept in, and then you will easily get out.”
moral: Greed can get you into trouble.
body_child: A very hungry fox saw food inside a hollow tree. She crawled in and ate a lot of bread and meat. The fox ate so much that she got very big! She couldn't get out of the hole. She cried and cried. Another fox came by and said, "You have to stay there until you get as skinny as you were when you went in. Then you will get out easily!"
moral_elaborated: Being too greedy can cause problems. Sometimes, having too much of a good thing can get you stuck. It's important to know when you've had enough.

title: The Two Frogs
body: TWO FROGS dwelt in the same pool. When the pool dried up under the summer’s heat, they left it and set out together for another home.
