As they went along they chanced to pass a deep well, amply supplied with water, and when they saw it, one of the Frogs said to the other, “Let us descend and make our abode in this well: it will furnish us with shelter and food.” The other replied with greater caution, “But suppose the water should fail us. How can we get out again from so great a depth?”
moral: Do nothing without a regard to the consequences.
body_child: Two frogs lived in a pond. The sun made the pond dry up. So, the frogs left to find a new home. They saw a deep well with lots of water. One frog said, “Let’s live here! It has water and food.” The other frog was more careful. He said, “What if the water dries up? How will we get out of this deep well?”
moral_elaborated: This moral means to think before you act. Always think about what might happen next. It helps you make good choices and stay safe.

title: The Lamp
body: A LAMP, soaked with too much oil and flaring brightly, boasted that it gave more light than the sun. Then a sudden puff of wind arose, and the Lamp was immediately extinguished. Its owner lit it again, and said: “Boast no more, but henceforth be content to give thy light in silence. Know that not even the stars need to be relit.”
moral: Do not boast or brag.
body_child: A lamp had too much oil. It burned very brightly. The lamp bragged, “I shine brighter than the sun!” Then, a gust of wind blew. The lamp went out right away. Its owner lit it again. He told the lamp, “Stop bragging. Just shine your light quietly. Even the stars do not need to be lit again.”
moral_elaborated: This moral tells us not to brag about ourselves. It's better to be humble and let your actions show what you can do. Bragging can sometimes lead to trouble or make others not like you.

title: The Camel and the Arab
body: AN ARAB Camel-driver, after completing the loading of his Camel, asked him which he would like best, to go up hill or down. The poor beast replied, not without a touch of reason: “Why do you ask me? Is it that the level way through the desert is closed?”
moral: Always choose the easiest path if possible.
body_child: An Arab loaded his camel. When he finished, he asked the camel, “Do you want to go up a hill or down a hill?” The smart camel answered, “Why do you ask me? Is the flat road through the desert closed?”
moral_elaborated: This moral means it's good to pick the easiest way to do things. Why make something harder if there's a simple path? Look for the simple answers first.

title: The Miller, His Son, and Their Ass
body: A MILLER and his son were driving their Ass to a neighboring fair to sell him. They had not gone far when they met with a troop of women collected round a well, talking and laughing. “Look there,” cried one of them, “did you ever see such fellows, to be trudging along the road on foot when they might ride?” The old man hearing this, quickly made his son mount the Ass, and continued to walk along merrily by his side. Presently they came up to a group of old men in earnest debate. “There,” said one of them, “it proves what I was a-saying. What respect is shown to old age in these days? Do you see that idle lad riding while his old father has to walk? Get down, you young scapegrace, and let the old man rest his weary limbs.” Upon this the old man made his son dismount, and got up himself. In this manner they had not proceeded far when they met a company of women and children: “Why, you lazy old fellow,” cried several tongues at once, “how can you ride upon the beast, while that poor little lad there can hardly keep pace by the side of you?” The good-natured Miller immediately took up his son behind him. They had now almost reached the town. “Pray, honest friend,” said a citizen, “is that Ass your own?” “Yes,” replied the old man. “O, one would not have thought so,” said the other, “by the way you load him. Why, you two fellows are better able to carry the poor beast than he you.” “Anything to please you,” said the old man; “we can but try.” So, alighting with his son, they tied the legs of the Ass together and with the help of a pole endeavored to carry him on their shoulders over a bridge near the entrance to the town. This entertaining sight brought the people in crowds to laugh at it, till the Ass, not liking the noise nor the strange handling that he was subject to, broke the cords that bound him and, tumbling off the pole, fell into the river. Upon this, the old man, vexed and ashamed, made the best of his way home again, convinced that by endeavoring to please everybody he had pleased nobody, and lost his Ass in the bargain.
moral: If you try to please everyone, you will please no one.
body_child: A farmer and his son were taking their donkey to the fair. They wanted to sell him. Soon, they saw some women by a well. One woman said, “Look! They are walking, but they could ride the donkey!” The farmer heard this. He told his son to ride the donkey. The farmer walked beside him. Later, they met some old men. One old man said, “Look at that lazy boy! His old father is walking, but the boy is riding.” So, the farmer told his son to get off. The farmer rode the donkey instead. They met more people, women and children. They cried, “Oh, you lazy old man! How can you ride while the poor boy walks?” The kind farmer then let his son ride behind him. They were almost at town. A man asked, “Is that your donkey?” The farmer said yes. The man said, “You load him too much! You two should carry the donkey, not the other way around!” The farmer wanted to please everyone. So, he and his son tied the donkey’s legs. They put a pole through them and tried to carry the donkey. People laughed at them. The donkey did not like this. He broke free and fell into the river! The farmer went home sad. He learned that if you try to please everyone, you please no one. And he lost his donkey!
moral_elaborated: This moral means it's impossible to make everyone happy all the time. Everyone has different ideas, so you should make choices that are right for you. Don't change what you believe just to try and please every single person.

title: The Cat and the Mice
body: A CERTAIN HOUSE was overrun with Mice. A Cat, discovering this, made her way into it and began to catch and eat them one by one. Fearing for their lives, the Mice kept themselves close in their holes. The Cat was no longer able to get at them and perceived that she must tempt them forth by some device. For this purpose she jumped upon a peg, and suspending herself from it, pretended to be dead. One of the Mice, peeping stealthily out, saw her and said, “Ah, my good madam, even though you should turn into a meal-bag, we will not come near you.”
moral: Be cautious of those who have tried to harm you before.
body_child: Many mice lived in a house. A cat found them. She started catching and eating them. The mice were scared. They stayed hidden in their holes. The cat could not catch them anymore. She thought of a trick. She jumped onto a hook and hung there. She pretended to be dead. One mouse peeked out carefully. He saw the cat. He said, “Oh, dear cat, even if you looked like a bag of food, we would not come near you!”
moral_elaborated: This moral teaches us to be very careful around people who have tried to hurt us. Even if they seem to change or act friendly, it's smart to stay away. Trust your gut and remember what happened before.

title: The Mouse and the Bull
body: A BULL was bitten by a Mouse and, angered by the wound, tried to capture him. But the Mouse reached his hole in safety. Though the Bull dug into the walls with his horns, he tired before he could rout out the Mouse, and crouching down, went to sleep outside the hole. The Mouse peeped out, crept furtively up his flank, and again biting him, retreated to his hole. The Bull rising up, and not knowing what to do, was sadly perplexed. At which the Mouse said, “The great do not always prevail. There are times when the small and lowly are the strongest to do mischief.”
moral: Even the smallest can cause trouble for the mighty.
body_child: A big bull was bitten by a tiny mouse. The bull was very mad! He tried to catch the mouse. But the mouse ran into its hole. The bull dug at the hole with his horns. He got tired and fell asleep. The mouse came out quietly. It bit the bull again! Then it ran back to its hole. The bull woke up. He didn't know what to do. The mouse said, "Big doesn't always mean strongest."
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, even a little person or a small animal can bother someone big and strong. It shows that being big doesn't mean you can't be tricked or annoyed by something small. Everyone has their own kind of power.

title: The Dog and the Cook
body: A RICH MAN gave a great feast, to which he invited many friends and acquaintances. His Dog availed himself of the occasion to invite a stranger Dog, a friend of his, saying, “My master gives a feast, and there is always much food remaining; come and sup with me tonight.” The Dog thus invited went at the hour appointed, and seeing the preparations for so grand an entertainment, said in the joy of his heart, “How glad I am that I came! I do not often get such a chance as this. I will take care and eat enough to last me both today and tomorrow.” While he was congratulating himself and wagging his tail to convey his pleasure to his friend, the Cook saw him moving about among his dishes and, seizing him by his fore and hind paws, bundled him without ceremony out of the window. He fell with force upon the ground and limped away, howling dreadfully. His yelling soon attracted other street dogs, who came up to him and inquired how he had enjoyed his supper. He replied, “Why, to tell you the truth, I drank so much wine that I remember nothing. I do not know how I got out of the house.”
moral: Don't boast or celebrate too soon.
body_child: A rich man had a big party. His dog asked his friend, another dog, to come. "My master has a party," he said. "There will be lots of extra food!" The friend dog came. He was so happy to see all the food. He thought, "I will eat enough for today and tomorrow!" He wagged his tail happily. But the cook saw him near the food. The cook grabbed the dog and threw him out the window! The dog fell hard and ran away, yelping. Other dogs asked how his dinner was. He said, "Oh, I drank too much. I don't remember leaving the house!"
moral_elaborated: It's not good to get too excited or brag about something before it actually happens. Things can change very quickly. It's better to be quiet and thankful when good things come, instead of showing off.

title: The Thieves and the Cock
body: SOME THIEVES broke into a house and found nothing but a Cock, whom they stole, and got off as fast as they could. Upon arriving at home they prepared to kill the Cock, who thus pleaded for his life: “Pray spare me; I am very serviceable to men. I wake them up in the night to their work.” “That is the very reason why we must the more kill you,” they replied; “for when you wake your neighbors, you entirely put an end to our business.”
moral: The safeguards of virtue are hateful to those with evil intentions.
body_child: Some robbers broke into a house. They only found a rooster. So they stole the rooster and ran away fast. When they got home, they planned to kill the rooster. The rooster begged, "Please don't kill me! I help people. I wake them up for work." The robbers said, "That's exactly why we *must* kill you! When you wake people up, you stop us from doing our sneaky work."
moral_elaborated: Good things that protect people, like a rooster waking everyone up, are bad for people who want to do mean things. Those who plan mischief don't like anything that stops them. It means good actions can spoil bad plans.

title: The Dancing Monkeys
body: A PRINCE had some Monkeys trained to dance. Being naturally great mimics of men’s actions, they showed themselves most apt pupils, and when arrayed in their rich clothes and masks, they danced as well as any of the courtiers. The spectacle was often repeated with great applause, till on one occasion a courtier, bent on mischief, took from his pocket a handful of nuts and threw them upon the stage. The Monkeys at the sight of the nuts forgot their dancing and became (as indeed they were) Monkeys instead of actors. Pulling off their masks and tearing their robes, they fought with one another for the nuts. The dancing spectacle thus came to an end amidst the laughter and ridicule of the audience.
moral: You cannot hide your true nature forever.
body_child: A prince taught some monkeys to dance. Monkeys are good at copying people. So they learned fast! They wore fancy clothes and masks. They danced just like the prince's friends. Everyone loved to watch them. One day, a man in the crowd wanted to cause trouble. He threw some nuts onto the stage. The monkeys saw the nuts and forgot all about dancing. They took off their masks and tore their clothes. They fought over the nuts! The show ended with everyone laughing at the monkeys.
moral_elaborated: Even if you try to act like someone else, your real self will show through eventually. Like the monkeys, even dressed up, they were still monkeys at heart. It's always best to be true to yourself.

title: The Farmer and the Fox
body: A FARMER, who bore a grudge against a Fox for robbing his poultry yard, caught him at last, and being determined to take an ample revenge, tied some rope well soaked in oil to his tail, and set it on fire. The Fox by a strange fatality rushed to the fields of the Farmer who had captured him. It was the time of the wheat harvest; but the Farmer reaped nothing that year and returned home grieving sorely.
moral: Revenge can hurt the one seeking it just as much.
body_child: A farmer was mad at a fox for eating his chickens. He finally caught the fox. The farmer wanted to get even. He tied a rope soaked in oil to the fox's tail. Then he set the rope on fire. The fox ran straight into the farmer's own fields! It was the time to pick the wheat. But the fire burned it all. The farmer had no food to gather that year. He went home very sad.
moral_elaborated: When you try to get back at someone, your plan can sometimes hurt you instead. The farmer wanted to hurt the fox, but his plan ended up burning his own farm. It shows that being kind is often better than trying to get even.

title: The Traveler and Fortune
body: A TRAVELER wearied from a long journey lay down, overcome with fatigue, on the very brink of a deep well. Just as he was about to fall into the water, Dame Fortune, it is said, appeared to him and waking him from his slumber thus addressed him: “Good Sir, pray wake up: for if you fall into the well, the blame will be thrown on me, and I shall get an ill name among mortals; for I find that men are sure to impute their calamities to me, however much by their own folly they have really brought them on themselves.”
moral: Everyone is more or less master of his own fate.
body_child:
A man was very tired after a long trip. He lay down to rest. He was right next to a deep hole in the ground. He almost fell in!
Then, a lady named Fortune showed up. She woke him up.
She said, "Wake up! If you fall in, people will blame me. They will say bad things about me. People always blame me for their troubles, even when it's their own fault!"
moral_elaborated: This means you are mostly in charge of what happens in your life. Your choices and actions make a big difference. Don't always blame others for your problems.

title: The Seagull and the Kite
body: A SEAGULL having bolted down too large a fish, burst its deep gullet-bag and lay down on the shore to die. A Kite saw him and exclaimed: “You richly deserve your fate; for a bird of the air has no business to seek its food from the sea.”
moral: Every man should be content to mind his own business.
body_child:
A seagull ate a fish that was too big. Its throat tore, and it fell to the shore to die.
A kite bird saw it. The kite said, "You deserve this! A bird that flies in the air should not try to find food in the sea."
moral_elaborated: This means you should focus on your own life and what you are good at. Don't try to do things that are not meant for you. It's best to stick to what you know.

title: The Lion, the Bear, and the Fox
body: A LION and a Bear seized a Kid at the same moment, and fought fiercely for its possession. When they had fearfully lacerated each other and were faint from the long combat, they lay down exhausted with fatigue. A Fox, who had gone round them at a distance several times, saw them both stretched on the ground with the Kid lying untouched in the middle. He ran in between them, and seizing the Kid scampered off as fast as he could. The Lion and the Bear saw him, but not being able to get up, said, “Woe be to us, that we should have fought and belabored ourselves only to serve the turn of a Fox.”
moral: It sometimes happens that one man has all the toil, and another all the profit.
body_child:
A strong lion and a big bear both grabbed a baby goat at the same time. They fought very hard for it. They hurt each other badly. They were very tired from the long fight.
They both lay down on the ground, too tired to move.
A clever fox had been watching them from far away. The fox saw them both lying down. The baby goat was in the middle, not touched.
The fox ran in, grabbed the goat, and ran away as fast as he could!
The lion and the bear saw him. But they couldn't get up. They said, "Oh no! We fought so hard and got so hurt, just so the fox could get the goat!"
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, people work very hard and get nothing for it. Then, someone else comes along and gets all the good stuff without doing any work. It's not fair, but it can happen.

title: The Philosopher, the Ants, and Mercury
body: A PHILOSOPHER witnessed from the shore the shipwreck of a vessel, of which the crew and passengers were all drowned. He inveighed against the injustice of Providence, which would for the sake of one criminal perchance sailing in the ship allow so many innocent persons to perish. As he was indulging in these reflections, he found himself surrounded by a whole army of Ants, near whose nest he was standing. One of them climbed up and stung him, and he immediately trampled them all to death with his foot. Mercury presented himself, and striking the Philosopher with his wand, said, “And are you indeed to make yourself a judge of the dealings of Providence, who hast thyself in a similar manner treated these poor Ants?”
moral: Don't judge others when you do similar wrongs yourself.
body_child:
A smart man called a philosopher watched from the beach. A ship crashed, and everyone on it drowned.
He was angry at how unfair life seemed. He thought, "Maybe there was one bad person on the ship. But why did so many good people have to die too?"
As he thought this, he stood near an ant nest. Many ants came around him. One ant climbed up and bit him.
The philosopher got mad and stomped on all the ants, killing them.
Then, a god named Mercury appeared. He tapped the philosopher with his magic stick. Mercury said, "You think you can judge life and how things happen? But you just did the same thing to these poor ants!"
moral_elaborated: This means you should not be quick to judge or blame others for their actions. Especially if you do similar things yourself. Think about your own actions before you criticize someone else.

title: The Peasant and the Eagle
body: A PEASANT found an Eagle captured in a trap, and much admiring the bird, set him free. The Eagle did not prove ungrateful to his deliverer, for seeing the Peasant sitting under a wall which was not safe, he flew toward him and with his talons snatched a bundle from his head. When the Peasant rose in pursuit, the Eagle let the bundle fall again. Taking it up, the man returned to the same place, to find that the wall under which he had been sitting had fallen to pieces; and he marvelled at the service rendered him by the Eagle.
moral: A kindness is never thrown away.
body_child:
A farmer found a big eagle caught in a trap. He liked the eagle very much. So, he helped it get free.
The eagle did not forget the farmer's kindness. One day, the farmer was sitting under a wall that was not safe. The eagle saw him.
The eagle flew down and used its claws to snatch a bundle from the farmer's head.
The farmer got up to chase the eagle. The eagle then dropped the bundle.
The man picked up his bundle. He went back to where he was sitting. But the wall he had been under had fallen down!
He was amazed at how the eagle had saved him.
moral_elaborated: When you are kind to someone, they will often remember it. Your good deed might come back to help you later. It's always good to be kind.

title: The Fox and the Leopard
body: THE FOX and the Leopard disputed which was the more beautiful of the two. The Leopard exhibited one by one the various spots which decorated his skin. But the Fox, interrupting him, said, “And how much more beautiful than you am I, who am decorated, not in body, but in mind.”
moral: True beauty comes from within.
body_child: The Fox and the Leopard argued. They wanted to know who was prettier. The Leopard showed his spots. He had many pretty spots on his skin. But the Fox stopped him. The Fox said, "I am much prettier than you!" He said, "My beauty is inside my mind, not on my body."
moral_elaborated: It's better to be smart and kind than just pretty on the outside. What you think and how you act are more important than how you look. Be a good person inside your heart.

title: The Lion and the Hare
body: A LION came across a Hare, who was fast asleep. He was just in the act of seizing her, when a fine young Hart trotted by, and he left the Hare to follow him. The Hare, scared by the noise, awoke and scudded away. The Lion was unable after a long chase to catch the Hart, and returned to feed upon the Hare. On finding that the Hare also had run off, he said, “I am rightly served, for having let go of the food that I had in my hand for the chance of obtaining more.”
moral: Do not be greedy.
body_child: A Lion saw a Hare sleeping. He was about to catch her. Then a fast young deer ran by. The Lion let go of the Hare to chase the deer. The Hare woke up from the noise. She quickly ran away. The Lion could not catch the deer. He chased it for a long time. So, he went back to eat the Hare. But the Hare was gone too! The Lion said, "I deserved this!" He let go of food he had for a chance at more.
moral_elaborated: It's smart to keep what you have instead of risking it for something bigger. Don't be too greedy and wish for more when you already have enough. Sometimes, wanting too much can make you lose everything.

title: The Image of Mercury and the Carpenter
body: A VERY POOR MAN, a Carpenter by trade, had a wooden image of Mercury, before which he made offerings day by day, and begged the idol to make him rich, but in spite of his entreaties he became poorer and poorer. At last, being very angry, he took his image down from its pedestal and dashed it against the wall. When its head was knocked off, out came a stream of gold, which the Carpenter quickly picked up and said, “Well, I think thou art altogether contradictory and unreasonable; for when I paid you honour, I reaped no benefits: but now that I maltreat you I am loaded with an abundance of riches.”
moral: Adversity can reveal hidden blessings.
body_child: A very poor Carpenter had a wooden statue of Mercury. Every day, he gave gifts to the statue. He asked the statue to make him rich. But he stayed poor, even more poor! He got very angry. He took the statue and threw it at the wall. The statue's head broke off. Gold coins spilled out! The Carpenter quickly picked them up. He said, "You are very strange! When I was nice to you, I got nothing. But when I hurt you, you gave me lots of money!"
moral_elaborated: Good things can happen in surprising ways. Sometimes, when you try something new or get upset, a hidden treasure might appear. Don't always expect things to work the way you think they will.

title: The Lion, the Fox, and the Ass
body: THE LION, the Fox and the Ass entered into an agreement to assist each other in the chase. Having secured a large booty, the Lion on their return from the forest asked the Ass to allot his due portion to each of the three partners in the treaty. The Ass carefully divided the spoil into three equal shares and modestly requested the two others to make the first choice. The Lion, bursting out into a great rage, devoured the Ass. Then he requested the Fox to do him the favour to make a division. The Fox accumulated all that they had killed into one large heap and left to himself the smallest possible morsel. The Lion said, “Who has taught you, my very excellent fellow, the art of division? You are perfect to a fraction.” He replied, “I learned it from the Ass, by witnessing his fate.”
moral: Happy is the man who learns from the misfortunes of others.
body_child: The Lion, the Fox, and the Donkey agreed to hunt together. They caught many animals. When they came back, the Lion asked the Donkey to share the food. The Donkey divided the food into three equal parts. He asked the Lion and Fox to pick first. The Lion got very angry! He ate the Donkey! Then the Lion asked the Fox to divide the food. The Fox put almost all the food in one big pile for the Lion. He took only a tiny piece for himself. The Lion said, "Who taught you to share so well?" The Fox answered, "I learned it from the Donkey, by seeing what happened to him."
moral_elaborated: It's smart to watch what happens to other people. If someone makes a mistake and gets into trouble, you can learn from it. Then you won't make the same mistake yourself.

title: The Bull and the Goat
body: A BULL, escaping from a Lion, hid in a cave which some shepherds had recently occupied. As soon as he entered, a He-Goat left in the cave sharply attacked him with his horns. The Bull quietly addressed him: “Butt away as much as you will. I have no fear of you, but of the Lion. Let that monster go away and I will soon let you know what is the respective strength of a Goat and a Bull.”
moral: It shows an evil disposition to take advantage of a friend in distress.
body_child: A Bull was running from a Lion. He hid in a cave where shepherds had been. A Goat was also in the cave. The Goat used his horns to hit the Bull right away. The Bull calmly said, "Hit me all you want. I am not scared of you. I am scared of the Lion." He said, "Let that big monster go away. Then I will show you who is stronger, a Goat or a Bull!"
moral_elaborated: It's mean to bother someone when they are already having a hard time. A good friend helps when you are in trouble, instead of making things worse. Don't pick on someone who is already down.

title: The Bald Knight
body: A BALD KNIGHT, who wore a wig, went out to hunt. A sudden puff of wind blew off his hat and wig, at which a loud laugh rang forth from his companions. He pulled up his horse, and with great glee joined in the joke by saying, “What a marvel it is that hairs which are not mine should fly from me, when they have forsaken even the man on whose head they grew.”
body_child: A knight was bald. He wore a wig. One day, he went hunting. A strong wind blew his hat and wig off! His friends laughed loudly. The knight laughed too! He said, "It's funny that hair not mine would fly away, when my own hair already left my head!"
moral: It is good to laugh at yourself.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes silly things happen to us. If you can laugh at yourself, it makes things better. It shows you are strong and happy.

title: The Oaks and Jupiter
body: THE OAKS presented a complaint to Jupiter, saying, “We bear for no purpose the burden of life, as of all the trees that grow we are the most continually in peril of the axe.” Jupiter made answer: “You have only to thank yourselves for the misfortunes to which you are exposed: for if you did not make such excellent pillars and posts, and prove yourselves so serviceable to the carpenters and the farmers, the axe would not so frequently be laid to your roots.”
body_child: Some big oak trees talked to Jupiter. They said, "Life is hard for us! We are always in danger of the axe." Jupiter answered, "It's your own fault." He said, "You are very good for making things like posts and pillars. If you were not so useful, no one would cut you down."
moral: Being very good at something can sometimes bring trouble.
moral_elaborated: When you are very useful or special, many people might want you. This can be good, but it can also make things harder sometimes. Just like the strong oak trees were cut down because they were good for building.

title: The Monkeys and Their Mother
body: THE MONKEY, it is said, has two young ones at each birth. The Mother fondles one and nurtures it with the greatest affection and care, but hates and neglects the other. It happened once that the young one which was caressed and loved was smothered by the too great affection of the Mother, while the despised one was nurtured and reared in spite of the neglect to which it was exposed.
body_child: A mother monkey had two babies. She loved one baby very much. She hugged it and took great care of it. But she did not like the other baby. She left it alone. One day, she hugged her favorite baby too hard. The baby was smothered and died. The baby she did not like grew up strong and healthy, even though it was alone.
moral: The best intentions will not always ensure success.
moral_elaborated: Even if you try your very best to do something good, it might not always work out the way you want. Sometimes, trying too hard can even cause problems. It's like the mother monkey who loved her baby too much.

title: The Hare and the Hound
body: A HOUND started a Hare from his lair, but after a long run, gave up the chase. A goat-herd seeing him stop, mocked him, saying “The little one is the best runner of the two.” The Hound replied, “You do not see the difference between us: I was only running for a dinner, but he for his life.”
body_child: A dog was chasing a rabbit. The dog ran very fast for a long time. But then the dog stopped chasing. A man watching said, "The rabbit is a better runner than you!" The dog answered, "No, you don't understand. I was running to get a meal, but the rabbit was running to save his life!"
moral: You try harder when something very important is at stake.
moral_elaborated: When you are trying to get something small, you might not try your hardest. But when something really big or important is on the line, you will give it your all. Like the rabbit running to stay alive, it ran much faster than the dog who just wanted dinner.

title: The Shepherd and the Dog
body: A SHEPHERD penning his sheep in the fold for the night was about to shut up a wolf with them, when his Dog perceiving the wolf said, “Master, how can you expect the sheep to be safe if you admit a wolf into the fold?”
body_child: A shepherd was putting his sheep in their pen for the night. He was going to close the gate. His dog saw a wolf. The shepherd was about to put the wolf in with the sheep! The dog said, "Master, how can the sheep be safe if you let a wolf into their pen?"
moral: Never trust an enemy with something precious.
moral_elaborated: It is never a good idea to put someone who means harm in a place where they can hurt what you care about. An enemy will always try to do bad things if they get the chance. So, keep important things far away from those who are not friends.

title: The Oak and the Woodcutters
body: THE WOODCUTTER cut down a Mountain Oak and split it in pieces, making wedges of its own branches for dividing the trunk. The Oak said with a sigh, “I do not care about the blows of the axe aimed at my roots, but I do grieve at being torn in pieces by these wedges made from my own branches.”
moral: Misfortunes springing from ourselves are the hardest to bear.
body_child: A woodcutter chopped down a big oak tree. He used parts of the tree's own branches. He made small wedges from them. Then he used these wedges to split the tree's trunk. The oak tree sighed. It said, “I do not mind the axe hitting my roots. But it hurts so much to be cut apart by pieces from my own self.”
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, bad things happen because of our own choices or actions. These kinds of problems can feel the worst. It's harder when we hurt ourselves, even by accident.

title: The Wasp and the Snake
body: A WASP seated himself upon the head of a Snake and, striking him unceasingly with his stings, wounded him to death. The Snake, being in great torment and not knowing how to rid himself of his enemy, saw a wagon heavily laden with wood, and went and purposely placed his head under the wheels, saying, “At least my enemy and I shall perish together.”
moral: Revenge can hurt you too.
body_child: A wasp landed on a snake's head. It stung the snake again and again. The snake was hurt very badly. It did not know how to get the wasp off. The snake saw a big wagon with lots of wood. It put its head under the wagon wheels on purpose. The snake said, “At least we will both die together.”
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, we want to hurt someone who has hurt us. But trying to get revenge can also harm us. It's better to find safer ways to solve problems.

title: The Peacock and the Crane
body: A PEACOCK spreading its gorgeous tail mocked a Crane that passed by, ridiculing the ashen hue of its plumage and saying, “I am robed, like a king, in gold and purple and all the colors of the rainbow; while you have not a bit of color on your wings.” “True,” replied the Crane; “but I soar to the heights of heaven and lift up my voice to the stars, while you walk below, like a cock, among the birds of the dunghill.”
moral: Fine feathers don’t make fine birds.
body_child: A peacock showed off its beautiful tail. It made fun of a crane walking by. The peacock said, “My feathers are like a king's, full of gold and purple! But your wings have no color at all.” The crane answered, “Yes, that's true. But I can fly high up in the sky, all the way to the stars. You just walk on the ground with the other birds.”
moral_elaborated: Having pretty things on the outside isn't everything. What you can *do* or how you *act* is more important. Being kind and useful matters more than just looking good.

title: The Hen and the Golden Eggs
body: A COTTAGER and his wife had a Hen that laid a golden egg every day. They supposed that the Hen must contain a great lump of gold in its inside, and in order to get the gold they killed it. Having done so, they found to their surprise that the Hen differed in no respect from their other hens.
moral: The foolish pair, thus hoping to become rich all at once, deprived themselves of the gain of which they were assured day by day.
body_child: A farmer and his wife had a special hen. This hen laid one golden egg every day! The farmer and his wife thought, “There must be a lot of gold inside this hen.” So, they killed the hen to get all the gold at once. But when they looked inside, the hen was just like any other hen. They did not find any extra gold.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, we get a little bit of something good every day. If we try to get everything all at once, we might lose it all. Be happy with what you get steadily, and don't be too greedy.

title: The Ass and the Frogs
body: AN ASS, carrying a load of wood, passed through a pond. As he was crossing through the water he lost his footing, stumbled and fell, and not being able to rise on account of his load, groaned heavily. Some Frogs frequenting the pool heard his lamentation, and said, “What would you do if you had to live here always as we do, when you make such a fuss about a mere fall into the water?”
moral: Men often bear little grievances with less courage than they do large misfortunes.
body_child: An old donkey was carrying wood. He walked through a pond. In the water, he tripped and fell down. He could not get up because his load was too heavy. The donkey groaned very loudly. Some frogs living in the pond heard him. They said, “You are making a big fuss about falling in! What if you had to live in this water all the time, like us?”
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, we complain a lot about small problems. But people who have big problems might not complain as much. It's good to remember that others might have harder lives than us.

title: The Crow and the Raven
body: A CROW was jealous of the Raven, because he was considered a bird of good omen and always attracted the attention of men, who noted by his flight the good or evil course of future events. Seeing some travelers approaching, the Crow flew up into a tree, and perching herself on one of the branches, cawed as loudly as she could. The travelers turned towards the sound and wondered what it foreboded, when one of them said to his companion, “Let us proceed on our journey, my friend, for it is only the caw of a crow, and her cry, you know, is no omen.”
moral: Those who assume a character which does not belong to them, only make themselves ridiculous.
body_child: A crow was jealous of a raven. People thought the raven was special. They watched the raven fly to guess what would happen next. The crow saw some people walking nearby. She flew to a tree branch and cawed very loudly. The travelers looked up. They wondered what the sound meant. But one person said, “Let's keep going. It's just a crow. Her caw doesn't mean anything special.”
moral_elaborated: This means you should always be yourself. Don't pretend to be someone you are not. When you try to be someone else, people might not take you seriously or believe you.

title: The Trees and the Axe
body: A MAN came into a forest and asked the Trees to provide him a handle for his axe. The Trees consented to his request and gave him a young ash-tree. No sooner had the man fitted a new handle to his axe from it, than he began to use it and quickly felled with his strokes the noblest giants of the forest. An old oak, lamenting when too late the destruction of his companions, said to a neighboring cedar, “The first step has lost us all. If we had not given up the rights of the ash, we might yet have retained our own privileges and have stood for ages.”
moral: Beware of giving up small things, as it might lead to losing much more.
body_child: A man went to a forest. He asked the trees for a handle for his axe. The trees said yes. They gave him a small ash tree. The man made a new handle for his axe. Then, he used the axe to chop down the biggest trees in the forest. An old oak tree was sad. It was too late. All its friends were gone. The oak told a nearby cedar, “It all started when we gave him that small tree. If we hadn't, we would still be here today.”
moral_elaborated: This means be careful about giving away even a little bit. Sometimes, giving away a small thing can cause you to lose many important things later on. Think carefully before you agree to something.

title: The Wolves and the Sheepdogs
body: THE WOLVES thus addressed the Sheepdogs: “Why should you, who are like us in so many things, not be entirely of one mind with us, and live with us as brothers should? We differ from you in one point only. We live in freedom, but you bow down to and slave for men, who in return for your services flog you with whips and put collars on your necks. They make you also guard their sheep, and while they eat the mutton throw only the bones to you. If you will be persuaded by us, you will give us the sheep, and we will enjoy them in common, till we all are surfeited.” The Dogs listened favourably to these proposals, and, entering the den of the Wolves, they were set upon and torn to pieces.
moral: Never trust your enemies, even when they seem friendly.
body_child: The wolves spoke to the sheepdogs. “Why do you work for humans?” they asked. “You are like us! We are free, but you wear collars and get hit. You guard their sheep, but they only give you bones to eat. Come join us! We can share the sheep. We will all eat until we are full.” The dogs thought this was a good idea. They went into the wolves' den. But the wolves attacked them and tore them to pieces.
moral_elaborated: This story teaches us to be careful of people who are not our friends, even if they seem kind. They might pretend to be nice to hurt you later. Always be smart and protect yourself.

title: The Bull, the Lioness, and the Wild-Boar Hunter
body: A BULL finding a lion’s cub asleep gored him to death with his horns. The Lioness came up, and bitterly lamented the death of her whelp. A wild-boar Hunter, seeing her distress, stood at a distance and said to her, “Think how many men there are who have reason to lament the loss of their children, whose deaths have been caused by you.”
moral: Do not complain about a bad thing happening to you if you have done the same to others.
body_child: A bull found a baby lion sleeping. The bull used its horns and killed the cub. The mother lioness came and cried sadly for her baby. A hunter who hunted wild boars saw her. He stood far away and said to the lioness, “Think about how many people cry for their children. You have caused many of those deaths.”
moral_elaborated: This means it's not fair to be sad about something bad happening to you if you have made that same bad thing happen to others. We should always think about how our actions affect everyone. It reminds us to be kind.

title: The Bowman and Lion
body: A VERY SKILLFUL BOWMAN went to the mountains in search of game, but all the beasts of the forest fled at his approach. The Lion alone challenged him to combat. The Bowman immediately shot out an arrow and said to the Lion: “I send thee my messenger, that from him thou mayest learn what I myself shall be when I assail thee.” The wounded Lion rushed away in great fear, and when a Fox who had seen it all happen told him to be of good courage and not to back off at the first attack he replied: “You counsel me in vain; for if he sends so fearful a messenger, how shall I abide the attack of the man himself?”
moral: Be on guard against men who can strike from a distance.
body_child: A very good archer went to the mountains. He wanted to hunt animals. All the animals ran away when he came near. Only a lion stayed and wanted to fight him. The archer quickly shot an arrow at the lion. He told the lion, “This arrow is my helper. It will show you how strong I am when I truly fight you.” The lion was hurt and ran away, very scared. A fox saw everything. The fox told the lion to be brave and not run away after just one hit. But the lion answered, “It's no use telling me that. If his helper (the arrow) is so scary, how will I fight the man himself?”
moral_elaborated: This means you should be careful of people who can hurt you from far away. They might have hidden strengths or tools you don't expect. It's smart to be cautious when you don't know someone's full power.

title: The Camel
body: WHEN MAN first saw the Camel, he was so frightened at his vast size that he ran away. After a time, perceiving the meekness and gentleness of the beast’s temper, he summoned courage enough to approach him. Soon afterwards, observing that he was an animal altogether deficient in spirit, he assumed such boldness as to put a bridle in his mouth, and to let a child drive him.
moral: Use serves to overcome dread.
body_child: A man saw a camel for the first time. The camel was very big. The man was scared and ran away. Later, he saw the camel was kind and calm. He got brave and went closer. Then, he saw the camel was not scary at all. He put a rope in its mouth. A child could even drive it.
moral_elaborated: When you get used to something new, it stops being scary. The more you do something, the less you will be afraid of it.

title: The Crab and the Fox
body: A CRAB, forsaking the seashore, chose a neighboring green meadow as its feeding ground. A Fox came across him, and being very hungry ate him up. Just as he was on the point of being eaten, the Crab said, “I well deserve my fate, for what business had I on the land, when by my nature and habits I am only adapted for the sea?”
moral: Contentment with our lot is an element of happiness.
body_child: A crab left the ocean beach. It went to a green field to find food. A hungry fox saw the crab. The fox ate the crab. Just before it was eaten, the crab said, "I deserve this. Why was I on land? I belong in the sea."
moral_elaborated: It is good to be happy with what you have and where you belong. Trying to be something you are not can lead to trouble. Stay true to yourself and your place.

title: The Ass and the Old Shepherd
body: A SHEPHERD, watching his Ass feeding in a meadow, was alarmed all of a sudden by the cries of the enemy. He appealed to the Ass to fly with him, lest they should both be captured, but the animal lazily replied, “Why should I, pray? Do you think it likely the conqueror will place on me two sets of panniers?” “No,” rejoined the Shepherd. “Then,” said the Ass, “as long as I carry the panniers, what matters it to me whom I serve?”
moral: In a change of government the poor change nothing beyond the name of their master.
body_child: A shepherd watched his donkey eat grass. Suddenly, he heard the enemy coming! The shepherd told the donkey to run away with him. He was scared they would both be caught. But the donkey was lazy. It said, "Why should I run? Do you think the new people will make me carry two bags instead of one?" The shepherd said, "No." The donkey then said, "If I still carry the same bags, it doesn't matter who I work for."
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, when big changes happen, it doesn't really change things for everyone. For some, life stays mostly the same. They still have their work to do, no matter who is in charge.

title: The Fox and the Hedgehog
body: A FOX swimming across a rapid river was carried by the force of the current into a very deep ravine, where he lay for a long time very much bruised, sick, and unable to move. A swarm of hungry blood-sucking flies settled upon him. A Hedgehog, passing by, saw his anguish and inquired if he should drive away the flies that were tormenting him. “By no means,” replied the Fox; “pray do not molest them.” “How is this?” said the Hedgehog; “do you not want to be rid of them?” “No,” returned the Fox, “for these flies which you see are full of blood, and sting me but little, and if you rid me of these which are already satiated, others more hungry will come in their place, and will drink up all the blood I have left.”
moral: Sometimes it's better to deal with a problem you know, than to invite a worse one you don't.
body_child: A fox was swimming across a fast river. The strong water carried him into a deep ditch. He was hurt and sick and couldn't move. Many hungry flies came and bit him. A hedgehog walked by and saw the fox hurting. The hedgehog asked if he should shoo away the flies. "No, please don't touch them!" said the fox. "Why?" asked the hedgehog. "Don't you want them gone?" "No," the fox said. "These flies have already eaten a lot of my blood. They don't hurt much now. If you scare them away, new, hungrier flies will come. They will drink all the blood I have left."
moral_elaborated: It is sometimes smarter to keep a small problem you understand. If you try to fix it, you might get a bigger problem. Think carefully before making big changes.

title: The Woman and Her Hen
body: A WOMAN possessed a Hen that gave her an egg every day. She often pondered how she might obtain two eggs daily instead of one, and at last, to gain her purpose, determined to give the Hen a double allowance of barley. From that day the Hen became fat and sleek, and never once laid another egg.
moral: Greed can make you lose everything.
body_child: A woman had a hen. This hen laid one egg every day. The woman wished she could get two eggs a day. She thought about it a lot. Finally, she decided to give the hen twice as much food. From that day on, the hen got very fat. It looked healthy, but it never laid another egg again.
moral_elaborated: Being too greedy can make you lose what you already have. It's better to be happy with enough than to wish for too much. Sometimes, trying to get more can leave you with nothing.

title: The Kites and the Swans
body: TEE KITES of olden times, as well as the Swans, had the privilege of song. But having heard the neigh of the horse, they were so enchanted with the sound, that they tried to imitate it; and, in trying to neigh, they forgot how to sing.
moral: The desire for imaginary benefits often involves the loss of present blessings.
body_child: Kites and swans used to sing beautiful songs. One day, they heard a horse neigh. They loved the sound so much! They wanted to neigh just like the horse. But when they tried to neigh, they forgot how to sing their own songs.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes we want something new and exciting, but it might not be good for us. We might lose something good we already have. It's important to be happy with what you have.

title: The Dog and the Hare
body: A HOUND having started a Hare on the hillside pursued her for some distance, at one time biting her with his teeth as if he would take her life, and at another fawning upon her, as if in play with another dog. The Hare said to him, “I wish you would act sincerely by me, and show yourself in your true colors. If you are a friend, why do you bite me so hard? If an enemy, why do you fawn on me?”
moral: No one can be a friend if you know not whether to trust or distrust him.
body_child: A dog chased a hare. Sometimes the dog bit the hare, like it wanted to hurt her. Other times, the dog acted friendly, like it wanted to play. The hare said, "Please be honest with me. Are you my friend or my enemy? If you are a friend, why do you bite me? If you are an enemy, why do you act so nice?"
moral_elaborated: It's hard to be friends with someone who acts both kind and mean. A true friend is always honest and acts the same way all the time. You need to know if you can truly trust someone.

title: The Hares and the Foxes
body: THE HARES waged war with the Eagles, and called upon the Foxes to help them. They replied, “We would willingly have helped you, if we had not known who you were, and with whom you were fighting.”
moral: Count the cost before you commit yourselves.
body_child: The hares decided to fight the eagles. They asked the foxes to help them. The foxes said, "We would help you. But we know you are hares, and we know who you are fighting."
moral_elaborated: Always think carefully before you agree to do something big. Make sure you know all the facts about what you are getting into. Sometimes it's better not to get involved if it's too risky.

title: The Bull and the Calf
body: A BULL was striving with all his might to squeeze himself through a narrow passage which led to his stall. A young Calf came up, and offered to go before and show him the way by which he could manage to pass. “Save yourself the trouble,” said the Bull; “I knew that way long before you were born.”
moral: Older people often know more than younger ones.
body_child: A big bull tried hard to get through a small path to his home. A young calf came up. The calf wanted to show the bull the best way to get through. The bull said, "Don't bother! I knew how to get through this path long before you were born."
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, older people have more experience and wisdom. They have lived longer and learned many things. It's a good idea to listen to what they have to say.

title: The Stag, the Wolf, and the Sheep
body: A STAG asked a Sheep to lend him a measure of wheat, and said that the Wolf would be his surety. The Sheep, fearing some fraud was intended, excused herself, saying, “The Wolf is accustomed to seize what he wants and to run off; and you, too, can quickly outstrip me in your rapid flight. How then shall I be able to find you, when the day of payment comes?”
moral: Two blacks do not make one white.
body_child: A stag asked a sheep to lend him some wheat. The stag said that the wolf would promise he would pay it back. The sheep was scared something bad was planned. She said, "The wolf always takes what he wants and runs away. And you, Mr. Stag, are very fast! You can run away quickly too. How will I ever find you both when it's time to pay me back?"
moral_elaborated: It is not wise to trust bad people, even if another bad person says they are good. One bad action doesn't become good just because another bad person is involved. Always choose your friends and helpers carefully.

title: The Eagle, the Cat, and the Wild Sow
body: AN EAGLE made her nest at the top of a lofty oak; a Cat, having found a convenient hole, moved into the middle of the trunk; and a Wild Sow, with her young, took shelter in a hollow at its foot. The Cat cunningly resolved to destroy this chance-made colony. To carry out her design, she climbed to the nest of the Eagle, and said, “Destruction is preparing for you, and for me too, unfortunately. The Wild Sow, whom you see daily digging up the earth, wishes to uproot the oak, so she may on its fall seize our families as food for her young.” Having thus frightened the Eagle out of her senses, she crept down to the cave of the Sow, and said, “Your children are in great danger; for as soon as you go out with your litter to find food, the Eagle is prepared to pounce upon one of your little pigs.” Having instilled these fears into the Sow, she went and pretended to hide herself in the hollow of the tree. When night came she went forth with silent foot and obtained food for herself and her kittens, but feigning to be afraid, she kept a lookout all through the day. Meanwhile, the Eagle, full of fear of the Sow, sat still on the branches, and the Sow, terrified by the Eagle, did not dare to go out from her cave. And thus they both, along with their families, perished from hunger, and afforded ample provision for the Cat and her kittens.
moral: A cunning liar can cause harm to others for their own gain.
body_child: An Eagle built her nest high in a tall tree. A Cat found a cozy hole in the middle of the tree trunk. A Wild Sow lived at the bottom of the tree with her baby pigs. The Cat was very tricky. She wanted to get rid of the others. First, she climbed to the Eagle's nest. She whispered, "Oh no, there's danger coming for us! The Sow is digging to knock down the tree. She wants to eat our babies!" The Eagle was very scared. Then the Cat crept down to the Sow's home. She whispered, "Your babies are in great danger! The Eagle is waiting to grab one of your little pigs when you go out." The Sow was very scared too. The Cat then pretended to hide. At night, the Cat went out to find food for her kittens. But all day, she stayed hidden, pretending to be afraid. The Eagle was too scared of the Sow to leave her nest. The Sow was too scared of the Eagle to leave her cave. So, both the Eagle and the Sow, and their families, became hungry and died. The tricky Cat and her kittens had lots of food to eat.
moral_elaborated: The Cat was very mean and tricky. She told lies to the Eagle and the Sow. These lies made them scared of each other. Because they were so scared, they didn't get food and died. The Cat got what she wanted.

title: The Wolf and the Fox
body: AT ONE TIME a very large and strong Wolf was born among the wolves, who exceeded all his fellow-wolves in strength, size, and swiftness, so that they unanimously decided to call him “Lion.” The Wolf, with a lack of sense proportioned to his enormous size, thought that they gave him this name in earnest, and, leaving his own race, consorted exclusively with the lions. An old sly Fox, seeing this, said, “May I never make myself so ridiculous as you do in your pride and self-conceit; for even though you have the size of a lion among wolves, in a herd of lions you are definitely a wolf.”
moral: Don't let pride make you think you are better than you are.
body_child: There was a very big and strong Wolf. He was bigger, stronger, and faster than all other wolves. So, the other wolves called him "Lion." The Wolf thought they called him "Lion" because he really was a lion. He felt very proud. He stopped being with other wolves and only spent time with lions. An old, smart Fox saw this. The Fox said, "I hope I never act as silly as you do. You might look like a lion among wolves. But when you are with real lions, you are still just a wolf."
moral_elaborated: The Wolf was proud because he was big among wolves. He thought he was a real lion. But when he was with real lions, he was still just a wolf. It's good to know who you are and not be too proud, or you might look silly.

title: The Mule
body: A MULE, frolicsome from lack of work and from too much corn, galloped about in a very extravagant manner, and said to himself: “My father surely was a high-mettled racer, and I am his own child in speed and spirit.” On the next day, being driven a long journey, and feeling very wearied, he exclaimed in a disconsolate tone: “I must have made a mistake; my father, after all, could have been only an ass.”
moral: Don't boast about yourself until you have truly proven what you can do.
body_child: A Mule felt happy because he had no work and lots of food. He ran around and kicked his legs high. He said to himself, "My dad must have been a fast racehorse! I am just as fast and spirited as him." The next day, he had to travel a very long way. He felt very, very tired. He then said sadly, "Oh, I was wrong! My dad must have just been a donkey after all."
moral_elaborated: The Mule was proud and boasted about being like a fast horse. But when he had to do hard work, he quickly got tired. It's easy to be proud when things are easy. Real strength shows when things are hard.

title: The Prophet
body: A WIZARD, sitting in the marketplace, was telling the fortunes of the passers-by when a person ran up in great haste, and announced to him that the doors of his house had been broken open and that all his goods were being stolen. He sighed heavily and hastened away as fast as he could run. A neighbor saw him running and said, “Oh! you fellow there! you say you can foretell the fortunes of others; how is it you did not foresee your own?”
moral: It is easier to give advice to others than to follow it yourself.
body_child: A man who told the future sat in the market. He told people what would happen to them. Suddenly, a person ran up to him very fast. The person said, "Oh no! The doors to your house are broken! All your things are being stolen!" The fortune-teller sighed loudly and ran home as fast as he could. A neighbor saw him running. The neighbor said, "Hey! You tell others what will happen to them. Why didn't you know this would happen to your own house?"
moral_elaborated: The fortune-teller told other people about their future. But he didn't know his own house was in danger. This shows that sometimes we can help others, but forget to help ourselves or see our own problems.

title: The Two Frogs
body: TWO FROGS were neighbors. One inhabited a deep pond, far removed from public view; the other lived in a gully containing little water, and traversed by a country road. The Frog that lived in the pond warned his friend to change his residence and entreated him to come and live with him, saying that he would enjoy greater safety from danger and more abundant food. The other refused, saying that he felt it so very hard to leave a place to which he had become accustomed. A few days afterwards a heavy wagon passed through the gully and crushed him to death under its wheels.
moral: A willful man will have his way to his own hurt.
body_child: There were two Frogs who were friends. One Frog lived in a deep pond where no one could see him. The other Frog lived in a small ditch with not much water. A busy road ran by it. The Frog in the deep pond told his friend, "Come live with me! It's safer here, and there's lots of food." But the other Frog said no. He said it was too hard to leave the place he was used to. A few days later, a big, heavy wagon drove through the ditch. It ran over the Frog and crushed him.
moral_elaborated: The Frog in the ditch did not want to move, even though it was dangerous. He was stubborn and wanted to stay where he was used to. Because he was stubborn, he got hurt. It's important to listen to good advice.

title: The Serpent and the Eagle
body: A SERPENT and an Eagle were struggling with each other in deadly conflict. The Serpent had the advantage, and was about to strangle the bird. A countryman saw them, and running up, loosed the coil of the Serpent and let the Eagle go free. The Serpent, irritated at the escape of his prey, injected his poison into the drinking horn of the countryman. The rustic, ignorant of his danger, was about to drink, when the Eagle struck his hand with his wing, and, seizing the drinking horn in his talons, carried it aloft.
moral: One good turn deserves another.
body_child: A snake and an eagle were fighting. The snake was winning and trying to squeeze the eagle. A man saw them and helped the eagle get free. The snake was mad. It put poison in the man's cup. The man did not know it was dangerous. He was about to drink. But the eagle hit his hand with its wing. The eagle took the cup and flew high up.
moral_elaborated: When someone helps you, it is good to help them back. The eagle saved the man because the man had saved it. It shows we should be kind and thankful to others.

title: The Crow and the Pitcher
body: A CROW perishing with thirst saw a pitcher, and hoping to find water, flew to it with delight. When he reached it, he discovered to his grief that it contained so little water that he could not possibly get at it. He tried everything he could think of to reach the water, but all his efforts were in vain. At last he collected as many stones as he could carry and dropped them one by one with his beak into the pitcher, until he brought the water within his reach and thus saved his life.
moral: Necessity is the mother of invention.
body_child: A thirsty crow saw a water pot. He flew to it, hoping for a drink. But there was only a little water, and he could not reach it. The crow tried many things, but nothing worked. Then, he picked up small stones. He dropped them into the pot, one by one. The water level slowly rose. At last, the crow could drink and saved himself!
moral_elaborated: When you really need something, it helps you think of new ways to solve a problem. The crow needed water very badly, so he found a clever way to get it. If you are determined, you can find a solution even when things are hard.

title: The Thief and the Innkeeper
body: A THIEF hired a room in a tavern and stayed a while in the hope of stealing something which should enable him to pay his reckoning. When he had waited some days in vain, he saw the Innkeeper dressed in a new and handsome coat and sitting before his door. The Thief sat down beside him and talked with him. As the conversation began to flag, the Thief yawned terribly and at the same time howled like a wolf. The Innkeeper said, “Why do you howl so fearfully?” “I will tell you,” said the Thief, “but first let me ask you to hold my clothes, or I shall tear them to pieces. I know not, sir, when I got this habit of yawning, nor whether these attacks of howling were inflicted on me as a judgment for my crimes, or for any other cause; but this I do know, that when I yawn for the third time, I actually turn into a wolf and attack men.” With this speech he commenced a second fit of yawning and again howled like a wolf, as he had at first. The Innkeeper, hearing his tale and believing what he said, became greatly alarmed and, rising from his seat, attempted to run away. The Thief laid hold of his coat and entreated him to stop, saying, “Pray wait, sir, and hold my clothes, or I shall tear them to pieces in my fury, when I turn into a wolf.” At the same moment he yawned the third time and set up a terrible howl. The Innkeeper, frightened lest he should be attacked, left his new coat in the Thief’s hand and ran as fast as he could into the inn for safety. The Thief made off with the coat and did not return again to the inn.
moral: Every tale is not to be believed.
body_child: A thief stayed at an inn. He wanted to steal something to pay his bill. One day, he saw the innkeeper in a nice new coat. The thief sat with the innkeeper and talked. Then, the thief yawned big and howled like a wolf. The innkeeper asked, "Why did you howl?" The thief said, "When I yawn three times, I turn into a wolf and attack people!" He said, "Please hold my clothes so I don't tear them." The thief howled a second time. The innkeeper was scared. The thief howled a third time. The innkeeper got very scared and ran away, leaving his new coat. The thief took the coat and left the inn.
moral_elaborated: It is important not to believe everything people tell you, especially if it sounds strange. Sometimes people tell untrue stories to trick others. Always think carefully before believing a wild tale.

title: The Hart and the Vine
body: A HART, hard pressed in the chase, hid himself beneath the large leaves of a Vine. The huntsmen, in their haste, overshot the place of his concealment. Supposing all danger to have passed, the Hart began to nibble the tendrils of the Vine. One of the huntsmen, attracted by the rustling of the leaves, looked back, and seeing the Hart, shot an arrow from his bow and struck it. The Hart, at the point of death, groaned: “I am rightly served, for I should not have maltreated the Vine that saved me.”
moral: Do not harm those who help you.
body_child: A deer was running from hunters. It hid under a big leafy vine. The hunters ran past without seeing it. The deer thought it was safe. Then, it started to eat the leaves of the vine that hid it. One hunter heard the leaves rustle. He looked back, saw the deer, and shot it with an arrow. As it was dying, the deer said, "I deserve this. I should not have hurt the vine that saved me."
moral_elaborated: It is wrong to hurt or be mean to someone who has helped you. The deer was punished because it hurt the very vine that kept it safe. Always be grateful and kind to those who offer you protection or help.

title: The Gnat and the Lion
body: A GNAT came and said to a Lion, “I do not in the least fear you, nor are you stronger than I am. For in what does your strength consist? You can scratch with your claws and bite with your teeth an a woman in her quarrels. I repeat that I am altogether more powerful than you; and if you doubt it, let us fight and see who will conquer.” The Gnat, having sounded his horn, fastened himself upon the Lion and stung him on the nostrils and the parts of the face devoid of hair. While trying to crush him, the Lion tore himself with his claws, until he punished himself severely. The Gnat thus prevailed over the Lion, and, buzzing about in a song of triumph, flew away. But shortly afterwards he became entangled in the meshes of a cobweb and was eaten by a spider. He greatly lamented his fate, saying, “Woe is me! that I, who can wage war successfully with the hugest beasts, should perish myself from this spider, the most inconsiderable of insects!”
moral: Pride goes before a fall.
body_child: A tiny gnat told a big lion, "I am not afraid of you! You are not stronger than me." "Your strength is just scratching and biting. Let's fight!" The gnat buzzed and stung the lion's nose and face. The lion tried to swat the gnat, but he scratched himself instead. The gnat won against the big lion and flew away, buzzing happily. But soon, the gnat flew into a spider's web. A tiny spider caught and ate the gnat. The gnat cried, "Oh no! I beat a huge lion, but a tiny spider got me!"
moral_elaborated: Even if you are very good at something, don't be too proud or boastful. The gnat beat the lion, but then its pride led it to a tiny spider it didn't expect. It is wise to stay humble, because even small things can cause big problems.

title: The Fox and the Grapes
body: A FAMISHED FOX saw some clusters of ripe black grapes hanging from a trellised vine. She resorted to all her tricks to get at them, but wearied herself in vain, for she could not reach them. At last she turned away, hiding her disappointment and saying: “The Grapes are sour, and not ripe as I thought.”
moral: It is easy to despise what you cannot get.
body_child:
A hungry fox saw some purple grapes.
They hung high on a vine.
The fox tried many times to reach them.
But she could not.
She got tired.
Then she walked away.
"Those grapes are sour," she said.
"I don't want them anyway."
moral_elaborated:
Sometimes we want something very much.
But we can't have it.
Then we might pretend we didn't want it anyway. This helps us feel better.

title: The Walnut-Tree
body: A WALNUT TREE standing by the roadside bore an abundant crop of fruit. For the sake of the nuts, the passers-by broke its branches with stones and sticks. The Walnut-Tree piteously exclaimed, “O wretched me! that those whom I cheer with my fruit should repay me with these painful requitals!”
moral: Some people repay kindness with injury.
body_child:
A walnut tree grew by the road.
It had many nuts.
People walked by and wanted the nuts.
They threw stones and hit the tree with sticks.
They broke its branches to get the nuts.
The tree cried, "Oh dear! I give them yummy fruit.
But they hurt me in return!"
moral_elaborated:
Sometimes, when someone helps us or gives us something good, we might still act mean.
It's not fair to hurt someone who is kind to you.
Always be grateful for good things and treat others well.

title: The Kid and the Wolf
body: A KID, returning without protection from the pasture, was pursued by a Wolf. Seeing he could not escape, he turned round, and said: “I know, friend Wolf, that I must be your prey, but before I die I would ask of you one favour you will play me a tune to which I may dance.” The Wolf complied, and while he was piping and the Kid was dancing, some hounds hearing the sound ran up and began chasing the Wolf. Turning to the Kid, he said, “It is just what I deserve; for I, who am only a butcher, should not have turned piper to please you.”
moral: Do not try to do things that are not your business.
body_child:
A little goat was walking home alone.
A hungry wolf chased him.
The goat knew he could not get away.
He turned to the wolf and said, "Dear Wolf, I know you will eat me.
But please play a song for me first. I want to dance one last time."
The wolf started to play music.
The little goat danced.
Some dogs heard the music. They ran to see what it was.
The dogs saw the wolf and chased him away!
The wolf looked back at the goat. "This is my fault," he said.
"I should have stayed a hunter, not a musician!"
moral_elaborated:
It's best to do what you are good at and what you usually do.
Sometimes trying to do something new, especially for someone else's trick, can lead to trouble.
Focus on your own job or role to avoid problems.

title: The Monkey and the Dolphin
body: A SAILOR, bound on a long voyage, took with him a Monkey to amuse him while on shipboard. As he sailed off the coast of Greece, a violent tempest arose in which the ship was wrecked and he, his Monkey, and all the crew were obliged to swim for their lives. A Dolphin saw the Monkey contending with the waves, and supposing him to be a man (whom he is always said to befriend), came and placed himself under him, to convey him on his back in safety to the shore. When the Dolphin arrived with his burden in sight of land not far from Athens, he asked the Monkey if he were an Athenian. The latter replied that he was, and that he was descended from one of the most noble families in that city. The Dolphin then inquired if he knew the Piræus (the famous harbor of Athens). Supposing that a man was meant, the Monkey answered that he knew him very well and that he was an intimate friend. The Dolphin, indignant at these falsehoods, dipped the Monkey under the water and drowned him.
moral: Boasting and falsehoods often lead to ruin.
body_child:
A sailor went on a long trip.
He brought a monkey to play with.
Their ship crashed in a big storm.
Everyone had to swim.
A kind dolphin saw the monkey in the water.
The dolphin thought the monkey was a person.
Dolphins like to help people.
So, the dolphin let the monkey ride on his back to safety.
Near the land, the dolphin asked, "Are you from Athens?"
The monkey said, "Yes, I am from a very important family there!"
The dolphin then asked, "Do you know the Piræus?" (That's a port city near Athens).
The monkey thought Piræus was a person.
He said, "Oh yes, he is a good friend of mine!"
The dolphin was angry because the monkey told so many lies.
The dolphin pushed the monkey underwater and he drowned.
moral_elaborated:
It is important to always tell the truth.
Pretending to be someone you're not or knowing things you don't can get you into big trouble.
Be honest, even if it's hard, because lies can hurt you in the end.

title: The Horse and the Stag
body: AT ONE TIME the Horse had the plain entirely to himself. Then a Stag intruded into his domain and shared his pasture. The Horse, desiring to revenge himself on the stranger, asked a man if he were willing to help him in punishing the Stag. The man replied that if the Horse would receive a bit in his mouth and agree to carry him, he would contrive effective weapons against the Stag. The Horse consented and allowed the man to mount him. From that hour he found that instead of obtaining revenge on the Stag, he had enslaved himself to the service of man.
moral: In seeking revenge, we often punish ourselves.
body_child:
Once, a horse lived all alone on a wide field.
Then, a deer came and ate the grass with him.
The horse did not like sharing. He wanted to get rid of the deer.
He asked a man for help to chase the deer away.
The man said, "I will help you. But you must let me put a bit in your mouth.
And you must let me ride on your back."
The horse agreed. The man got on his back.
From that day on, the horse was no longer free.
He had to work for the man forever.
He never got rid of the deer, but he lost his own freedom.
moral_elaborated:
Sometimes we get so angry that we want to get back at someone.
But trying to hurt someone else can end up hurting us more.
It's better to let go of anger than to lose something important by seeking revenge.

title: The Jackdaw and the Doves
body: A JACKDAW, seeing some Doves in a cote abundantly provided with food, painted himself white and joined them in order to share their plentiful maintenance. The Doves, as long as he was silent, supposed him to be one of themselves and admitted him to their cote. But when one day he forgot himself and began to chatter, they discovered his true character and drove him forth, pecking him with their beaks. Failing to obtain food among the Doves, he returned to the Jackdaws. They too, not recognizing him on account of his color, expelled him from living with them. So desiring two ends, he obtained neither.
body_child: A bird named a Jackdaw saw some Doves. The Doves lived in a house with lots of food. The Jackdaw wanted their food. So, he painted himself white. He pretended to be a Dove. The Doves let him in because he was quiet. One day, he forgot and made his own sounds. The Doves knew he was not one of them. They chased him away. The Jackdaw went back to his own kind. But they did not know him either because he was white. They also chased him away. The Jackdaw wanted two things, but he got nothing.
moral: Trying to be someone you're not will leave you with nothing.
moral_elaborated: It's not good to pretend to be someone else. People will find out the truth. And then you might lose your real friends too.

title: The Fox and the Monkey
body: A FOX and a Monkey were traveling together on the same road. As they journeyed, they passed through a cemetery full of monuments. “All these monuments which you see,” said the Monkey, “are erected in honour of my ancestors, who were in their day freedmen and citizens of great renown.” The Fox replied, “You have chosen a most appropriate subject for your falsehoods, as I am sure none of your ancestors will be able to contradict you.”
body_child: A Fox and a Monkey were walking together. They walked past a graveyard. There were many statues there. The Monkey said, "Look at all these statues! They are for my family who were famous!" The Fox replied, "That's a good story, Monkey. Because no one from your family who is dead can say it's not true!"
moral: A false tale often betrays itself.
moral_elaborated: It means that a lie can often be easy to spot. If someone tells a big, unbelievable story, it might not be true. Think carefully about what people say.

title: The Man and His Wife
body: A MAN had a Wife who made herself hated by all the members of his household. Wishing to find out if she had the same effect on the persons in her father’s house, he made some excuse to send her home on a visit to her father. After a short time she returned, and when he inquired how she had got on and how the servants had treated her, she replied, “The herdsmen and shepherds cast on me looks of aversion.” He said, “O Wife, if you were disliked by those who go out early in the morning with their flocks and return late in the evening, what must have been felt towards you by those with whom you passed the whole day!”
body_child: A man had a wife. Everyone in his home did not like her. The man wanted to know if her own family liked her. So, he sent her to visit her father. After a while, she came back. He asked how it went. She said, "The farm workers did not like me." The man said, "Oh no, Wife! If people who only see you for a short time did not like you, imagine how those who spend all day with you must feel!"
moral: Straws show how the wind blows.
moral_elaborated: This means small things can tell you a lot. Even little hints can show what someone is really like. Pay attention to small clues.

title: The Man, the Horse, the Ox, and the Dog
body: A HORSE, Ox, and Dog, driven to great straits by the cold, sought shelter and protection from Man. He received them kindly, lighted a fire, and warmed them. He let the Horse make free with his oats, gave the Ox an abundance of hay, and fed the Dog with meat from his own table. Grateful for these favours, the animals determined to repay him to the best of their ability. For this purpose, they divided the term of his life between them, and each endowed one portion of it with the qualities which chiefly characterized himself. The Horse chose his earliest years and gave them his own attributes: hence every man is in his youth impetuous, headstrong, and obstinate in maintaining his own opinion. The Ox took under his patronage the next term of life, and therefore man in his middle age is fond of work, devoted to labor, and resolute to amass wealth and to husband his resources. The end of life was reserved for the Dog, wherefore the old man is often snappish, irritable, hard to please, and selfish, tolerant only of his own household, but averse to strangers and to all who do not administer to his comfort or to his necessities.
body_child: A Horse, an Ox, and a Dog were very cold. They asked a Man for help. The Man was kind. He made a fire and warmed them. He gave the Horse oats. He gave the Ox lots of hay. He gave the Dog meat from his own food. The animals were thankful. They wanted to thank the Man. They decided to give him parts of their lives. The Horse chose the Man's young years.
