So, young people are often wild and want their own way. The Ox chose the Man's middle years. So, grown-ups like to work hard and save money. The Dog chose the Man's old years. So, old people can sometimes be grumpy and only like their own family.
moral: Life has different stages, and each stage brings new behaviors.
moral_elaborated: People change as they get older. When you are young, you might be like a horse, full of energy! When you are grown up, you might be like an ox, working hard. And when you are very old, you might be like a dog, wanting comfort.

title: The Thief and the Housedog
body: A THIEF came in the night to break into a house. He brought with him several slices of meat in order to pacify the Housedog, so that he would not alarm his master by barking. As the Thief threw him the pieces of meat, the Dog said, “If you think to stop my mouth, you will be greatly mistaken. This sudden kindness at your hands will only make me more watchful, lest under these unexpected favours to myself, you have some private ends to accomplish for your own benefit, and for my master’s injury.”
body_child: A thief came to a house at night. He wanted to break in. He brought some meat for the dog. He hoped the dog would eat the meat and not bark. The thief threw the dog some meat. The Dog said, "You think this meat will make me quiet? You are wrong! Your sudden kindness makes me even more careful. I think you are trying to hurt my owner!"
moral: Do not trust gifts from strangers, especially when they seem too good to be true.
moral_elaborated: If someone you don't know gives you a gift, be careful. They might want something from you. Always think about why someone is being extra nice.

title: The Apes and the Two Travelers
body: TWO MEN, one who always spoke the truth and the other who told nothing but lies, were traveling together and by chance came to the land of Apes. One of the Apes, who had raised himself to be king, commanded them to be seized and brought before him, that he might know what was said of him among men. He ordered at the same time that all the Apes be arranged in a long row on his right hand and on his left, and that a throne be placed for him, as was the custom among men. After these preparations he signified that the two men should be brought before him, and greeted them with this salutation: “What sort of a king do I seem to you to be, O strangers?” The Lying Traveler replied, “You seem to me a most mighty king.” “And what is your estimate of those you see around me?” “These,” he made answer, “are worthy companions of yourself, fit at least to be ambassadors and leaders of armies.” The Ape and all his court, gratified with the lie, commanded that a handsome present be given to the flatterer. On this the truthful Traveler thought to himself, “If so great a reward be given for a lie, with what gift may not I be rewarded, if, according to my custom, I tell the truth?” The Ape quickly turned to him. “And pray how do I and these my friends around me seem to you?” “Thou art,” he said, “a most excellent Ape, and all these thy companions after thy example are excellent Apes too.” The King of the Apes, enraged at hearing these truths, gave him over to the teeth and claws of his companions.
moral: It is dangerous to tell the truth to those who prefer flattery.
body_child: Two men were traveling. One always told the truth. The other always told lies. They came to a land where apes lived. An ape king ruled there. The king wanted to know what people said about him. He made the men come before him. He asked, "What kind of king am I?" The lying man said, "You are a great king!" He said the other apes were important too. The ape king liked this. He gave the lying man a gift. The truthful man thought, "If lies get gifts, truth must get more!" The ape king asked him, "What do you think of me and my friends?" The truthful man said, "You are a very good ape. And your friends are good apes too." The ape king was very angry to hear the truth. He told his apes to hurt the truthful man.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, people like to hear nice lies more than hard truths. Being honest can be brave, but it might make some people mad. It's important to know who will listen to the truth and who will get upset.

title: The Fox and the Lion
body: WHEN A FOX who had never yet seen a Lion, fell in with him by chance for the first time in the forest, he was so frightened that he nearly died with fear. On meeting him for the second time, he was still much alarmed, but not to the same extent as at first. On seeing him the third time, he so increased in boldness that he went up to him and commenced a familiar conversation with him.
moral: Acquaintance softens prejudices.
body_child: A fox had never seen a lion before. One day, he met a lion in the forest. The fox was very scared! He almost died of fear. Later, he saw the lion a second time. He was still scared, but not as much. The third time he saw the lion, the fox was brave. He walked right up to the lion and started talking to him like a friend.
moral_elaborated: When you meet someone new, you might be shy or scared. But the more you get to know them, the easier it becomes. You might even become friends!

title: The Weasel and the Mice
body: A WEASEL, inactive from age and infirmities, was not able to catch mice as he once did. He therefore rolled himself in flour and lay down in a dark corner. A Mouse, supposing him to be food, leaped upon him, and was instantly caught and squeezed to death. Another perished in a similar manner, and then a third, and still others after them. A very old Mouse, who had escaped many a trap and snare, observed from a safe distance the trick of his crafty foe and said, “Ah! you that lie there, may you prosper just in the same proportion as you are what you pretend to be!”
moral: Beware of those who pretend to be something they are not.
body_child: A weasel was very old and sick. He could not catch mice anymore. So, he rolled himself in flour. He lay in a dark corner. A mouse saw him. The mouse thought he was food. The mouse jumped on the weasel and was caught! The weasel squeezed him to death. Another mouse came and then another. They all got caught the same way. An old, smart mouse saw what was happening from far away. He knew it was a trick. He said, "I hope you get what you deserve for pretending to be something you are not!"
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, bad things can look like good things. It's important to be careful and not trust everything you see. Always look closely before you get too close to something new or strange.

title: The Boy Bathing
body: A BOY bathing in a river was in danger of being drowned. He called out to a passing traveler for help, but instead of holding out a helping hand, the man stood by unconcernedly, and scolded the boy for his imprudence. “Oh, sir!” cried the youth, “pray help me now and scold me afterwards.”
moral: Counsel without help is useless.
body_child: A boy was swimming in a river. He started to drown. He called out for help to a man walking by. But the man did not help. He just stood there. He started scolding the boy for being careless. The boy cried, "Oh, please help me now! You can scold me later!"
moral_elaborated: It's good to give advice, but sometimes actions are more important. When someone is in trouble, helping them first is best. You can talk about what went wrong after they are safe.

title: The Peacock and Juno
body: THE PEACOCK made complaint to Juno that, while the nightingale pleased every ear with his song, he himself no sooner opened his mouth than he became a laughingstock to all who heard him. The Goddess, to console him, said, “But you far excel in beauty and in size. The splendor of the emerald shines in your neck and you unfold a tail gorgeous with painted plumage.” “But for what purpose have I,” said the bird, “this dumb beauty so long as I am surpassed in song?” “The lot of each,” replied Juno, “has been assigned by the will of the Fates—to thee, beauty; to the eagle, strength; to the nightingale, song; to the raven, favourable, and to the crow, unfavourable auguries. These are all contented with the endowments allotted to them.”
moral: Be content with your own unique gifts and talents.
body_child: A peacock complained to the goddess Juno. He said, "The nightingale sings so beautifully, everyone loves his song. But when I open my mouth, everyone laughs at me!" Juno tried to make him feel better. She said, "But you are so beautiful and big! Your neck shines like an emerald. Your tail has many colorful feathers." The peacock said, "What good is all this beauty if I cannot sing?" Juno replied, "Everyone has special gifts. You have beauty. The eagle has strength. The nightingale has a song. The raven and crow have other gifts." She said, "They are all happy with what they have. You should be happy with yours too."
moral_elaborated: Everyone is special and has different strengths. Don't wish for what others have. Instead, be happy and proud of your own amazing qualities!

title: The Wolf and the Shepherd
body: A WOLF followed a flock of sheep for a long time and did not attempt to injure one of them. The Shepherd at first stood on his guard against him, as against an enemy, and kept a strict watch over his movements. But when the Wolf, day after day, kept in the company of the sheep and did not make the slightest effort to seize them, the Shepherd began to look upon him as a guardian of his flock rather than as a plotter of evil against it; and when occasion called him one day into the city, he left the sheep entirely in his charge. The Wolf, now that he had the opportunity, fell upon the sheep, and destroyed the greater part of the flock. When the Shepherd returned to find his flock destroyed, he exclaimed: “I have been rightly served; why did I trust my sheep to a Wolf?”
moral: Never trust a known enemy.
body_child: A wolf watched a flock of sheep for a long time. He did not hurt any of them. The shepherd was careful at first. He watched the wolf closely. But the wolf stayed with the sheep every day. He never tried to catch them. The shepherd started to think the wolf was a helper, not an enemy. One day, the shepherd had to go to town. He left the sheep with the wolf. The wolf had his chance! He attacked the sheep and killed many. When the shepherd came back, his sheep were gone. He cried, "I deserve this! Why did I trust a wolf with my sheep?"
moral_elaborated: Do not trust someone who has shown they are not good. Even if they act nice for a while, their true nature might come out. It's smart to be careful with people you know can be dangerous.

title: The Hares and the Lions
body: THE HARES harangued the assembly, and argued that all should be equal. The Lions made this reply: “Your words, O Hares! are good; but they lack both claws and teeth such as we have.”
moral: Power speaks louder than words.
body_child: The hares spoke to a big meeting. They said everyone should be equal. The lions answered, "Hares, your words sound good! But you don't have strong claws and teeth like we do."
moral_elaborated: It means that sometimes, strength and power are more important than just talking. Even good ideas might not work if you don't have the power to make them happen. Strong animals often get their way.

title: The Seller of Images
body: A CERTAIN MAN made a wooden image of Mercury and offered it for sale. When no one appeared willing to buy it, in order to attract purchasers, he cried out that he had the statue to sell of a benefactor who bestowed wealth and helped to heap up riches. One of the bystanders said to him, “My good fellow, why do you sell him, being such a one as you describe, when you may yourself enjoy the good things he has to give?” “Why,” he replied, “I am in need of immediate help, and he is wont to give his good gifts very slowly.”
moral: Don't believe what a seller says about his own wares.
body_child: A man made a wooden statue of a god named Mercury. He tried to sell it. No one wanted to buy it. To get people to buy, he shouted that it was a special statue. He said it would bring money and make people rich. Someone nearby asked him, "Why do you sell it if it's so good? You could keep it and get rich yourself!" The man answered, "I need money right now. But this god gives his gifts very slowly."
moral_elaborated: This fable teaches us to be smart about what people say. If someone says something is amazing but they don't use it themselves, it might not be true. Look at what people do, not just what they say.

title: The Hawk and the Nightingale
body: A NIGHTINGALE, sitting aloft upon an oak and singing according to his wont, was seen by a Hawk who, being in need of food, swooped down and seized him. The Nightingale, about to lose his life, earnestly begged the Hawk to let him go, saying that he was not big enough to satisfy the hunger of a Hawk who, if he wanted food, ought to pursue the larger birds. The Hawk, interrupting him, said: “I should indeed have lost my senses if I should let go food ready in my hand, for the sake of pursuing birds which are not yet even within sight.”
moral: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
body_child: A nightingale was singing high in an oak tree. A hungry hawk saw him. The hawk flew down fast and caught the nightingale. The nightingale was about to die. He begged the hawk to let him go. He said, "I am too small for you. If you are hungry, you should go hunt bigger birds!" The hawk stopped him. He said, "I would be silly to let go of food I already have! Why would I chase birds I cannot even see yet?"
moral_elaborated: It means it is better to keep something good you already have. Don't let it go to try and get something bigger or better that you might not get. What you have for sure is often more valuable than a promise of more.

title: The Lark and Her Young Ones
body: A LARK had made her nest in the early spring on the young green wheat. The brood had almost grown to their full strength and attained the use of their wings and the full plumage of their feathers, when the owner of the field, looking over his ripe crop, said, “The time has come when I must ask all my neighbors to help me with my harvest.” One of the young Larks heard his speech and related it to his mother, inquiring of her to what place they should move for safety. “There is no occasion to move yet, my son,” she replied; “the man who only sends to his friends to help him with his harvest is not really in earnest.” The owner of the field came again a few days later and saw the wheat shedding the grain from excess of ripeness. He said, “I will come myself tomorrow with my laborers, and with as many reapers as I can hire, and will get in the harvest.” The Lark on hearing these words said to her brood, “It is time now to be off, my little ones, for the man is in earnest this time; he no longer trusts his friends, but will reap the field himself.”
moral: Self-help is the best help.
body_child: In spring, a mother lark built her nest in a field of young green wheat. Her baby birds grew big and almost learned to fly. One day, the farmer looked at his ripe wheat. He said, "It's time to cut the wheat! I will ask my neighbors to help me." A young lark heard this and told his mother. He asked where they should go to be safe. "Not yet, my son," she said. "A man who only asks friends to help is not truly ready." A few days later, the farmer came back. The wheat was very ripe. He said, "Tomorrow, I will come myself with my workers. We will cut the wheat!" When the mother lark heard this, she told her babies, "Now it's time to go, little ones! The man is truly ready this time. He won't wait for friends; he will do the work himself."
moral_elaborated: This means it's best to do things yourself if you want them done. Don't just wait for others to help you. If you rely on your own hard work, things will get finished.

title: The Dog, the Cock, and the Fox
body: A DOG and a Cock being great friends, agreed to travel together. At nightfall they took shelter in a thick wood. The Cock flying up, perched himself on the branches of a tree, while the Dog found a bed beneath in the hollow trunk. When the morning dawned, the Cock, as usual, crowed very loudly several times. A Fox heard the sound, and wishing to make a breakfast on him, came and stood under the branches, saying how earnestly he desired to make the acquaintance of the owner of so magnificent a voice. The Cock, suspecting his civilities, said: “Sir, I wish you would do me the favour of going around to the hollow trunk below me, and waking my porter, so that he may open the door and let you in.” When the Fox approached the tree, the Dog sprang out and caught him, and tore him to pieces.
moral: It is good to have a loyal friend.
body_child: A dog and a rooster were good friends. They went on a trip together. When it got dark, they found a wood to sleep in. The rooster flew up into a tree. The dog slept in a hollow log below. In the morning, the rooster crowed very loudly. A fox heard him. The fox wanted to eat the rooster for breakfast. He came under the tree. "What a wonderful voice you have!" said the fox. "I want to meet you!" The rooster was smart. He knew the fox was tricky. "Sir," said the rooster, "please go wake up my helper in the log below. He will open the door for you." The fox went to the log. The dog jumped out and caught the fox. The fox ran away scared!
moral_elaborated: Having a good friend is very helpful. They can protect you from danger or tricky people. Always stick together with your true friends.

title: The Geese and the Cranes
body: THE GEESE and the Cranes were feeding in the same meadow, when a birdcatcher came to ensnare them in his nets. The Cranes, being light of wing, fled away at his approach; while the Geese, being slower of flight and heavier in their bodies, were captured.
moral: The swift are often safer than the slow.
body_child: Geese and cranes were eating in a field. A man came to catch birds with nets. The cranes were light and could fly fast. They flew away when they saw the man. The geese were heavy and flew slowly. They could not get away. The man caught them in his nets.
moral_elaborated: If you can act fast, you might escape trouble. Being quick can help you stay safe. Slow ones might get caught in danger.

title: The Ass and the Wolf
body: AN ASS feeding in a meadow saw a Wolf approaching to seize him, and immediately pretended to be lame. The Wolf, coming up, inquired the cause of his lameness. The Ass replied that passing through a hedge he had trod with his foot upon a sharp thorn. He requested that the Wolf pull it out, lest when he ate him it should injure his throat. The Wolf consented and lifted up the foot, and was giving his whole mind to the discovery of the thorn, when the Ass, with his heels, kicked his teeth into his mouth and galloped away. The Wolf, being thus fearfully mauled, said, “I am rightly served, for why did I attempt the art of healing, when my father only taught me the trade of a butcher?”
moral: Stick to your own trade.
body_child: A donkey was eating grass. He saw a wolf coming to catch him. The donkey quickly pretended to have a sore leg. The wolf came closer and asked, "Why are you limping?" The donkey said, "I stepped on a sharp thorn. Please pull it out. If you eat me, the thorn might hurt your throat." The wolf agreed. He picked up the donkey's foot to look for the thorn. The donkey kicked the wolf hard in the mouth! Then the donkey ran away fast. The wolf learned a lesson. "I should stick to what I know," he said.
moral_elaborated: It is best to do what you are good at. Don't try to do things you don't know how to do. You might get hurt if you try to do someone else's job.

title: The Goat and the Ass
body: A MAN once kept a Goat and an Ass. The Goat, envying the Ass on account of his greater abundance of food, said, “How shamefully you are treated: at one time grinding in the mill, and at another carrying heavy burdens;” and he further advised him to pretend to be epileptic and fall into a ditch and so obtain rest. The Ass listened to his words, and falling into a ditch, was very much bruised. His master, sending for a leech, asked his advice. He bade him pour upon the wounds the lungs of a Goat. They at once killed the Goat, and so healed the Ass.
moral: He who plots mischief against another is often caught in his own snare.
body_child: A farmer had a goat and a donkey. The goat was jealous because the donkey got more food. The goat said to the donkey, "You work so hard! You grind grain and carry heavy things." The goat told the donkey to pretend to be sick. He told him to fall into a ditch and rest. The donkey listened to the goat. He fell into a ditch and got badly hurt. The farmer called a doctor for the donkey. The doctor said, "To make the donkey better, you need a goat's lungs." So, they killed the goat to save the donkey.
moral_elaborated: If you try to hurt someone, you might hurt yourself instead. Being jealous and giving bad advice can cause big trouble. Be kind and helpful, not tricky.

title: The Lion and the Bull
body: A LION, greatly desiring to capture a Bull, and yet afraid to attack him on account of his great size, resorted to a trick to ensure his destruction. He approached the Bull and said, “I have slain a fine sheep, my friend; and if you will come home and partake of him with me, I shall be delighted to have your company.” The Lion said this in the hope that, as the Bull was in the act of reclining to eat, he might attack him to advantage, and make his meal on him. The Bull, on approaching the Lion’s den, saw the huge spits and giant caldrons, and no sign whatever of the sheep, and, without saying a word, quietly took his departure. The Lion inquired why he went off so abruptly without a word of salutation to his host, who had not given him any cause for offense. “I have reasons enough,” said the Bull. “I see no indication whatever of your having slaughtered a sheep, while I do see very plainly every preparation for your dining on a bull.”
moral: Always inspect a situation carefully.
body_child: A lion wanted to catch a big bull. But the bull was very strong, so the lion was scared to attack him. The lion thought of a trick. He went to the bull and said, "My friend, I have caught a tasty sheep! Come to my home and eat with me." The lion hoped that when the bull sat down to eat, he could easily catch him. The bull went to the lion's den. He saw big cooking tools and pots, but no sheep. The bull knew something was wrong. He left quietly without saying a word. The lion asked, "Why are you leaving so fast?" The bull replied, "I see no sheep here. But I see everything ready for a big bull dinner!"
moral_elaborated: Always be careful, especially if someone who isn't a friend invites you. Look closely at things before you act. Sometimes, things are not what they seem, and someone might be trying to trick you.

title: The Fox and the Mask
body: A FOX entered the house of an actor and, rummaging through all his properties, came upon a Mask, an admirable imitation of a human head. He placed his paws on it and said, “What a beautiful head! Yet it is of no value, as it entirely lacks brains.”
body_child: A fox went into an actor's house. He looked at all the actor's things. He found a mask that looked like a human head. The fox put his paws on it. He said, "This head is pretty! But it's not good for anything. It has no brains inside."
moral: What looks good on the outside may not be useful without intelligence.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes things look nice on the outside. But if they don't have good ideas or smarts inside, they aren't very useful. It's more important to be smart than just pretty.

title: The Grasshopper and the Owl
body: AN OWL, accustomed to feed at night and to sleep during the day, was greatly disturbed by the noise of a Grasshopper and earnestly besought her to stop chirping. The Grasshopper refused to desist, and chirped louder and louder the more the Owl entreated. When she saw that she could get no redress and that her words were despised, the Owl attacked the chatterer by a stratagem. “Since I cannot sleep,” she said, “on account of your song which, believe me, is sweet as the lyre of Apollo, I shall indulge myself in drinking some nectar which Pallas lately gave me. If you do not dislike it, come to me and we will drink it together.” The Grasshopper, who was thirsty, and pleased with the praise of her voice, eagerly flew up. The Owl came forth from her hollow, seized her, and put her to death.
body_child: An owl liked to eat at night and sleep during the day. A loud grasshopper made too much noise. The owl asked the grasshopper to stop chirping. But the grasshopper chirped even louder! The owl got a clever idea. She told the grasshopper, "Your song is so sweet! I can't sleep. I have some special drink. Come share it with me!" The grasshopper was thirsty and happy about the praise. She flew right to the owl. The owl grabbed her and ate her.
moral: Never trust a flatterer.
moral_elaborated: Be careful when someone says very nice things to you. They might be trying to trick you. Always think if what they say is true, or if they want something from you.

title: The Fowler and the Viper
body: A FOWLER, taking his bird-lime and his twigs, went out to catch birds. Seeing a thrush sitting upon a tree, he wished to take it, and fitting his twigs to a proper length, watched intently, having his whole thoughts directed towards the sky. While thus looking upwards, he unknowingly trod upon a Viper asleep just before his feet. The Viper, turning about, stung him, and falling into a swoon, the man said to himself, “Woe is me! that while I purposed to hunt another, I am myself fallen unawares into the snares of death.”
body_child: A bird catcher went out to catch birds. He had sticky stuff and sticks. He saw a thrush in a tree. He wanted to catch it. He looked up at the sky very carefully, thinking only about the bird. He didn't see a sleeping snake on the ground. He stepped on the snake! The snake bit him. The man fell down, feeling sick. He said, "Oh no! I wanted to catch a bird, but now I am caught by death."
moral: Often, while we are intent on harming others, we fall into our own traps.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, when people try to hurt others, they end up hurting themselves instead. It's better to be kind and careful. If you focus on doing bad things, bad things might happen to you too.

title: The Horse and the Ass
body: A HORSE, proud of his fine trappings, met an Ass on the highway. The Ass, being heavily laden, moved slowly out of the way. “Hardly,” said the Horse, “can I resist kicking you with my heels.” The Ass held his peace, and made only a silent appeal to the justice of the gods. Not long afterwards the Horse, having become broken-winded, was sent by his owner to the farm. The Ass, seeing him drawing a dungcart, thus derided him: “Where, O boaster, are now all thy gay trappings, thou who are thyself reduced to the condition you so lately treated with contempt?”
body_child: A proud horse, wearing fancy gear, met a donkey on the road. The donkey was carrying a heavy load and moved slowly out of the way. The horse said, "I want to kick you!" The donkey stayed quiet. He just wished things would be fair. Not long after, the horse got sick and couldn't run fast. His owner sent him to work on the farm. The donkey saw him pulling a cart of manure. The donkey said, "Where are your fancy clothes now, Mr. Boaster? You made fun of me, but now you do the same work!"
moral: Pride goes before a fall.
moral_elaborated: Don't be too proud or make fun of others. Things can change quickly. Someone who is high up today might be low tomorrow. Be kind to everyone, no matter their situation.

title: The Lion and the Three Bulls
body: THREE BULLS for a long time pastured together. A Lion lay in ambush in the hope of making them his prey, but was afraid to attack them while they kept together. Having at last by guileful speeches succeeded in separating them, he attacked them without fear as they fed alone, and feasted on them one by one at his own leisure.
body_child: Three bulls lived and ate grass together for a long time. A lion hid, hoping to catch them. But the lion was scared to attack them when they were all together. The lion used clever words to make the bulls fight and separate. Then, the lion was not scared. He attacked them one by one when they were alone. He ate them all.
moral: Union is strength.
moral_elaborated: When people work together, they are strong. It's hard for others to hurt them. But if they fight and go their separate ways, they become weak. It's always better to be a team!

title: The Wolf and the Goat
body: A WOLF saw a Goat feeding at the summit of a steep precipice, where he had no chance of reaching her. He called to her and earnestly begged her to come lower down, lest she fall by some mishap; and he added that the meadows lay where he was standing, and that the herbage was most tender. She replied, “No, my friend, it is not for the pasture that you invite me, but for yourself, who are in want of food.”
moral: Beware of those who offer help with selfish motives.
body_child:
A wolf saw a goat. The goat was eating grass on a tall, rocky hill. The wolf could not reach her.
"Come down here!" called the wolf. "You might fall! The grass is much better down here, where I am."
The goat replied, "No, wolf. You don't want me to eat grass. You want to eat *me*!"
moral_elaborated: Some people pretend to be kind, but they only want something for themselves. It's smart to think about why someone is offering help. Always be careful and think if their help is truly good for you.

title: The Fly and the Draught-Mule
body: A FLY sat on the axle-tree of a chariot, and addressing the Draught-Mule said, “How slow you are! Why do you not go faster? See if I do not prick your neck with my sting.” The Draught-Mule replied, “I do not heed your threats; I only care for him who sits above you, and who quickens my pace with his whip, or holds me back with the reins. Away, therefore, with your insolence, for I know well when to go fast, and when to go slow.”
moral: It's easy for small people to brag about big things others do.
body_child:
A little fly sat on a wagon wheel. It buzzed at the big mule pulling the wagon.
"You are so slow!" said the fly. "Why don't you go faster? I might sting you!"
The mule answered, "I don't care about your stings. I only listen to the driver. He tells me when to go fast and when to go slow. Go away with your rude words!"
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, people who are not important try to act like they are in charge. They might take credit for someone else's hard work. True leaders and workers know their own job and don't listen to boastful talk.

title: The Fishermen
body: SOME FISHERMEN were out trawling their nets. Perceiving them to be very heavy, they danced about for joy and supposed that they had taken a large catch. When they had dragged the nets to the shore they found but few fish: the nets were full of sand and stones, and the men were beyond measure cast down so much at the disappointment which had befallen them, but because they had formed such very different expectations. One of their company, an old man, said, “Let us cease lamenting, my mates, for, as it seems to me, sorrow is always the twin sister of joy; and it was only to be looked for that we, who just now were over-rejoiced, should next have something to make us sad.”
moral: Joy and sorrow often follow each other.
body_child:
Some fishermen were pulling in their nets. The nets felt very heavy. The men jumped up and down with joy! They thought they had caught many fish.
But when they pulled the nets to the beach, there were only a few fish. The nets were full of sand and rocks. The men felt very sad. They were sad because they had hoped for so much more.
An old man said, "Stop being sad, friends. Being sad often comes after being very happy. We were so happy just now, so it makes sense to feel sad next."
moral_elaborated: Life has happy times and sad times. When we feel very, very happy, we should remember that sad times might come too. And when we are sad, we can hope for happy times ahead. It's okay to feel both.

title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
body: A COUNTRY MOUSE invited a Town Mouse, an intimate friend, to pay him a visit and partake of his country fare. As they were on the bare plowlands, eating there wheat-stocks and roots pulled up from the hedgerow, the Town Mouse said to his friend, “You live here the life of the ants, while in my house is the horn of plenty. I am surrounded by every luxury, and if you will come with me, as I wish you would, you shall have an ample share of my dainties.” The Country Mouse was easily persuaded, and returned to town with his friend. On his arrival, the Town Mouse placed before him bread, barley, beans, dried figs, honey, raisins, and, last of all, brought a dainty piece of cheese from a basket. The Country Mouse, being much delighted at the sight of such good cheer, expressed his satisfaction in warm terms and lamented his own hard fate. Just as they were beginning to eat, someone opened the door, and they both ran off squeaking, as fast as they could, to a hole so narrow that two could only find room in it by squeezing. They had scarcely begun their repast again when someone else entered to take something out of a cupboard, whereupon the two Mice, more frightened than before, ran away and hid themselves. At last the Country Mouse, almost famished, said to his friend: “Although you have prepared for me so dainty a feast, I must leave you to enjoy it by yourself. It is surrounded by too many dangers to please me. I prefer my bare plowlands and roots from the hedgerow, where I can live in safety, and without fear.”
moral: A simple life with peace is better than a rich life with fear.
body_child:
A Country Mouse invited his friend, a Town Mouse, to visit. They ate simple food like wheat and roots.
The Town Mouse said, "Your life is like an ant's! My house has so much good food. Come live with me, and you will have many treats."
The Country Mouse agreed and went to town. The Town Mouse showed him bread, beans, honey, cheese, and more! The Country Mouse was very happy and wished he had such food.
But just as they started to eat, a door opened. They both squeaked and ran into a tiny hole.
Soon, someone else came in. The mice were even more scared and hid again.
Finally, the Country Mouse, very hungry, told his friend, "Your food is good, but it's too dangerous here. I like my simple life in the country better. There, I am safe and not afraid."
moral_elaborated: Having lots of nice things might seem good, but sometimes it comes with many worries or dangers. It is often better to live a simple life where you feel safe and happy. Peace of mind is more valuable than fancy food or big houses.

title: The Wolf, the Fox, and the Ape
body: A WOLF accused a Fox of theft, but the Fox entirely denied the charge. An Ape undertook to adjudge the matter between them. When each had fully stated his case the Ape announced this sentence: “I do not think you, Wolf, ever lost what you claim; and I do believe you, Fox, to have stolen what you so stoutly deny.”
moral: The dishonest, if they act honestly, get no credit.
body_child:
A wolf said a fox stole something from him. The fox said, "No, I did not!"
An ape was asked to decide who was right. Both the wolf and the fox told their stories.
Then the ape said, "Wolf, I don't think you ever lost what you say. And Fox, I do think you stole what you say you didn't!"
moral_elaborated: If someone is known for not being honest, people might not believe them even when they tell the truth. It's important to always try to be honest, so others can trust you. Being trustworthy helps everyone believe you more.

title: The Wasps, the Partridges, and the Farmer
body: THE WASPS and the Partridges, overcome with thirst, came to a Farmer and besought him to give them some water to drink. They promised amply to repay him the favour which they asked. The Partridges declared that they would dig around his vines and make them produce finer grapes. The Wasps said that they would keep guard and drive off thieves with their stings. But the Farmer interrupted them, saying: “I have already two oxen, who, without making any promises, do all these things. It is surely better for me to give the water to them than to you.”
moral: Actions speak louder than words.
body_child: The Wasps and the Partridges were very thirsty. They went to a farmer and asked for water. They promised to help him if he did. The Partridges said they would dig around his grapevines so they would grow well. The Wasps said they would scare away thieves with their stings. But the farmer stopped them. He said, 'I already have two oxen. They do all these things without even promising!' 'It is better for me to give the water to them than to you.'
moral_elaborated: This means that doing good things is better than just saying you will. The farmer liked his oxen because they already helped him every day. He didn't need new helpers who only talked about what they would do.

title: The Brother and the Sister
body: A FATHER had one son and one daughter, the former remarkable for his good looks, the latter for her extraordinary ugliness. While they were playing one day as children, they happened by chance to look together into a mirror that was placed on their mother’s chair. The boy congratulated himself on his good looks; the girl grew angry, and could not bear the self-praises of her Brother, interpreting all he said (and how could she do otherwise?) into reflection on herself. She ran off to her father, to be avenged on her Brother, and spitefully accused him of having, as a boy, made use of that which belonged only to girls. The father embraced them both, and bestowing his kisses and affection impartially on each, said, “I wish you both would look into the mirror every day: you, my son, that you may not spoil your beauty by evil conduct; and you, my daughter, that you may make up for your lack of beauty by your virtues.”
moral: True beauty comes from within.
body_child: A father had a son and a daughter. The son was very handsome. The daughter was not as pretty. One day, they both looked into a mirror together. The boy was happy about his good looks. The girl got angry because she thought he was making fun of her. She ran to her father to complain. The father hugged them both. He said, 'I want you both to look in the mirror every day.' 'Son, don't let your good looks make you act badly.' 'Daughter, let your kind heart make you truly beautiful.'
moral_elaborated: This story teaches us that what's inside a person is most important. Being kind, honest, and good makes you truly beautiful. It's better to have a good heart than just a pretty face.

title: The Dogs and the Fox
body: SOME DOGS, finding the skin of a lion, began to tear it in pieces with their teeth. A Fox, seeing them, said, “If this lion were alive, you would soon find out that his claws were stronger than your teeth.”
moral: It is easy to kick a man that is down.
body_child: Some dogs found a lion's skin. They started to rip it apart with their teeth. A fox saw them doing this. The fox said, 'If this lion were alive, you would quickly learn that his claws are much stronger than your teeth!'
moral_elaborated: This means it's easy to be brave or strong when someone can't fight back. The dogs were brave with a dead lion's skin because it posed no danger. But they wouldn't be brave if the lion was alive and could defend itself.

title: The Blind Man and the Whelp
body: A BLIND MAN was accustomed to distinguishing different animals by touching them with his hands. The whelp of a Wolf was brought him, with a request that he would feel it, and say what it was. He felt it, and being in doubt, said: “I do not quite know whether it is the cub of a Fox, or the whelp of a Wolf, but this I know full well. It would not be safe to admit him to the sheepfold.”
moral: Evil tendencies are shown in early life.
body_child: A blind man could tell different animals apart just by touching them. Someone brought him a baby wolf and asked him to feel it. He touched it, but he was not sure what kind of animal it was. He said, 'I don't really know if it's a baby fox or a baby wolf.' 'But I do know one thing for sure: it would not be safe to let him near the sheep!'
moral_elaborated: This means you can often see if someone might cause trouble, even when they are young. The blind man sensed danger from the baby wolf. He knew it would not be safe around sheep, even if it was small.

title: The Cobbler Turned Doctor
body: A COBBLER unable to make a living by his trade and made desperate by poverty, began to practice medicine in a town in which he was not known. He sold a drug, pretending that it was an antidote to all poisons, and obtained a great name for himself by long-winded puffs and advertisements. When the Cobbler happened to fall sick himself of a serious illness, the Governor of the town determined to test his skill. For this purpose he called for a cup, and while filling it with water, pretended to mix poison with the Cobbler’s antidote, commanding him to drink it on the promise of a reward. The Cobbler, under the fear of death, confessed that he had no knowledge of medicine, and was only made famous by the stupid clamors of the crowd. The Governor then called a public assembly and addressed the citizens: “Of what folly have you been guilty? You have not hesitated to entrust your heads to a man, whom no one could employ to make even the shoes for their feet.”
moral: Do not trust those who pretend to be something they are not.
body_child: A cobbler, who fixed shoes, was very poor and could not make enough money. He moved to a new town and pretended to be a doctor. He sold fake medicine, saying it was a cure for all poisons. People believed his big stories and thought he was a great doctor. One day, the cobbler got very sick himself. The town's leader wanted to see if he was really a doctor. He filled a cup with water and pretended to put poison in it, telling the cobbler to drink his own medicine. Scared of dying, the cobbler told the truth. He said he knew nothing about medicine and only fooled people. The leader then told everyone, 'How silly you were! You trusted your lives to a man who couldn't even make your shoes!'
moral_elaborated: This fable teaches us not to trust people who lie about what they can do. The cobbler pretended to be a doctor, but he was not good at it at all. It's important to make sure someone is truly good at what they say they are before you trust them.

title: The Wolf and the Horse
body: A WOLF coming out of a field of oats met a Horse and thus addressed him: “I would advise you to go into that field. It is full of fine oats, which I have left untouched for you, as you are a friend whom I would love to hear enjoying good eating.” The Horse replied, “If oats had been the food of wolves, you would never have indulged your ears at the cost of your belly.”
body_child: A wolf saw a horse. The wolf said, "Go into that field. It has yummy oats. I saved them for you.". The horse said, "If wolves ate oats, you wouldn't talk so much." He meant the wolf was tricky.
moral: Men of evil reputation, when they perform a good deed, fail to get credit for it.
moral_elaborated: If people don't trust you, they won't believe you are being nice. Even if you do something good, they might think you have a hidden trick. It's hard to change a bad name.

title: The Two Men Who Were Enemies
body: TWO MEN, deadly enemies to each other, were sailing in the same vessel. Determined to keep as far apart as possible, the one seated himself in the stem, and the other in the prow of the ship. A violent storm arose, and with the vessel in great danger of sinking, the one in the stern inquired of the pilot which of the two ends of the ship would go down first. On his replying that he supposed it would be the prow, the Man said, “Death would not be grievous to me, if I could only see my Enemy die before me.”
body_child: Two men hated each other. They were on a boat together. One sat at the front, and one sat at the back. A big storm came. The boat was in danger. One man asked which part would sink first. When he heard it was the front, he said he wouldn't mind dying if his enemy died first.
moral: Hatred can make people wish for terrible things, even for themselves, just to see their enemy suffer.
moral_elaborated: Being very angry at someone can make you want bad things to happen. Sometimes, you might even want bad things to happen to yourself if it means your enemy gets hurt. It's not good to let anger control you like that.

title: The Gamecocks and the Partridge
body: A MAN had two Gamecocks in his poultry-yard. One day by chance he found a tame Partridge for sale. He purchased it and brought it home to be reared with his Gamecocks. When the Partridge was put into the poultry-yard, they struck at it and followed it about, so that the Partridge became grievously troubled and supposed that he was thus evilly treated because he was a stranger. Not long afterwards he saw the Cocks fighting together and not separating before one had well beaten the other. He then said to himself, “I shall no longer distress myself at being struck at by these Gamecocks, when I see that they cannot even refrain from quarreling with each other.”
body_child: A man had two fighting chickens. He bought a partridge. He put the partridge with the chickens. The chickens pecked and chased the partridge. The partridge felt sad and thought they were mean because it was new. Then, the partridge saw the chickens fight each other. One chicken beat the other. The partridge thought, "It's okay they peck me. They even peck each other!"
moral: We should not be too troubled by the ill-treatment of strangers, when we see that those who are intimate with us can hardly refrain from quarreling with each other.
moral_elaborated: If people you know fight with each other, don't feel too bad if they are a little rough with you. They are acting like that because they are used to being competitive. It's normal for them to argue sometimes.

title: The Fox and the Lion
body: A FOX saw a Lion confined in a cage, and standing near him, bitterly reviled him. The Lion said to the Fox, “It is not thou who revilest me; but this mischance which has befallen me.”
body_child: A fox saw a lion in a cage. The fox yelled mean things at the lion. The lion said, "You are not really calling me names. It's just my bad luck that I'm stuck here."
moral: It is often our misfortunes, and not ourselves, that are the object of reproach.
moral_elaborated: When something bad happens, people might say mean things. But it's not really you they are mad at, it's the situation. It's your bad luck that is causing the trouble, not you personally.

title: The Quack Frog
body: A FROG once upon a time came forth from his home in the marsh and proclaimed to all the beasts that he was a learned physician, skilled in the use of drugs and able to heal all diseases. A Fox asked him, “How can you pretend to prescribe for others, when you are unable to heal your own lame gait and wrinkled skin?”
body_child: A frog said he was a great doctor. He told everyone he could cure any sickness. A fox asked him, "How can you help others when you can't even fix your own wobbly walk or wrinkly skin?"
moral: Those who pretend to possess qualities which they do not, are easily found out.
moral_elaborated: If you pretend to be good at something you're not, people will notice. They will see that you can't even do it for yourself. It's better to be honest about what you can and cannot do.

title: The Lion, the Wolf, and the Fox
body: A LION, growing old, lay sick in his cave. All the beasts came to visit their king, except the Fox. The Wolf therefore, thinking that he had a capital opportunity, accused the Fox to the Lion of not paying any respect to him who had the rule over them all and of not coming to visit him. At that very moment the Fox came in and heard these last words of the Wolf. The Lion roaring out in a rage against him, the Fox sought an opportunity to defend himself and said, “And who of all those who have come to you have benefited you so much as I, who have traveled from place to place in every direction, and have sought and learnt from the physicians the means of healing you?” The Lion commanded him immediately to tell him the cure, when he replied, “You must flay a wolf alive and wrap his skin yet warm around you.” The Wolf was at once taken and flayed; whereon the Fox, turning to him, said with a smile, “You should have moved your master not to ill, but to good, will.”
body_child: The old Lion was sick. All the animals visited him, but the Fox did not. The Wolf told the Lion that the Fox did not care. The Fox came then. He told the Lion he found a cure for him. The cure was to flay a wolf. The Wolf was flayed. The Fox told the Wolf he should have been kind to the Lion.
moral: It is better to do good than to cause harm.
moral_elaborated: When you want to help someone, you should be kind. Causing harm to others, even if you think it will help, is not the right way. Always try to be good to everyone.

title: The Dog’s House
body: IN THE WINTERTIME, a Dog curled up in as small a space as possible on account of the cold, determined to make himself a house. However when the summer returned again, he lay asleep stretched at his full length and appeared to himself to be of a great size. Now he considered that it would be neither an easy nor a necessary work to make himself such a house as would accommodate him.
body_child: It was cold. A Dog wanted to make a house. When summer came, the Dog stretched out. He was big! He thought he did not need a house anymore. He was too big for the house he wanted to make.
moral: Do not put off until tomorrow what you can do today.
moral_elaborated: When it is cold, the Dog wants a house. But then it gets warm, and he forgets. Do not wait to do things you need to do. It is better to do them when you have the chance.

title: The North Wind and the Sun
body: THE NORTH WIND and the Sun disputed as to which was the most powerful, and agreed that he should be declared the victor who could first strip a wayfaring man of his clothes. The North Wind first tried his power and blew with all his might, but the keener his blasts, the closer the Traveler wrapped his cloak around him, until at last, resigning all hope of victory, the Wind called upon the Sun to see what he could do. The Sun suddenly shone out with all his warmth. The Traveler no sooner felt his genial rays than he took off one garment after another, and at last, fairly overcome with heat, undressed and bathed in a stream that lay in his path.
body_child: The North Wind and the Sun wanted to see who was stronger. They decided to see who could take a man's coat off first. The North Wind blew very hard. The man held his coat tighter. Then the Sun shone warm. The man took off his coat because he was hot. The Sun won!
moral: Persuasion is better than Force.
moral_elaborated: The North Wind was strong and loud, but it did not work. The Sun was warm and gentle, and it worked. Being kind and gentle can help you more than being loud and forceful. Sometimes, the best way to get what you want is to be nice.

title: The Crow and Mercury
body: A CROW caught in a snare prayed to Apollo to release him, making a vow to offer some frankincense at his shrine. But when rescued from his danger, he forgot his promise. Shortly afterwards, again caught in a snare, he passed by Apollo and made the same promise to offer frankincense to Mercury. Mercury soon appeared and said to him, “O thou most base fellow? how can I believe thee, who hast disowned and wronged thy former patron?”
body_child: A Crow got caught. He prayed to Apollo for help and promised a gift. The Crow was freed but forgot his promise. Later, he got caught again. He prayed to Mercury and promised a gift. Mercury came and said, "How can I believe you? You broke your promise to Apollo."
moral: Keep your promises.
moral_elaborated: When you make a promise, you should keep it. If you break a promise, people will not trust you. It is important to be honest and do what you say you will do.

title: The Fox and the Crane
body: A FOX invited a Crane to supper and provided nothing for his entertainment but some soup made of pulse, which was poured out into a broad flat stone dish. The soup fell out of the long bill of the Crane at every mouthful, and his vexation at not being able to eat afforded the Fox much amusement. The Crane, in his turn, asked the Fox to sup with him, and set before her a flagon with a long narrow mouth, so that he could easily insert his neck and enjoy its contents at his leisure. The Fox, unable even to taste it, met with a fitting requital, after the fashion of her own hospitality.
body_child: A Fox invited a Crane to dinner. The Fox gave soup on a flat plate. The Crane's long beak could not eat the soup. The Fox laughed. Then the Crane invited the Fox to dinner. The Crane gave food in a tall jar with a long neck. The Fox could not eat the food. The Crane ate it easily. The Fox got what she deserved.
moral: Treat others as you would like to be treated.
moral_elaborated: The Fox was not nice to the Crane when she gave dinner. So, the Crane was not nice back. When you are kind to others, they will be kind to you. When you are not kind, they might not be kind back.

title: The Wolf and the Lion
body: ROAMING BY the mountainside at sundown, a Wolf saw his own shadow become greatly extended and magnified, and he said to himself, “Why should I, being of such an immense size and extending nearly an acre in length, be afraid of the Lion? Ought I not to be acknowledged as King of all the collected beasts?” While he was indulging in these proud thoughts, a Lion fell upon him and killed him. He exclaimed with a too late repentance, “Wretched me! this overestimation of myself is the cause of my destruction.”
body_child: A wolf saw his shadow. It looked very big! He thought, "I am so big, I am not scared of the lion! I should be king!" But then, a lion came and ate him. The wolf wished he had not thought he was so great.
moral: Do not boast about yourself. Be humble.
moral_elaborated: It's good to know what you are good at. But it's not good to think you are better than everyone else. Be humble, and you will be safer.

title: The Birds, the Beasts, and the Bat
body: THE BIRDS waged war with the Beasts, and each were by turns the conquerors. A Bat, fearing the uncertain issues of the fight, always fought on the side which he felt was the strongest. When peace was proclaimed, his deceitful conduct was apparent to both combatants.
body_child: The birds and the animals were fighting. A bat was scared. He would fly with whichever side was winning. When they stopped fighting, everyone saw what the bat did. They did not like that he was tricky.
moral: Therefore being condemned by each for his treachery, he was driven forth from the light of day, and henceforth concealed himself in dark hiding-places, flying always alone and at night.
moral_elaborated: If you are not honest, others will not trust you. Being tricky can make you lonely and sad. It is better to be truthful.

title: The Spendthrift and the Swallow
body: A YOUNG MAN, a great spendthrift, had run through all his patrimony and had but one good cloak left. One day he happened to see a Swallow, which had appeared before its season, skimming along a pool and twittering gaily. He supposed that summer had come, and went and sold his cloak. Not many days later, winter set in again with renewed frost and cold. When he found the unfortunate Swallow lifeless on the ground, he said, “Unhappy bird! what have you done? By thus appearing before the springtime you have not only killed yourself, but you have wrought my destruction also.”
body_child: A young man spent all his money. He only had one coat left. He saw a little bird. The bird was out early, before it was warm. The young man thought, "Summer is here!" He sold his coat. Then, it got cold again. The bird froze. The young man was sad. He lost his coat and the bird died too soon.
moral: Do not be too quick to judge or act.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes things are not what they seem at first. It's important to wait and see what really happens. Don't make big decisions too fast or you might regret it.

title: The Trumpeter Taken Prisoner
body: A TRUMPETER, bravely leading on the soldiers, was captured by the enemy. He cried out to his captors, “Pray spare me, and do not take my life without cause or without inquiry. I have not slain a single man of your troop. I have no arms, and carry nothing but this one brass trumpet.” “That is the very reason for which you should be put to death,” they said; “for, while you do not fight yourself, your trumpet stirs all the others to battle.”
body_child: A trumpet player was captured by enemies. He begged them, "Please don't hurt me! I didn't fight anyone. I don't have a weapon, just my trumpet." The enemies said, "That's why we will hurt you! Your trumpet makes others want to fight."
moral: Your actions have consequences, even if you don't directly cause harm.
moral_elaborated: Even if you don't fight, your words or actions can make others want to fight. What you do can still cause trouble. Think about how your actions affect others.

title: The Owl and the Birds
body: AN OWL, in her wisdom, counseled the Birds that when the acorn first began to sprout, to pull it all up out of the ground and not allow it to grow. She said acorns would produce mistletoe, from which an irremediable poison, the bird-lime, would be extracted and by which they would be captured. The Owl next advised them to pluck up the seed of the flax, which men had sown, as it was a plant which boded no good to them. And, lastly, the Owl, seeing an archer approach, predicted that this man, being on foot, would contrive darts armed with feathers which would fly faster than the wings of the Birds themselves. The Birds gave no credence to these warning words, but considered the Owl to be beside herself and said that she was mad. But afterwards, finding her words were true, they wondered at her knowledge and deemed her to be the wisest of birds.
body_child: An owl was very wise. She told the birds to pull up acorn plants. She said they would make sticky stuff to catch them. She also told them to pull up flax plants. Then she saw a man and said he would make flying arrows. The birds did not listen. They thought she was crazy. But later, everything the owl said came true. The birds then knew she was very smart.
moral: Hence it is that when she appears they look to her as knowing all things, while she no longer gives them advice, but in solitude laments their past folly.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes people don't believe good advice when they hear it. They might think it's silly. But when bad things happen, they realize the advice was wise. It's important to listen to wise words.

title: The Goods and the Ills
body: ALL the Goods were once driven out by the Ills from that common share which they each had in the affairs of mankind; for the Ills by reason of their numbers had prevailed to possess the earth. The Goods wafted themselves to heaven and asked for a righteous vengeance on their persecutors. They entreated Jupiter that they might no longer be associated with the Ills, as they had nothing in common and could not live together, but were engaged in unceasing warfare; and that an indissoluble law might be laid down for their future protection. Jupiter granted their request and decreed that henceforth the Ills should visit the earth in company with each other, but that the Goods should one by one enter the habitations of men. Hence it arises that Ills abound, for they come not one by one, but in troops, and by no means singly: while the Goods proceed from Jupiter, and are given, not alike to all, but singly, and separately; and one by one to those who are able to discern them.
body_child: Bad things and good things used to share the world. But the bad things became many and took over. The good things went to heaven and asked for help. They said they didn't want to be with the bad things anymore because they always fought. So, the god Jupiter said the bad things would come to Earth together, but the good things would come one by one. That's why there are so many bad things all at once! But good things come slowly, to people who can see them.
moral: Good things and bad things are different and should be kept apart.
moral_elaborated: Good and bad things do not go well together. It is better to keep them separate. This is why bad things often come in big groups, while good things come one at a time.

title: The Ass in the Lion’s Skin
body: AN ASS, having put on the Lion’s skin, roamed about in the forest and amused himself by frightening all the foolish animals he met in his wanderings. At last coming upon a Fox, he tried to frighten him also, but the Fox no sooner heard the sound of his voice than he exclaimed, “I might possibly have been frightened myself, if I had not heard your bray.”
body_child: An ass wore a lion's skin. He walked in the forest and scared the other animals. He met a fox. He tried to scare the fox too. But the fox heard the ass make a sound. The fox said, "I might have been scared if I didn't hear your bray!" The ass made a loud "hee-haw" sound. It sounded like an ass, not a lion.
moral: Appearances can be deceiving.
moral_elaborated: Things might look one way, but they can be different on the inside. Just because someone or something looks scary or important, it doesn't mean they are. You can often tell what something really is by listening or paying close attention.

title: The Sparrow and the Hare
body: A HARE pounced upon by an eagle sobbed very much and uttered cries like a child. A Sparrow upbraided her and said, “Where now is thy remarkable swiftness of foot? Why were your feet so slow?” While the Sparrow was thus speaking, a hawk suddenly seized him and killed him. The Hare was comforted in her death, and expiring said, “Ah! you who so lately, when you supposed yourself safe, exulted over my calamity, have now reason to deplore a similar misfortune.”
body_child: A hare was caught by an eagle. She cried a lot like a baby. A sparrow saw her and said, "Where is your fast running now? Why were you so slow?" While the sparrow was talking, a hawk grabbed the sparrow and killed him. The hare felt a little better when she died. She thought, "You made fun of me when I was in trouble. Now you are in trouble too!"
moral: Do not mock others in their misfortune, for you may soon face a similar fate.
moral_elaborated: It's not nice to laugh at someone when they are having a hard time. You never know when bad things might happen to you too. It's better to be kind and understand, rather than to make fun of others.

title: The Flea and the Ox
body: A FLEA thus questioned an Ox: “What ails you, that being so huge and strong, you submit to the wrongs you receive from men and slave for them day by day, while I, being so small a creature, mercilessly feed on their flesh and drink their blood without stint?” The Ox replied: “I do not wish to be ungrateful, for I am loved and well cared for by men, and they often pat my head and shoulders.” “Woe’s me!” said the flea; “this very patting which you like, whenever it happens to me, brings with it my inevitable destruction.”
body_child: A little flea asked an ox, "Why are you so big and strong, but you work for people? I am small, but I bite them and drink their blood!" The ox said, "I like the people. They take care of me and pet me." The flea said, "Oh no! When they pet you, it's nice. When they pet me, it means they are going to squish me!"
moral: What is beneficial to one may be destructive to another.
moral_elaborated: Something that is good for one person might be very bad for another. What one creature can handle, another might not survive. We are all different and need different things to be okay.

title: The Ass and His Purchaser
body: A MAN wished to purchase an Ass, and agreed with its owner that he should try out the animal before he bought him. He took the Ass home and put him in the straw-yard with his other Asses, upon which the new animal left all the others and at once joined the one that was most idle and the greatest eater of them all. Seeing this, the man put a halter on him and led him back to his owner. On being asked how, in so short a time, he could have made a trial of him, he answered, “I do not need a trial; I know that he will be just the same as the one he chose for his companion.”
body_child: A man wanted to buy a donkey. He got to try the donkey before he bought it. He took the donkey home and put it with his other donkeys. The new donkey ignored the others and went right to the laziest donkey, the one who ate the most food. The man saw this and took the donkey back. The owner asked how he knew so fast. The man said, "I don't need to try him. I know he will be like the donkey he picked to be friends with."
moral: A man is known by the company he keeps.
moral_elaborated: The friends we choose show what we are like. If you spend time with people who are lazy or mean, people might think you are lazy or mean too. It's important to choose good friends who make you want to be your best self.

title: The Dove and the Crow
body: A DOVE shut up in a cage was boasting of the large number of young ones which she had hatched. A Crow hearing her, said: “My good friend, cease from this unseasonable boasting. The larger the number of your family, the greater your cause of sorrow, in seeing them shut up in this prison-house.”
body_child: A dove was in a cage. She told a crow that she had many babies. The crow said, “It is sad that your babies are stuck in a cage with you.”
moral: Do not boast about things that do not bring true happiness.
moral_elaborated: Boasting about something that makes you sad is not good. It is better to be content with what you have and focus on true happiness. Freedom and well-being are more important than just having a lot of things.

title: The Man and the Satyr
body: A MAN and a Satyr once drank together in token of a bond of alliance being formed between them. One very cold wintry day, as they talked, the Man put his fingers to his mouth and blew on them. When the Satyr asked the reason for this, he told him that he did it to warm his hands because they were so cold. Later on in the day they sat down to eat, and the food prepared was quite scalding. The Man raised one of the dishes a little towards his mouth and blew in it. When the Satyr again inquired the reason, he said that he did it to cool the meat, which was too hot. “I can no longer consider you as a friend,” said the Satyr, “a fellow who with the same breath blows hot and cold.”
body_child: A man and a Satyr were friends. One cold day, the man blew on his hands to warm them. Later, they ate food that was too hot. The man blew on the food to cool it. The Satyr said, “I can't be friends with someone who blows hot and cold.”
moral: Be consistent in your words and actions.
moral_elaborated: Be honest and do what you say you will do. People do not like it when someone says one thing and does the opposite. Being dependable makes you a good friend.

title: Jupiter, Neptune, Minerva, and Momus
body: ACCORDING to an ancient legend, the first man was made by Jupiter, the first bull by Neptune, and the first house by Minerva. On the completion of their labours, a dispute arose as to which had made the most perfect work. They agreed to appoint Momus as judge, and to abide by his decision. Momus, however, being very envious of the handicraft of each, found fault with all. He first blamed the work of Neptune because he had not made the horns of the bull below his eyes, so he might better see where to strike. He then condemned the work of Jupiter, because he had not placed the heart of man on the outside, that everyone might read the thoughts of the evil disposed and take precautions against the intended mischief. And, lastly, he inveighed against Minerva because she had not contrived iron wheels in the foundation of her house, so its inhabitants might more easily remove if a neighbor proved unpleasant.
moral: Jupiter, indignant at such inveterate faultfinding, drove him from his office of judge, and expelled him from the mansions of Olympus.
body_child: Jupiter made the first man. Neptune made the first bull. Minerva made the first house. They asked Momus to say whose work was best. Momus found fault with everything. He said Neptune should have put the bull's horns lower. He said Jupiter should have put man's heart outside. He said Minerva should have put wheels on her house. Jupiter was angry and kicked Momus out.
moral_elaborated: Always being critical is not nice. Momus was rude and didn't appreciate the work. It's better to be kind and look for good things in others.

title: The Eagle and the Jackdaw
body: AN EAGLE, flying down from his perch on a lofty rock, seized upon a lamb and carried him aloft in his talons. A Jackdaw, who witnessed the capture of the lamb, was stirred with envy and determined to emulate the strength and flight of the Eagle. He flew around with a great whir of his wings and settled upon a large ram, with the intention of carrying him off, but his claws became entangled in the ram’s fleece and he was not able to release himself, although he fluttered with his feathers as much as he could. The shepherd, seeing what had happened, ran up and caught him. He at once clipped the Jackdaw’s wings, and taking him home at night, gave him to his children. On their saying, “Father, what kind of bird is it?” he replied, “To my certain knowledge he is a Daw; but he would like you to think an Eagle.”
body_child: An eagle caught a lamb. A jackdaw saw this and wanted to be like the eagle. He tried to carry off a big ram, but got stuck in its wool. A shepherd caught the jackdaw. He cut its wings and told his kids it was a jackdaw trying to pretend to be an eagle.
moral: Do not try to be someone you are not.
moral_elaborated: It's not good to act like someone you're not. The jackdaw got stuck because he tried to be an eagle. Be happy with who you are and don't try to fool others.

title: The Eagle and the Fox
body: AN EAGLE and a Fox formed an intimate friendship and decided to live near each other. The Eagle built her nest in the branches of a tall tree, while the Fox crept into the underwood and there produced her young. Not long after they had agreed upon this plan, the Eagle, being in want of provision for her young ones, swooped down while the Fox was out, seized upon one of the little cubs, and feasted herself and her brood. The Fox on her return, discovered what had happened, but was less grieved for the death of her young than for her inability to avenge them. A just retribution, however, quickly fell upon the Eagle. While hovering near an altar, on which some villagers were sacrificing a goat, she suddenly seized a piece of the flesh, and carried it, along with a burning cinder, to her nest. A strong breeze soon fanned the spark into a flame, and the eaglets, as yet unfledged and helpless, were roasted in their nest and dropped down dead at the bottom of the tree. There, in the sight of the Eagle, the Fox gobbled them up.
body_child: An eagle and a fox were friends. The eagle lived in a tree, and the fox lived nearby. One day, the eagle ate one of the fox's babies. Later, the eagle took some meat from an altar, but it had a burning coal. The coal burned her nest, and her babies died. The fox ate the eagle's babies.
moral: Those who harm others will suffer the same fate.
moral_elaborated: If you do something mean to someone, something mean might happen to you. The eagle ate the fox's baby. Then the eagle's babies died. It's good to be kind to everyone.

title: The Two Bags
body: EVERY MAN, according to an ancient legend, is born into the world with two bags suspended from his neck all bag in front full of his neighbors’ faults, and a large bag behind filled with his own faults.
body_child: Everyone has two bags. One bag is in front and holds everyone else's mistakes. The other bag is behind and holds our own mistakes. We can see other people's mistakes easily. But we don't often see our own mistakes.
moral: Hence it is that men are quick to see the faults of others, and yet are often blind to their own failings.
moral_elaborated: It is easy to see when other people make mistakes. But it is hard to see our own mistakes. We should try to see our own mistakes too.

title: The Bitch and Her Whelps
body: A BITCH, ready to whelp, earnestly begged a shepherd for a place where she might litter. When her request was granted, she besought permission to rear her puppies in the same spot. The shepherd again consented. But at last the Bitch, protected by the bodyguard of her Whelps, who had now grown up and were able to defend themselves, asserted her exclusive right to the place and would not permit the shepherd to approach.
body_child: A mother dog wanted a safe place to have her puppies. The shepherd let her have a spot. Then she asked to keep her puppies there until they grew up. The shepherd said yes again. When the puppies were big and strong, they helped the mother dog. Now, the mother dog said the spot was only for them. She would not let the shepherd come near.
moral: Do not be greedy, or you will lose all that you have.
moral_elaborated: The mother dog was greedy. She wanted to keep the whole spot for herself and her puppies. Because she was greedy, she lost the kindness the shepherd had shown her. She should have been thankful and shared.

title: The Stag at the Pool
body: A STAG overpowered by heat came to a spring to drink. Seeing his own shadow reflected in the water, he greatly admired the size and variety of his horns, but felt angry with himself for having such slender and weak feet. While he was thus contemplating himself, a Lion appeared at the pool and crouched to spring upon him. The Stag immediately took to flight, and exerting his utmost speed, as long as the plain was smooth and open kept himself easily at a safe distance from the Lion. But entering a wood he became entangled by his horns, and the Lion quickly came up to him and caught him. When too late, he thus reproached himself: “Woe is me! How I have deceived myself! These feet which would have saved me I despised, and I gloried in these antlers which have proved my destruction.”
body_child: A thirsty deer went to a pool to drink. He saw his reflection in the water. He loved his big, fancy antlers. But he did not like his skinny legs. Suddenly, a lion jumped out! The deer ran away very fast. His long legs helped him run far away on the open ground. But then he ran into some trees. His antlers got stuck in the branches. The lion caught him. The deer said, 'I wish I had not liked my antlers so much. My fast legs could have saved me!'
moral: What is most truly valuable is often underrated.
moral_elaborated: The deer thought his antlers were the best. But his thin legs were actually more important for saving his life. We should not judge things by how they look. We should think about what is really useful and important.

title: The Lark Burying Her Father
body: THE LARK (according to an ancient legend) was created before the earth itself, and when her father died, as there was no earth, she could find no place of burial for him. She let him lie uninterred for five days, and on the sixth day, not knowing what else to do, she buried him in her own head. Hence she obtained her crest, which is popularly said to be her father’s grave-hillock.
body_child: A long, long time ago, there was no land. A baby bird called a lark's father died. The lark had no place to bury him. She waited five days. On the sixth day, she didn't know what to do. So, she buried her father in her own head! That is why larks have a crest of feathers on their heads. People say it is like a little hill where her father is buried.
moral: Youth’s first duty is reverence to parents.
moral_elaborated: It is important to respect and care for our parents. The lark showed great love for her father. Even when she had no place to bury him, she found a way to honor him.

title: The Gnat and the Bull
body: A GNAT settled on the horn of a Bull, and sat there a long time. Just as he was about to fly off, he made a buzzing noise, and inquired of the Bull if he would like him to go. The Bull replied, “I did not know you had come, and I shall not miss you when you go away.”
body_child: A tiny gnat landed on a bull's horn. He sat there for a long time. When he was ready to fly away, he buzzed loudly. He asked the bull if he wanted him to leave. The bull said, 'I didn't even know you were here. I won't miss you when you leave.'
moral: Some men are of more consequence in their own eyes than in the eyes of their neighbors.
moral_elaborated: The gnat thought he was very important. He thought the bull would miss him. But the bull didn't even notice he was there. This shows that sometimes we think we are more important than we really are to others.

title: The Monkey and the Camel
body: THE BEASTS of the forest gave a splendid entertainment at which the Monkey stood up and danced. Having vastly delighted the assembly, he sat down amidst universal applause. The Camel, envious of the praises bestowed on the Monkey and desiring to divert to himself the favour of the guests, proposed to stand up in his turn and dance for their amusement. He moved about in so utterly ridiculous a manner that the Beasts, in a fit of indignation, set upon him with clubs and drove him out of the assembly.
body_child: The Monkey danced for all the forest animals. Everyone clapped and cheered! The Camel was jealous. He wanted everyone to cheer for him. So, the Camel tried to dance too. But he looked so silly! The animals got mad and chased him away with sticks.
moral: It is absurd to ape our betters.
moral_elaborated: Trying to be like someone else when you can't do it well makes you look silly. It's better to be yourself and do things you are good at.

title: The Dogs and the Hides
body: SOME DOGS famished with hunger saw a number of cowhides steeping in a river. Not being able to reach them, they agreed to drink up the river, but it happened that they burst themselves with drinking long before they reached the hides.
body_child: Some hungry dogs saw yummy cow hides in a river. They wanted to eat them! But the river was too wide. So, the dogs decided to drink all the water. They drank and drank and drank. But they drank too much and their tummies got too big! They burst before they could eat the hides.
moral: Attempt not impossibilities.
moral_elaborated: Don't try to do things that are impossible. You might hurt yourself trying. It's better to think of a plan that can actually work.

title: The Jackdaw and the Fox
body: A HALF-FAMISHED JACKDAW seated himself on a fig-tree, which had produced some fruit entirely out of season, and waited in the hope that the figs would ripen. A Fox seeing him sitting so long and learning the reason of his doing so, said to him, “You are indeed, sir, sadly deceiving yourself; you are indulging a hope strong enough to cheat you, but which will never reward you with enjoyment.”
