body_child: A hungry Jackdaw sat in a tree. He saw some figs that were not ripe yet. He hoped they would get ripe soon so he could eat them. A Fox saw him. The Fox said, "You are tricking yourself! You hope for something that will never happen. You won't get to eat those figs."
moral: Hope for what is possible, not what is impossible.
moral_elaborated: It's good to have hope, but make sure you are hoping for something that can actually happen. Don't waste your time wishing for things that are impossible. Be realistic.

title: Mercury and the Workmen
body: A WORKMAN, felling wood by the side of a river, let his axe drop by accident into a deep pool. Being thus deprived of the means of his livelihood, he sat down on the bank and lamented his hard fate. Mercury appeared and demanded the cause of his tears. After he told him his misfortune, Mercury plunged into the stream, and, bringing up a golden axe, inquired if that were the one he had lost. On his saying that it was not, Mercury disappeared beneath the water a second time, returned with a silver axe in his hand, and again asked the Workman if it were his. When the Workman said it was not, he dived into the pool for the third time and brought up the axe that had been lost. The Workman claimed it and expressed his joy at its recovery. Mercury, pleased with his honesty, gave him the golden and silver axes in addition to his own. The Workman, on his return to his house, related to his companions all that had happened. One of them at once resolved to try and secure the same good fortune for himself. He ran to the river and threw his axe on purpose into the pool at the same place, and sat down on the bank to weep. Mercury appeared to him just as he hoped he would; and having learned the cause of his grief, plunged into the stream and brought up a golden axe, inquiring if he had lost it. The Workman seized it greedily, and declared that truly it was the very same axe that he had lost. Mercury, displeased at his knavery, not only took away the golden axe, but refused to recover for him the axe he had thrown into the pool.
body_child: A woodcutter accidentally dropped his axe into a river. He was very sad because he needed his axe to work. The god Mercury appeared. Mercury dove into the river and found a golden axe. He asked the woodcutter if it was his. The woodcutter said no. Mercury found a silver axe and asked again. The woodcutter said no. Then Mercury found the woodcutter's real axe. The woodcutter was happy and told the truth. Mercury was pleased and gave him the golden and silver axes too! Another worker saw this and wanted the gold axe. He threw his axe in the river on purpose. When Mercury asked if he lost his axe, the worker lied and said yes to the gold axe. Mercury knew he was lying and took the gold axe away. He didn't give him his own axe back either.
moral: Honesty is rewarded.
moral_elaborated: When you are honest, good things can happen to you. Telling the truth is always the best choice. Cheating or lying will not bring you happiness.

title: The Peasant and the Apple-Tree
body: A PEASANT had in his garden an Apple-Tree which bore no fruit but only served as a harbor for the sparrows and grasshoppers. He resolved to cut it down, and taking his axe in his hand, made a bold stroke at its roots. The grasshoppers and sparrows entreated him not to cut down the tree that sheltered them, but to spare it, and they would sing to him and lighten his labours. He paid no attention to their request, but gave the tree a second and a third blow with his axe. When he reached the hollow of the tree, he found a hive full of honey. Having tasted the honeycomb, he threw down his axe, and looking on the tree as sacred, took great care of it.
body_child: A farmer had an apple tree that didn't grow apples. Birds and bugs lived in it. The farmer wanted to cut it down. The birds and bugs begged him not to. They said they would sing for him. But the farmer kept chopping. He chopped into the tree and found honey! He tasted the honey and decided to keep the tree safe and sound. It was a special tree after all.
moral: Self-interest alone moves some men.
moral_elaborated: Some people only care about what they can get for themselves. They don't do things to be nice unless they get something good in return. It's important to remember that not everyone is motivated by kindness.

title: The Two Soldiers and the Robber
body: TWO SOLDIERS traveling together were set upon by a Robber. The one fled away; the other stood his ground and defended himself with his stout right hand. The Robber being slain, the timid companion ran up and drew his sword, and then, throwing back his traveling cloak said, “I’ll at him, and I’ll take care he shall learn whom he has attacked.” On this, he who had fought with the Robber made answer, “I only wish that you had helped me just now, even if it had been only with those words, for I should have been the more encouraged, believing them to be true; but now put up your sword in its sheath and hold your equally useless tongue, till you can deceive others who do not know you. I, indeed, who have experienced with what speed you run away, know right well that no dependence can be placed on your valor.”
body_child: Two soldiers were walking. A robber jumped out! One soldier ran away. The other soldier fought the robber. The robber was hurt. The other soldier came back. He said, "I will fight him too!" But he had already run away. The first soldier said, "You didn't help me. You only said brave words. Your words are not helpful because you ran away." The first soldier told him to put his sword away.
moral: Empty boasts are useless; actions speak louder than words.
moral_elaborated: It's easy to say brave things. But it's much harder to actually do them. True bravery is shown by what you do, not by what you say.

title: The Shepherd and the Sheep
body: A SHEPHERD driving his Sheep to a wood, saw an oak of unusual size full of acorns, and spreading his cloak under the branches, he climbed up into the tree and shook them down. The Sheep eating the acorns inadvertently frayed and tore the cloak. When the Shepherd came down and saw what was done, he said, “O you most ungrateful creatures! You provide wool to make garments for all other men, but you destroy the clothes of him who feeds you.”
body_child: A shepherd had sheep. He was in the woods. He saw a big oak tree with acorns. He shook the acorns down for the sheep to eat. The sheep ate the acorns. They also chewed and tore his warm cloak. When the shepherd came down, he was sad. He said, "You are not thankful! You give wool to others. But you tore my cloak that keeps me warm."
moral: Do not harm those who help you.
moral_elaborated: The sheep ate the acorns the shepherd gave them. But they tore his cloak. We should be thankful for help. We should not hurt the people who are kind to us.

title: The Trees Under the Protection of the Gods
body: THE GODS, according to an ancient legend, made choice of certain trees to be under their special protection. Jupiter chose the oak, Venus the myrtle, Apollo the laurel, Cybele the pine, and Hercules the poplar. Minerva, wondering why they had preferred trees not yielding fruit, inquired the reason for their choice. Jupiter replied, “It is lest we should seem to covet the honour for the fruit.” But said Minerva, “Let anyone say what he will the olive is more dear to me on account of its fruit.” Then said Jupiter, “My daughter, you are rightly called wise; for unless what we do is useful, the glory of it is vain.”
body_child: The gods picked special trees. Jupiter chose the oak tree. Venus chose the myrtle tree. Apollo chose the laurel tree. The goddess Minerva asked why they picked trees without fruit. Jupiter said it was so people wouldn't think they wanted the fruit. Minerva said she liked the olive tree because it had fruit. Jupiter said Minerva was wise. He said that if something isn't useful, it's not really important.
moral: True worth is found in usefulness, not in empty show.
moral_elaborated: The gods chose trees that looked nice. But Minerva liked the olive tree because it gave food. Jupiter said she was wise. This means that things that are useful are more valuable than things that just look good.

title: The Flea and the Wrestler
body: A FLEA settled upon the bare foot of a Wrestler and bit him, causing the man to call loudly upon Hercules for help. When the Flea a second time hopped upon his foot, he groaned and said, “O Hercules! if you will not help me against a Flea, how can I hope for your assistance against greater antagonists?”
body_child: A tiny flea bit a wrestler's foot. The wrestler yelled for help from Hercules, a strong hero. The flea bit him again. The wrestler moaned. He said, "Hercules, if you can't help me with a little flea, how will you help me with bigger problems?"
moral: If you cannot overcome small difficulties, you will not be able to face larger ones.
moral_elaborated: The wrestler was upset about a tiny flea bite. He asked for help from a big hero. This shows that even small problems can be annoying. If you can't handle small problems, you won't be ready for big ones.

title: The Lion and the Fox
body: A FOX entered into partnership with a Lion on the pretense of becoming his servant. Each undertook his proper duty in accordance with his own nature and powers. The Fox discovered and pointed out the prey; the Lion sprang on it and seized it. The Fox soon became jealous of the Lion carrying off the Lion’s share, and said that he would no longer find out the prey, but would capture it on his own account. The next day he attempted to snatch a lamb from the fold, but he himself fell prey to the huntsmen and hounds.
body_child: A fox wanted to work with a lion. The fox said he would be the lion's helper. The fox would find food. The lion would catch the food. The fox got mad because the lion got the bigger part. The fox said he would catch food by himself. The next day, the fox tried to get a lamb. But he got caught by hunters.
moral: Greed leads to ruin.
moral_elaborated: The fox and the lion worked together. But the fox wanted more for himself. He was greedy. Because he was greedy, he got into trouble. He ended up being caught.

title: Truth and the Traveler
body: A WAYFARING MAN, traveling in the desert, met a woman standing alone and terribly dejected. He inquired of her, “Who art thou?” “My name is Truth,” she replied. “And for what cause,” he asked, “have you left the city to dwell alone here in the wilderness?” She made answer, “Because in former times, falsehood was with few, but is now with all men.”
body_child: A man was walking in the desert. He saw a woman who looked very sad. He asked her name. She said, "My name is Truth." He asked why she was all alone. She said, "A long time ago, not many people told lies. Now, almost everyone does."
moral: It is better to tell the truth.
moral_elaborated: Being truthful is important. Even when it's hard, telling the truth is the right thing to do. Lies can lead to sad things, but the truth will always be best.

title: The Manslayer
body: A MAN committed a murder, and was pursued by the relations of the man whom he murdered. On his reaching the river Nile he saw a Lion on its bank and being fearfully afraid, climbed up a tree. He found a serpent in the upper branches of the tree, and again being greatly alarmed, he threw himself into the river, where a crocodile caught him and ate him. Thus the earth, the air, and the water alike refused shelter to a murderer.
body_child: A man did a very bad thing. He hurt someone and ran away. People were chasing him. He ran to a big river. He saw a lion and climbed a tree. A snake was in the tree! He jumped into the river. A big fish ate him. The world did not want to help someone who did wrong.
moral: Those who do wrong will find no escape from justice.
moral_elaborated: If you do something very bad, you cannot hide from it. No matter where you go, bad actions can catch up with you. It is important to be good so you don't have to run away.

title: The Lion and the Eagle
body: AN EAGLE stayed his flight and entreated a Lion to make an alliance with him to their mutual advantage. The Lion replied, “I have no objection, but you must excuse me for requiring you to find surety for your good faith, for how can I trust anyone as a friend who is able to fly away from his bargain whenever he pleases?”
body_child: An eagle asked a lion to be friends. They could help each other. The lion said, "I want to be friends, but I need a promise. How can I trust you? You can fly away anytime you want."
moral: Try before you trust.
moral_elaborated: It's good to make new friends. But sometimes you need to wait and see if someone is a good friend. It takes time to know if you can really trust someone.

title: The Ass and His Driver
body: AN ASS, being driven along a high road, suddenly started off and bolted to the brink of a deep precipice. While he was in the act of throwing himself over, his owner seized him by the tail, endeavoring to pull him back. When the Ass persisted in his effort, the man let him go and said, “Conquer, but conquer to your cost.”
body_child: A man was leading a donkey. The donkey suddenly ran very fast. It ran to the edge of a very deep cliff! The man grabbed the donkey's tail to pull it back. The donkey kept trying to jump. So, the man let go. He said, "Go ahead, but you will be sorry."
moral: Let those who act unwisely learn from their own experience.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes people want to do something, even if it's a bad idea. If you try to stop them and they don't listen, they might learn a lesson by doing it themselves. They will have to deal with the results.

title: The Thrush and the Fowler
body: A THRUSH was feeding on a myrtle-tree and did not move from it because its berries were so delicious. A Fowler observed her staying so long in one spot, and having well bird-limed his reeds, caught her. The Thrush, being at the point of death, exclaimed, “O foolish creature that I am! For the sake of a little pleasant food I have deprived myself of my life.”
body_child: A little bird was eating yummy berries from a bush. It stayed there for a long time. A hunter saw the bird and caught it with sticky sticks. The bird said, "Oh no! I ate too much and forgot to be careful. Because I wanted tasty food, I lost my life."
moral: Do not let greed lead you into danger.
moral_elaborated: It's nice to enjoy good things. But if you want something too much, it can make you careless. Always be aware of your surroundings, even when you are enjoying something.

title: The Mother and the Wolf
body: A FAMISHED WOLF was prowling about in the morning in search of food. As he passed the door of a cottage built in the forest, he heard a Mother say to her child, “Be quiet, or I will throw you out of the window, and the Wolf shall eat you.” The Wolf sat all day waiting at the door. In the evening he heard the same woman fondling her child and saying: “You are quiet now, and if the Wolf should come, we will kill him.” The Wolf, hearing these words, went home, gasping with cold and hunger. When he reached his den, Mistress Wolf inquired of him why he returned wearied and supperless, so contrary to his wont. He replied: “Why, forsooth! use I gave credence to the words of a woman!”
body_child: A hungry wolf looked for food. He heard a mom tell her baby, “Be quiet or the wolf will eat you!” The wolf waited all day. Later, the mom said, “You are quiet now. If the wolf comes, we will hurt him.” The wolf went home hungry. He told his wife he did not believe what the woman said.
moral: Words are not always true.
moral_elaborated: People sometimes say different things. They might say one thing to scare someone. Then they say something else when that person is not around. It is hard to know what is true.

title: The Hen and the Swallow
body: A HEN finding the eggs of a viper and carefully keeping them warm, nourished them into life. A Swallow, observing what she had done, said, “You silly creature! why have you hatched these vipers which, when they shall have grown, will inflict injury on all, beginning with yourself?”
body_child: A hen found snake eggs. She kept them warm to hatch them. A bird saw this. The bird said, “You are silly! These snakes will hurt everyone, even you!”
moral: Beware of what you do, for it may bring harm to you.
moral_elaborated: Be careful about your actions. What you do can have bad results. Sometimes your own actions can hurt you the most.

title: The Rose and the Amaranth
body: AN AMARANTH planted in a garden near a Rose-Tree, thus addressed it: “What a lovely flower is the Rose, a favourite alike with Gods and with men. I envy you your beauty and your perfume.” The Rose replied, “I indeed, dear Amaranth, flourish but for a brief season! If no cruel hand pluck me from my stem, yet I must perish by an early doom. But thou art immortal and dost never fade, but bloomest for ever in renewed youth.”
body_child: A flower called Amaranth talked to a Rose. “You are so pretty,” said the Amaranth. “Everyone loves you.” The Rose said, “But I don’t last long. I will fall off soon. You are always beautiful and never fade.”
moral: Do not envy others their temporary gifts.
moral_elaborated: It is easy to be jealous of what others have. But remember that some good things do not last forever. Be happy with what you have and don't wish for what others have if it is only for a short time.

title: The Travelers and the Plane-Tree
body: TWO TRAVELERS, worn out by the heat of the summer’s sun, laid themselves down at noon under the widespreading branches of a Plane-Tree. As they rested under its shade, one of the Travelers said to the other, “What a singularly useless tree is the Plane! It bears no fruit, and is not of the least service to man.” The Plane-Tree, interrupting him, said, “You ungrateful fellows! Do you, while receiving benefits from me and resting under my shade, dare to describe me as useless, and unprofitable?”
body_child: Two friends were hot in the sun. They sat under a big tree for shade. One friend said, “This tree is not useful. It has no fruit.” The tree heard them. It said, “You are not thankful! You are resting in my shade, but you call me useless.”
moral: Some men underrate their best blessings.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes people don't see how good things are for them. They complain about something that is actually helping them. Be thankful for the good things you have.

title: The Ass and the Horse
body: AN ASS besought a Horse to spare him a small portion of his feed. “Yes,” said the Horse; “if any remains out of what I am now eating I will give it you for the sake of my own superior dignity, and if you will come when I reach my own stall in the evening, I will give you a little sack full of barley.” The Ass replied, “Thank you. But I can’t think that you, who refuse me a little matter now, will by and by confer on me a greater benefit.”
body_child: An ass asked a horse for some food. The horse said, “I will give you some later if I have extra. Come to my stall tonight, and I will give you barley.” The ass said, “Thank you. But I don’t think you will give me more later if you won’t give me a little now.”
moral: Promises are worth little when not backed by present action.
moral_elaborated: It is easy to promise things for the future. But if someone does not help you now, their promises might not mean much. We should be careful to trust people who show they are willing to help.

title: The Crow and the Sheep
body: A TROUBLESOME CROW seated herself on the back of a Sheep. The Sheep, much against his will, carried her backward and forward for a long time, and at last said, “If you had treated a dog in this way, you would have had your deserts from his sharp teeth.” To this the Crow replied, “I despise the weak and yield to the strong. I know whom I may bully and whom I must flatter; and I thus prolong my life to a good old age.”
body_child: A naughty crow sat on a sheep's back. The sheep did not like it. The sheep said, "If you did this to a dog, he would bite you." The crow said, "I am mean to weak things and nice to strong things. I know who to bother and who to be nice to. That's how I live a long time."
moral: Bully the weak and flatter the strong.
moral_elaborated: It is not good to be mean to those who are weaker than you. It is also not wise to only be nice to those who are strong. Everyone deserves kindness.

title: The Fox and the Bramble
body: A FOX was mounting a hedge when he lost his footing and caught hold of a Bramble to save himself. Having pricked and grievously torn the soles of his feet, he accused the Bramble because, when he had fled to her for assistance, she had used him worse than the hedge itself. The Bramble, interrupting him, said, “But you really must have been out of your senses to fasten yourself on me, who am myself always accustomed to fasten upon others.”
body_child: A fox was climbing a fence. He slipped and grabbed a thorny bush to stop himself. The bush hurt his feet badly. The fox blamed the bush. The bush said, "You are silly to grab me! I always prick things, that's what I do."
moral: Do not trust those who have a bad reputation.
moral_elaborated: If someone is known for being hurtful, it's not a good idea to rely on them. You might get hurt if you trust them. It's better to be careful and choose friends wisely.

title: The Ass and the Charger
body: AN ASS congratulated a Horse on being ungrudgingly and carefully provided for, while he himself had scarcely enough to eat and not even that without hard work. But when war broke out, a heavily armed soldier mounted the Horse, and riding him to the charge, rushed into the very midst of the enemy. The Horse was wounded and fell dead on the battlefield.
moral: Then the Ass, seeing all these things, changed his mind, and commiserated the Horse.
body_child: An ass was jealous of a horse. The horse had lots of food and didn't have to work hard. The ass had to work hard for little food. Then, a war started. A soldier rode the horse into battle. The horse was hurt and died. The ass felt sad for the horse.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, a hard life can be safer than an easy one. Things that seem good can also be dangerous. It's important to think carefully about what we want.

title: The Lion, Jupiter, and the Elephant
body: THE LION wearied Jupiter with his frequent complaints. “It is true, O Jupiter!” he said, “that I am gigantic in strength, handsome in shape, and powerful in attack. I have jaws well provided with teeth, and feet furnished with claws, and I lord it over all the beasts of the forest, and what a disgrace it is, that being such as I am, I should be frightened by the crowing of a cock.” Jupiter replied, “Why do you blame me without a cause? I have given you all the attributes which I possess myself, and your courage never fails you except in this one instance.” On hearing this the Lion groaned and lamented very much and, reproaching himself with his cowardice, wished that he might die. As these thoughts passed through his mind, he met an Elephant and came close to hold a conversation with him. After a time he observed that the Elephant shook his ears very often, and he inquired what was the matter and why his ears moved with such a tremor every now and then. Just at that moment a Gnat settled on the head of the Elephant, and he replied, “Do you see that little buzzing insect? If it enters my ear, my fate is sealed. I should die presently.” The Lion said, “Well, since so huge a beast is afraid of a tiny gnat, I will no more complain, nor wish myself dead. I find myself, even as I am, better off than the Elephant.”
body_child: The lion complained to Jupiter. He said, "I am strong and scary, but a rooster's crow frightens me." Jupiter said, "You are brave except for that one thing." The lion felt sad. He met an elephant. The elephant's ears twitched. The lion asked why. The elephant said, "A tiny bug might go in my ear and I would die." The lion thought, "Even a big elephant is scared of small things. I am lucky I am not like him."
moral: Be content with what you have.
moral_elaborated: It's not good to always wish for something else. Even people who seem to have it all have problems. Be happy with what you have and don't compare yourself to others.

title: The Dog and the Oyster
body: A DOG, used to eating eggs, saw an Oyster and, opening his mouth to its widest extent, swallowed it down with the utmost relish, supposing it to be an egg. Soon afterwards suffering great pain in his stomach, he said, “I deserve all this torment, for my folly in thinking that everything round must be an egg.”
body_child: A dog liked to eat eggs. He saw an oyster. He thought it was an egg and swallowed it whole. His tummy hurt very much. The dog said, "It's my fault. I thought everything round is an egg."
moral: They who act without sufficient thought, will often fall into unsuspected danger.
moral_elaborated: If you do things without thinking first, you might get into trouble. It's important to look carefully and think before you act. Otherwise, you might face unexpected problems.

title: The Mules and the Robbers
body: TWO MULES well-laden with packs were trudging along. One carried panniers filled with money, the other sacks weighted with grain. The Mule carrying the treasure walked with head erect, as if conscious of the value of his burden, and tossed up and down the clear-toned bells fastened to his neck. His companion followed with quiet and easy step. All of a sudden Robbers rushed upon them from their hiding-places, and in the scuffle with their owners, wounded with a sword the Mule carrying the treasure, which they greedily seized while taking no notice of the grain. The Mule which had been robbed and wounded bewailed his misfortunes. The other replied, “I am indeed glad that I was thought so little of, for I have lost nothing, nor am I hurt with any wound.”
body_child: Two mules walked down the road. One mule carried money. The other mule carried grain. The mule with the money walked tall. He had bells that jingled. The other mule walked slowly. Suddenly, bad men jumped out! They hurt the money mule and took his money. They did not take the grain. The money mule was sad. The grain mule said, "I am happy I was not hurt. I did not lose anything."
moral: Better to have less and be safe, than to have much and be in danger.
moral_elaborated: It is better to be safe than to have many possessions. Sometimes, having too much can bring you trouble. Being safe is more important than having many things.

title: The Lamb and the Wolf
body: A WOLF pursued a Lamb, which fled for refuge to a certain Temple. The Wolf called out to him and said, “The Priest will slay you in sacrifice, if he should catch you.” On which the Lamb replied, “It would be better for me to be sacrificed in the Temple than to be eaten by you.”
moral: It is better to face a greater danger bravely than to fall into a lesser one ignominiously.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, a hard choice can lead to a better outcome. It is better to face a difficult situation with courage. This is better than escaping to something bad that is worse.

title: The Partridge and the Fowler
body: A FOWLER caught a Partridge and was about to kill it. The Partridge earnestly begged him to spare his life, saying, “Pray, master, permit me to live and I will entice many Partridges to you in recompense for your mercy to me.” The Fowler replied, “I shall now with less scruple take your life, because you are willing to save it at the cost of betraying your friends and relations.”
moral: A traitor is worse than a victim.
moral_elaborated: It is not good to betray your friends. Even if you want to save yourself, it is wrong to hurt others. Trustworthy people are more valuable than traitors.

title: The Flea and the Man
body: A MAN, very much annoyed with a Flea, caught him at last, and said, “Who are you who dare to feed on my limbs, and to cost me so much trouble in catching you?” The Flea replied, “O my dear sir, pray spare my life, and destroy me not, for I cannot possibly do you much harm.” The Man, laughing, replied, “Now you shall certainly die by mine own hands, for no evil, whether it be small or large, ought to be tolerated.”
moral: No evil, however small, should be tolerated.
moral_elaborated: Even small problems can become big problems later. It is important to deal with bad things right away. Do not let small troubles grow larger.

title: The Rich Man and the Tanner
body: A RICH MAN lived near a Tanner, and not being able to bear the unpleasant smell of the tan-yard, he pressed his neighbor to go away. The Tanner put off his departure from time to time, saying that he would leave soon. But as he still continued to stay, as time went on, the rich man became accustomed to the smell, and feeling no manner of inconvenience, made no further complaints.
moral: Habits are formed by association, and what was once unpleasant may become agreeable.
moral_elaborated: When you get used to something, it is not so bad anymore. Things that seem yucky at first can become okay after a while. Our bodies and minds can get used to many things.

title: The Viper and the File
body: A VIPER, entering the workshop of a smith, sought from the tools the means of satisfying his hunger. He more particularly addressed himself to a File, and asked of him the favour of a meal. The File replied, “You must indeed be a simple-minded fellow if you expect to get anything from me, who am accustomed to take from everyone, and never to give anything in return.”
body_child: A snake went into a workshop. He was hungry. He asked a tool called a file for some food. The file said, "You are silly if you think I will give you food. I only take things away, I don't give them."
moral: The covetous are poor givers.
moral_elaborated: Greedy people do not like to share. They want everything for themselves. Because of this, they can't give anything to others.

title: The Lion and the Shepherd
body: A LION, roaming through a forest, trod upon a thorn. Soon afterward he came up to a Shepherd and fawned upon him, wagging his tail as if to say, “I am a suppliant, and seek your aid.” The Shepherd boldly examined the beast, discovered the thorn, and placing his paw upon his lap, pulled it out; thus relieved of his pain, the Lion returned into the forest. Some time after, the Shepherd, being imprisoned on a false accusation, was condemned “to be cast to the Lions” as the punishment for his imputed crime. But when the Lion was released from his cage, he recognized the Shepherd as the man who healed him, and instead of attacking him, approached and placed his foot upon his lap. The King, as soon as he heard the tale, ordered the Lion to be set free again in the forest, and the Shepherd to be pardoned and restored to his friends.
body_child: A lion hurt his paw on a thorn. He asked a shepherd for help. The shepherd was brave and pulled the thorn out. The lion was happy and went away. Later, the shepherd was put in jail. He was going to be thrown to the lions! When the lion saw the shepherd, he remembered who helped him. The lion did not hurt the shepherd. The king heard the story and let the shepherd go. The lion was also freed.
moral: Kindness is never lost, and often comes back to help you.
moral_elaborated: If you are kind to someone, they will remember it. That kindness can help you later, even if you don't expect it. Always try to help others when you can.

title: The Camel and Jupiter
body: THE CAMEL, when he saw the Bull adorned with horns, envied him and wished that he himself could obtain the same honours. He went to Jupiter, and besought him to give him horns. Jupiter, vexed at his request because he was not satisfied with his size and strength of body, and desired yet more, not only refused to give him horns, but even deprived him of a portion of his ears.
body_child: A camel saw a bull with horns. The camel was jealous. He wanted horns too. He asked a god named Jupiter for horns. Jupiter was angry. He thought the camel was already big and strong and should be happy. Jupiter said no to the horns. He even cut off some of the camel's ears.
moral: Be happy with what you have.
moral_elaborated: It's not good to be jealous of others. You should be happy with your own special gifts. Wanting too much can lead to losing what you already have.

title: The Panther and the Shepherds
body: A PANTHER, by some mischance, fell into a pit. The Shepherds discovered him, and some threw sticks at him and pelted him with stones, while others, moved with compassion towards one about to die even though no one should hurt him, threw in some food to prolong his life. At night they returned home, not dreaming of any danger, but supposing that on the morrow they would find him dead. The Panther, however, when he had recruited his feeble strength, freed himself with a sudden bound from the pit, and hastened to his den with rapid steps. After a few days he came forth and slaughtered the cattle, and, killing the Shepherds who had attacked him, raged with angry fury. Then they who had spared his life, fearing for their safety, surrendered to him their flocks and begged only for their lives. To them the Panther made this reply: “I remember alike those who sought my life with stones, and those who gave me food aside, therefore, your fears. I return as an enemy only to those who injured me.”
body_child: A panther fell into a deep hole. Some shepherds found him. Some shepherds threw rocks and sticks at the panther. Others felt sorry for him and gave him food. The next day, the panther was strong. He jumped out of the hole. He went and killed the sheep of the shepherds who threw rocks. He also hurt those shepherds. The shepherds who gave him food were scared. They gave the panther their sheep. The panther told them, "I remember who hurt me and who was kind to me. I will not hurt those who were kind."
moral: Do not reward evil with good, nor good with evil.
moral_elaborated: When someone is kind to you, it's good to be kind back. But if someone is mean, it's okay to protect yourself. You don't have to be nice to everyone if they are not nice to you.

title: The Eagle and the Kite
body: AN EAGLE, overwhelmed with sorrow, sat upon the branches of a tree in company with a Kite. “Why,” said the Kite, “do I see you with such a rueful look?” “I seek,” she replied, “a mate suitable for me, and am not able to find one.” “Take me,” returned the Kite, “I am much stronger than you are.” “Why, are you able to secure the means of living by your plunder?” “Well, I have often caught and carried away an ostrich in my talons.” The Eagle, persuaded by these words, accepted him as her mate. Shortly after the nuptials, the Eagle said, “Fly off and bring me back the ostrich you promised me.” The Kite, soaring aloft into the air, brought back the shabbiest possible mouse, stinking from the length of time it had lain about the fields. “Is this,” said the Eagle, “the faithful fulfillment of your promise to me?” The Kite replied, “That I might attain your royal hand, there is nothing that I would not have promised, however much I knew that I must fail in the performance.”
body_child: An eagle was sad. She wanted a mate. A kite saw her and asked why she was sad. The eagle said she couldn't find a good mate. The kite said, "Marry me! I am strong! I can catch an ostrich!" The eagle believed the kite and married him. Then the eagle asked the kite to bring her an ostrich. The kite flew away and came back with a dead mouse. The eagle was angry. She asked if this was the ostrich he promised. The kite said, "I would have promised anything to marry you, even if I knew I couldn't do it."
moral: Do not trust those who make promises they cannot keep.
moral_elaborated: Some people say things they don't mean. They might say they can do something, but they really can't. It's important to listen carefully and not believe every promise you hear. Only trust people who are honest and can really do what they say.

title: The Eagle and His Captor
body: AN EAGLE was once captured by a man, who immediately clipped his wings and put him into his poultry-yard with the other birds, at which treatment the Eagle was weighed down with grief. Later, another neighbor purchased him and allowed his feathers to grow again. The Eagle took flight, and pouncing upon a hare, brought it at once as an offering to his benefactor. A Fox, seeing this, exclaimed, “Do not cultivate the favour of this man, but of your former owner, lest he should again hunt for you and deprive you a second time of your wings.”
body_child: An eagle was caught by a man. The man cut off the eagle's wings. He put the eagle with the chickens. The eagle was very sad. Another man bought the eagle. He let the eagle's feathers grow back. The eagle could fly again! He caught a rabbit and gave it to the man. A fox saw this and said, "Don't be nice to this man. Be nice to the first man. He might catch you again and cut off your wings."
moral: Be grateful to those who help you.
moral_elaborated: When someone is kind to you, it's important to remember them. They helped you when you needed it. It's good to show them you appreciate their kindness.

title: The King’s Son and the Painted Lion
body:
A KING, whose only son was fond of martial exercises, had a dream in which he was warned that his son would be killed by a lion. Afraid the dream should prove true, he built for his son a pleasant palace and adorned its walls for his amusement with all kinds of life-sized animals, among which was the picture of a lion. When the young Prince saw this, his grief at being thus confined burst out afresh, and, standing near the lion, he said: “O you most detestable of animals! through a lying dream of my father’s, which he saw in his sleep, I am shut up on your account in this palace as if I had been a girl: what shall I now do to you?” With these words he stretched out his hands toward a thorn-tree, meaning to cut a stick from its branches so that he might beat the lion. But one of the tree’s prickles pierced his finger and caused great pain and inflammation, so that the young Prince fell down in a fainting fit. A violent fever suddenly set in, from which he died not many days later.

We had better bear our troubles bravely than try to escape them.
body_child: A king had a son who loved to play. The king had a scary dream. He dreamed his son would be hurt by a lion. The king made a nice palace for his son. He put pictures of animals on the walls. One picture was of a lion. The prince was sad he had to stay inside. He stood by the lion picture. He said, "I hate you, lion! My dad had a bad dream. Now I'm stuck here like a girl! What can I do to you?" He reached for a stick to hit the lion. But a sharp thorn from a tree poked his finger. His finger hurt a lot and got swollen. The prince felt faint and fell down. He got very sick and died soon after.
moral: We had better bear our troubles bravely than try to escape them.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes bad things happen. It's better to face your problems. Trying to run away from them might make things worse. Be brave and try your best to handle them.

title: The Cat and Venus
body: A CAT fell in love with a handsome young man, and entreated Venus to change her into the form of a woman. Venus consented to her request and transformed her into a beautiful damsel, so that the youth saw her and loved her, and took her home as his bride. While the two were reclining in their chamber, Venus wishing to discover if the Cat in her change of shape had also altered her habits of life, let down a mouse in the middle of the room. The Cat, quite forgetting her present condition, started up from the couch and pursued the mouse, wishing to eat it. Venus was much disappointed and again caused her to return to her former shape.
body_child: A cat liked a nice young man. She asked the goddess Venus to make her a woman. Venus agreed. She turned the cat into a pretty girl. The man saw her and liked her. He married her. One day, they were in their room. Venus wanted to see if the cat was still a cat inside. She let a little mouse run into the room. The girl forgot she was a woman. She jumped up and chased the mouse to eat it! Venus was sad. She turned the girl back into a cat.
moral: Nature exceeds nurture.
moral_elaborated: It's hard to change what you are deep down. Even if you look or act different, your true nature might show. What you are born as is very strong.

title: The Eagle and the Beetle
body: THE EAGLE and the Beetle were at enmity together, and they destroyed one another’s nests. The Eagle gave the first provocation in seizing upon and in eating the young ones of the Beetle. The Beetle got by stealth at the Eagle’s eggs, and rolled them out of the nest, and followed the Eagle even into the presence of Jupiter. On the Eagle making his complaint, Jupiter ordered him to make his nest in his lap; and while Jupiter had the eggs in his lap, the Beetle came flying about him, and Jupiter rising up unawares, to drive him away from his head, threw down the eggs, and broke them.
body_child: An eagle and a beetle were mad at each other. They broke each other's nests. The eagle was mean first. It ate the baby beetles. The beetle was clever. It stole the eagle's eggs and pushed them out of the nest. The beetle followed the eagle to Jupiter, the king of the gods. The eagle told Jupiter what happened. Jupiter said the eagle could build its nest in his lap. Then, the beetle flew near Jupiter's head. Jupiter stood up quickly to shoo the beetle away. He dropped the eagle's eggs, and they broke.
moral: The weak often revenge themselves on those who use them ill, even though they be more powerful.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, even if someone is much stronger than you, they can still be tricked. You can find ways to get back at them. Even small creatures can be clever and find ways to get revenge.

title: The She-Goats and Their Beards
body: THE SHE-GOATS having obtained a beard by request to Jupiter, the He-Goats were sorely displeased and made complaint that the females equaled them in dignity. “Allow them,” said Jupiter, “to enjoy an empty honour and to assume the badge of your nobler sex, so long as they are not your equals in strength or courage.”
body_child: The girl goats asked Jupiter for beards. The boy goats were angry. They said the girl goats were the same as them now. Jupiter said, "Let them have a pretend honor. Let them have beards. But they are not as strong or brave as you."
moral: It matters little if those who are inferior to us in merit should be like us in outside appearances.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes people want to look like others. They might copy how someone looks. But what is inside, like being brave or strong, is more important. How someone looks doesn't make them as good as someone else.

title: The Bald Man and the Fly
body: A FLY bit the bare head of a Bald Man. He tried to swat the fly, but he hit himself really hard on his head! The fly got away. The fly laughed and said, "You wanted to hurt me, but look what you did to yourself!" The Bald Man said, "I can forgive myself because I didn't mean to hurt myself. But you are a nasty fly that bites people. I wish I could have caught you, even if it hurt me more."
body_child: A fly landed on a bald man's head and bit him. The man tried to slap the fly, but he ended up hitting himself really hard! The fly flew away and teased him. The fly said, "You wanted to punish me, but you hurt yourself instead!" The bald man said, "I can forget about hitting myself because I didn't mean to. But I wish I could have caught you, you annoying fly!"
moral: Be careful not to hurt yourself worse trying to punish something small.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes when you try to punish someone for something small, you end up hurting yourself even more. It's important to think before you act so you don't cause bigger problems for yourself.

title: The Shipwrecked Man and the Sea
body: A man was shipwrecked and washed onto land. He was tired and fell asleep. When he woke up, he yelled at the sea. He said the sea looked calm and invited him in, but then it got rough and tried to drown him. The sea, which looked like a woman, answered, "Don't blame me. Blame the wind. The sea is usually calm, but the wind makes the waves."
body_child: A man's boat sank, and he washed up on a beach. He was so tired he fell asleep. When he woke up, he was mad at the sea. He said the sea looked nice, but then it made big waves and tried to hurt him. The sea changed into a woman and said, "It's not my fault! The wind makes the waves. The sea is usually calm."
moral: Do not blame the innocent for the faults of others.
moral_elaborated: It's not fair to blame someone for something they didn't do. The sea was calm, but the wind made it stormy. We should be careful not to blame the wrong thing when something bad happens.

title: The Buffoon and the Countryman
body: A rich man wanted to give a prize for a new show. A funny man, called a buffoon, said he had a new act. He came out and made a noise like a little pig. Everyone thought he had a real pig hidden and cheered for him. A countryman in the crowd said, "I can do that too!" The next day, even more people came. The buffoon did his pig noise again, and they cheered. Then the countryman tried. He had a real pig hidden, but he couldn't make it sound as good as the buffoon. The crowd didn't like his act and told him to leave. The countryman then showed them the real pig and said, "You people don't know a good act when you see one!"
body_child: A rich man wanted to give a prize for a new show. A funny man, the buffoon, said he had a new trick. He made a noise like a little pig! The people thought he had a real pig and clapped a lot. A countryman said, "I can do that too!" The next day, more people came. The buffoon made his pig noise again, and they cheered. Then the countryman tried. He had a real pig, but his act wasn't as good. The crowd didn't like it and told him to go away. The countryman showed them the real pig. He said, "You don't know what's good!"
moral: Often, the appearance of things is preferred to their reality.
moral_elaborated: People sometimes like things that seem real and good, even if they are not. The crowd liked the man who pretended to have a pig more than the man who actually had a pig. They thought the pretend sound was better than the real thing.

title: The Crow and the Serpent
body: A crow was very hungry. He saw a snake sleeping in the sun. The crow flew down and grabbed the snake. But the snake turned around and bit the crow. The crow was dying. He said, "Oh no! I thought I found a good meal, but it ended up hurting me."
body_child: A crow was very hungry and looking for food. He saw a snake sleeping in a sunny spot. The crow flew down and grabbed the snake! But the snake quickly bit the crow. The crow was very hurt. He said, "I thought I found something good to eat, but it ended up hurting me!"
moral: Do not mistake an enemy for a friend.
moral_elaborated: Things that look good might be bad. The crow thought the snake was a good meal, but it was dangerous. We should be careful and not trust everything that seems easy or good.

title: The Hunter and the Horseman
body: A hunter caught a hare. He put it on his shoulder to take it home. He met a man on a horse who wanted to buy the hare. When the horseman got the hare, he rode away fast. The hunter chased him. The horseman got farther and farther away. The hunter sadly called out, "Take it! I will give it to you!"
body_child: A hunter caught a hare. He was carrying it home. He met a man on a horse. The horseman asked for the hare, saying he would buy it. But once he had the hare, the horseman rode away very fast! The hunter ran after him. The horseman kept getting farther away. The hunter had to yell, "Just take it! I'll give it to you!"
moral: It is better to lose something than to pursue it to your own disadvantage.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, it's better to give up if you can't get something back easily. The hunter chased the horseman, but he couldn't catch him. It was better for the hunter to let the hare go than to keep trying and not succeed.

title: The Olive-Tree and the Fig-Tree
body: THE OLIVE-TREE ridiculed the Fig-Tree because, while she was green all the year round, the Fig-Tree changed its leaves with the seasons. A shower of snow fell upon them, and, finding the Olive full of foliage, it settled upon its branches and broke them down with its weight, at the once despoiling it of its beauty and killing the tree. But finding the Fig-Tree denuded of leaves, the snow fell through to the ground, and did not injure it at all.
body_child: The olive tree made fun of the fig tree. The olive tree stayed green all year. The fig tree changed its leaves with the seasons. Then, snow came. The snow sat on the olive tree's leaves and broke its branches. But the snow fell through the fig tree's bare branches. The fig tree was safe.
moral: Appearances can be deceiving.
moral_elaborated: Something that looks strong and good on the outside might not be. Sometimes, being able to change or adapt is what helps you stay safe.

title: The Frogs’ Complaint Against the Sun
body: ONCE UPON A TIME, when the Sun announced his intention to take a wife, the Frogs lifted up their voices in clamor to the sky. Jupiter, disturbed by the noise of their croaking, inquired the cause of their complaint. One of them said, “The Sun, now while he is single, parches up the marsh, and compels us to die miserably in our arid homes. What will be our future condition if he should beget other suns?”
body_child: The frogs were upset. The sun said he was going to get married. The frogs croaked loudly. Jupiter asked why they were so noisy. A frog said, "The sun dries up our homes now. What will happen if he has kids and there are more suns?"
moral: Be careful what you wish for.
moral_elaborated: Sometimes, things are not as bad as they seem. Complaining about a small problem might lead to a much bigger one.

title: The Brazier and His Dog
body: A BRAZIER had a little Dog, which was a great favourite with his master, and his constant companion. While he hammered away at his metals the Dog slept; but when, on the other hand, he went to dinner and began to eat, the Dog woke up and wagged his tail, as if he would ask for a share of his meal. His master one day, pretending to be angry and shaking his stick at him, said, “You wretched little sluggard! what shall I do to you? While I am hammering on the anvil, you sleep on the mat; and when I begin to eat after my toil, you wake up and wag your tail for food. Do you not know that labor is the source of every blessing, and that none but those who work are entitled to eat?”
body_child: A man who worked with metal had a dog. The dog was his best friend. When the man hammered, the dog slept. When the man ate, the dog woke up and wagged his tail for food. The man pretended to be mad and said, "You sleep when I work! You wake up when I eat! You should only eat if you work."
moral: Those who work deserve to eat.
moral_elaborated: It is important to work hard. People who put in effort to earn their food and other things are the ones who deserve them.
